title: Before You Reach a Conclusion
subtitle: How to Question What You Believe and Make Better Decisions
author: Sriram Srinivasan
description: Before You Reach a Conclusion explores how beliefs take shape, how evidence can mislead, and how to think more carefully without becoming trapped in endless doubt.
blurb: We make judgments every day—about people, information, opportunities and ourselves. Yet familiarity can feel like evidence, confidence can disguise uncertainty, and a convincing explanation can still be wrong.
Before You Reach a Conclusion explores how beliefs take shape, how evidence can mislead, and how to think more carefully without becoming trapped in endless doubt.
At its heart is the deliberate interval: knowing when to open a conclusion for examination, how to test it, and when to close the inquiry and act.

sections.title: Why Thinking Deserves More Attention
sections.label: Introduction — Why Thinking Deserves More Attention

runs.text: Most of the conclusions that shape a life are not reached at a desk. They form in the middle of other things: in a meeting that is running late, in a conversation with someone we already trust or distrust, while reading a headline on the way to somewhere else. By the time we notice that we hold a view, it rarely feels like something we decided. It feels like something we simply see. The manager who knows a candidate will not fit the team, the parent who is certain a child is being lazy, the investor sure that a trend will continue, the citizen convinced that a policy has failed: each is looking at the world through a conclusion that arrived before any examination did.

This book is about that order of events. Its argument is easy to state and difficult to practise. Better judgment begins with the willingness to examine what we believe before deciding what to conclude or how to act. The weight of that sentence falls on the word
before

. People are seldom short of conclusions. What they are often short of is a deliberate interval in which a conclusion is held up and inspected: where it came from, what it rests on, what else could explain the same facts, and what it would cost to be wrong.
John Dewey gave this interval a name more than a century ago. In
How We Think

, published in 1910, he separated the loose stream of ideas that passes through anyone’s head from what he called reflective thought: “Active, persistent, and careful consideration of any belief or supposed form of knowledge in the light of the grounds that support it, and the further conclusions to which it tends.” The definition repays slow reading. It asks us to look at a belief in two directions at once. We look backward at the grounds beneath it and forward at the conclusions it leads to. A belief is not only a claim about the world. It is a commitment that will carry us somewhere, and examining it properly means checking both its foundation and its destination.

Dewey also saw that the core of reflective thinking is a willingness to stay in doubt long enough to investigate, rather than seizing the first plausible answer. That willingness is uncomfortable. Uncertainty feels like a problem to be removed, and a conclusion, almost any conclusion, brings relief. I have come to think that a great deal of poor reasoning is not a failure of intelligence at all. It is a premature end to discomfort.
Why intelligence and information are not enough

It is natural to assume that good thinking is mainly a matter of being clever or well informed. The research does not support that assumption as strongly as we might hope. In a series of seven studies published in 2008, the psychologists Keith Stanovich and Richard West looked at performance on many classic reasoning tasks, including resistance to framing effects, anchoring and base-rate neglect. When the tasks were presented in a way that did not signal what was being tested, performance was largely unrelated to cognitive ability. In related work, the tendency to evaluate evidence in favour of one’s own prior view, which they call myside bias, showed little relationship with intelligence. Clever people are not immune to poor reasoning. Sometimes they are simply better at defending it.

Information does not solve the problem either. A person can know a great many things about a subject and still be unable to explain how its parts fit together, or to tell when a familiar rule no longer applies. Chapter 1 begins with that gap, because almost every later mistake is built on it.

What does seem to matter is something closer to a disposition: the habit of treating one’s own beliefs as things that can be examined, together with the skills to examine them well. Dispositions can be strengthened. They are shaped by attention, by practice, by the questions we routinely ask, and by the environments we work and live in.
Why the question has become more urgent

There is a further reason to take the examination of belief seriously now. For most of history, producing a well-organized explanation took effort. Someone had to research it, structure it and write it down, and the effort itself acted as a rough filter. Today, software can produce a fluent, confident and well-structured answer to almost any question in seconds. Some of those answers are excellent. Some are subtly wrong. Many look exactly alike.

This book is not mainly about artificial intelligence. Most of its chapters would have been worth writing in 1980. But machines that can sound more certain than they are make an old discipline newly important, and Part IV takes up what that changes.
What this book offers, and what it does not

This is not a textbook of logic, a catalogue of cognitive biases, or a programme for becoming perfectly rational. It will not promise to remove bias, because no reliable method for doing so exists, and a book that claimed otherwise would be guilty of the very overconfidence it warns against. Nor does it ask readers to doubt everything. A person who examined every belief before every action would never act at all.

What the book offers is narrower and, I think, more useful. It tries to show how beliefs are formed, where reasoning commonly goes astray, and what kinds of attention reliably improve judgment in the situations where judgment matters most. Its ambition is to help readers build the habit of asking four things before they settle: what they believe, why they believe it, what they do not know, and what would justify acting despite that uncertainty.
The interval, in practice
The deliberate interval is the book’s central idea, so it is worth saying plainly what it involves, because an interval with no limits would be paralysis.

It answers three questions: which conclusions deserve deliberate examination, how much examination is enough, and when to stop examining and act. It has three corresponding moves, and the rest of the book can be read as an account of each.
Open the interval.

The question is whether this conclusion matters enough to deserve examination. Most do not. A conclusion deserves the interval when it is about to carry weight: when acting on it would be costly or hard to reverse, when it will affect other people, when the situation is unfamiliar, or when one feels unusually certain about something complicated. That last signal is the least intuitive. Strong certainty about a complex matter is not, by itself, a sign that the work has been done, and several later chapters show how often it accompanies work that has been skipped.
Examine the conclusion.

Four things, in roughly this order: the source (where the belief came from, and whether that route is reliable here), the assumptions (what it depends on that has not been said), the alternatives (what else could explain the same facts), and the evidence that would change your mind. How much of this is enough depends on what is at stake and how easily the decision could be undone: a few minutes for a reversible choice, a good deal more for one that cannot be taken back. Parts I to III of the book are, in effect, an extended account of how to do each of these well.
Close the interval.

The interval should end when further examination is unlikely to improve the decision enough to justify its cost: when nothing further you could reasonably learn would change the decision, when waiting costs more than it could reveal, or when the remaining uncertainty can only be resolved by acting. A reversible decision deserves a shorter interval than an irreversible one. Chapter 4 discusses when to stop asking questions, Chapter 14 how to act once examination has done what it can, and Chapter 15 how to make the interval a habit rather than an occasional effort.
How the book is organized
Part I,
The Foundations of Good Thinking

, examines the raw material of judgment: the difference between knowing and understanding, the routes by which beliefs are formed, the hidden assumptions that sit beneath conclusions, and the questions that open or close an inquiry.
Part II,
Reasoning in an Uncertain World

, turns to evidence. It asks what evidence can and cannot justify, how causal claims go wrong, why the explanations we fail to consider matter as much as the ones we test, and how numbers can mislead even when every figure is accurate.
Part III,
The Human Mind and Its Blind Spots

, examines the forces that bend reasoning from within and around us: the preference for agreeable evidence, the problem of deciding whom to trust, the effects of pressure, and the difficulty of changing one’s mind for good reasons.
Part IV,
Thinking in the Age of AI

, considers how to verify fluent machine-generated answers, how to act when certainty is unavailable, and how occasional good reasoning can become a dependable habit. The book closes with two appendices designed as standalone tools: a framework for examining important claims and a set of questions worth asking before major decisions.
A note on examples and sources

Wherever the book describes a study, a historical case or a legal decision, it cites a source that readers can check, and the References section lists them by chapter. Where it uses an invented scenario to illustrate a point, the scenario is identified as hypothetical. I have tried to describe research at the strength it actually has, including where findings are contested or have failed to replicate. When I write in the first person, it is to offer an interpretation or a judgment, not to report an experience.

None of this is meant to make thinking heavier than it needs to be. Most conclusions do not deserve a second look, and life would be unbearable if they all received one. The skill this book is concerned with is narrower and more valuable. It lies in recognizing which conclusions are about to carry real weight, in our work, our relationships or our choices, and in giving those conclusions the examination they deserve before we let them carry it.

sections.title: The Foundations of Good Thinking
sections.label: Part I — The Foundations of Good Thinking

runs.text: Before we can weigh evidence, we need to see what we are weighing it with. Part I examines the raw materials of judgment, the things that shape a conclusion before any deliberate reasoning begins.

The chapters follow a chain of questions. Chapter 1 asks how we can tell whether we understand something or merely recognize it, since the feeling of understanding so easily outruns the real thing. If our sense of knowing is that unreliable, the next question is where our beliefs came from in the first place, and Chapter 2 traces the routes by which they form and why those routes so quickly disappear from view. Some of what we believe was never formed as a belief at all, which leads Chapter 3 to the assumptions that sit beneath conclusions unrecognized. And if what we find depends on what we never thought to examine, Chapter 4 asks how the questions that start every inquiry quietly decide what it can find.

Together these chapters make a single argument. Most errors of judgment are not failures of logic applied to good material. They begin earlier, in material we never examined: a sense of understanding we did not test, a belief whose route we forgot, a premise we never stated, a question that excluded the answer we needed. Examining that material is necessary, but it is not sufficient. Beliefs are claims about the world, and the next question is what the world’s evidence can actually tell us about them.

sections.title: Knowing Something Is Not the Same as Understanding It
sections.label: 1. Knowing Something Is Not the Same as Understanding It

runs.text: The difference between information, knowledge, understanding and judgment.

Ask most adults whether they understand how a zipper works and they will say yes without hesitation. They have used thousands of them. They can describe one, fix a stuck one, and recognize a broken one at a glance. Now ask them to explain, step by step, how the small slider joins two rows of teeth so that they hold together, and why pulling it the other way separates them. Most people who try discover, somewhere in the second sentence, that they do not know.

This small embarrassment was the subject of a series of studies published in 2002 by the Yale psychologists Leonid Rozenblit and Frank Keil. They asked participants to rate how well they understood everyday devices such as zippers, flush toilets and cylinder locks. Then they asked them to write detailed explanations of how each device worked, answer a diagnostic question about it, and read an expert explanation. After each step, participants rated their understanding again. The ratings fell. People had confused familiarity with a thing for an understanding of how it works. The participants were university students rating everyday objects in a laboratory, so the studies show that the illusion is real and easy to produce, not how large it is in any particular person’s knowledge of their own professional field. What I take from it goes slightly beyond what the researchers claimed. If people overrate their grasp of zippers, which they handle daily and can inspect at will, there is little reason to think they rate more accurately their grasp of a pension scheme, a colleague’s motives or a policy they have read one article about. Rozenblit and Keil called this the illusion of explanatory depth, and they found it was strongest for objects with visible parts, where seeing a mechanism made people feel they grasped it.

The finding is easy to treat as a curiosity about household objects. I think it points to something much larger. Much of what we call knowing is a kind of recognition. We recognize a term, a pattern, a situation, and recognition comes with a feeling of competence. The feeling is real, but it reports on our familiarity, not on the structure of our knowledge. This chapter is about the distance between those two things, and about why that distance matters more for judgment than almost any other gap in our thinking.
Four things we run together
Everyday language uses “knowing” for several different achievements. It helps to pull them apart.
Information

is a claim or record that can be passed from one person to another: the boiling point of water, a company’s quarterly revenue, the name of a medication. Information can be stored, copied and searched. It does not require anyone to understand it. A database contains information. So does a page that nobody has read.
Knowledge

, in the ordinary sense, is information that a person holds and has some reason to accept as true. If I know that a medication should not be combined with alcohol, I am carrying a true belief that I acquired from a source I had grounds to trust. Philosophers have argued for centuries about exactly what turns a true belief into knowledge, and those debates are not settled. For practical purposes, the important point is that knowledge in this sense can be isolated. I can know that the medication interacts with alcohol without knowing why.
Understanding

is different in kind. To understand something is to grasp how its parts relate: what causes what, what depends on what, and what would change if one element changed. The philosopher Jonathan Kvanvig has argued that understanding, unlike knowledge of isolated facts, involves grasping the explanatory and coherence relations among a body of information. That is a technical way of saying something most good teachers recognize. A student who understands a subject can do things with it. They can explain it in their own words, predict what will happen in a new case, notice when an answer is implausible, and see where a general rule stops applying.
Judgment

is understanding brought to bear on a particular situation where something is at stake. It involves deciding what matters here, which general principles apply, what is unusual about this case, and what to do. Judgment draws on understanding but adds something more: attention to the specific, and a willingness to commit.

These four layers are not a strict ladder, and real thinking moves between them constantly. But the distinctions are useful because the feelings that accompany them are not reliable guides to which one we have. Information that has been encountered often feels like knowledge. Knowledge that is familiar feels like understanding. And understanding of a general principle can feel like judgment about a particular case, even when the case is unlike anything the principle was built for.
Why familiarity feels like understanding
The illusion of explanatory depth is not the result of carelessness. It follows from the way understanding usually works.

In daily life we rarely need to explain how things work. We need to use them. Use requires only a shallow model: pull the slider up to close, down to open. That shallow model is enough for nearly every purpose, and because it never fails us, we never discover how shallow it is. Each successful use quietly reinforces the sense that we know what we are dealing with.

There is also a structural reason. Rozenblit and Keil noted that explanations are layered. A zipper can be explained at the level of the slider, at the level of the interlocking teeth, at the level of the geometry that holds the teeth together, and so on. When we think about a device, we see the top layer clearly and assume, without checking, that the layers beneath it are equally available to us. They usually are not. We know where the explanation begins, and we mistake knowing where it begins for knowing where it goes.

The same pattern appears well beyond household objects. In 2013, Philip Fernbach, Todd Rogers, Craig Fox and Steven Sloman asked people to rate their understanding of political policies, such as a national flat tax or a cap-and-trade system for carbon emissions, and to state how strongly they supported or opposed them. Participants were then asked to explain, mechanistically, how each policy would work. After trying, they rated their understanding lower and expressed more moderate positions. A second condition is just as revealing: when people were asked only to list their reasons for supporting or opposing a policy, rather than explain how it worked, their positions did not moderate. Reasons for a view are not the same as an understanding of what the view is about, and only the second exposed the gap.

That difference is one of the most practically useful findings in this book. Listing reasons tends to strengthen a position because it rehearses the case for it. Explaining a mechanism tends to reveal the limits of what one knows. If you want to find out whether you understand something, the better test is not “Why do I believe this?” but “Can I explain how this actually works, step by step, to someone who will ask what happens next?”
The name of the bird
The physicist Richard Feynman described a lesson from his childhood in his memoir
What Do You Care What Other People Think?

His father pointed out that you could learn the name of a bird in many languages and still know nothing about the bird itself: what it does, how it lives, why it behaves as it does. Names are information. They let us refer to a thing and exchange claims about it. They can also give us the satisfying sense of having dealt with a subject when we have only labelled it.

Professional life is full of names that work this way. Consider a hypothetical analyst who can define every common financial ratio, recite the formula for each and say whether a given number is “good” or “bad” by industry standard. That analyst has a great deal of information and some knowledge. Now consider a colleague who, looking at the same ratios, notices that a company’s current ratio has improved only because it has delayed paying its suppliers. The second analyst understands what the ratio is measuring and therefore what it can hide. Both can use the vocabulary. Only one can tell when the vocabulary has stopped describing reality.

The example is invented, but the pattern is familiar in almost every field. A new manager can quote the principles of delegation. A student can recite the definition of statistical significance. A patient can name their diagnosis. In each case the name is a starting point that can easily be mistaken for an arrival.
Knowing how and knowing that
In 1949 the philosopher Gilbert Ryle drew a distinction in
The Concept of Mind

that is still useful here. He separated “knowing that”, the possession of facts and propositions, from “knowing how”, the capacity to perform an activity well. A person can know that a bicycle stays upright through a combination of steering and momentum without being able to ride one. A skilled cyclist may ride beautifully without being able to explain the physics.

Ryle’s distinction cuts in a direction that is easy to miss. It warns us not only against mistaking information for understanding but also against assuming that understanding must always be articulate. Experienced practitioners often understand their domain in ways they cannot fully explain. A seasoned nurse may sense that a patient is deteriorating before the measurements confirm it. Later chapters will examine when such intuitions deserve trust and when they do not. For now, the point is that understanding is not one thing. It includes the ability to explain, the ability to predict, and the ability to act appropriately in new conditions. A person may be strong in one and weak in another.

This matters for how we test ourselves. Explanation is a good test for the kind of understanding that can be put into words. Prediction is a better test for practical understanding: if you understand a system, you should be able to say what it will do when something changes, and be right more often than chance. And transfer, the ability to apply what you know to a situation that does not look like the ones you learned from, is perhaps the strongest test of all.
Where understanding ends

The most valuable thing understanding provides may be a sense of its own boundaries. A person who understands why a rule works also has some idea of when it will stop working. A person who has only memorized the rule does not.

This is why shallow knowledge is dangerous in a specific way. It is not that shallow knowledge is always wrong. Often it gives the right answer. The danger is that it gives no warning when it is about to give the wrong one. The rule-follower and the person who understands will usually agree. They part company in unusual cases, and unusual cases are where judgment is most needed.

Consider another hypothetical. A team has learned that customers who use a particular product feature tend to renew their subscriptions. Someone who holds this as information may propose pushing every customer toward the feature. Someone who understands it will want to know why the relationship exists. Perhaps the feature itself creates value. Perhaps it is simply used by customers who were already committed for other reasons. The two possibilities produce identical numbers in the past and very different results from the proposed intervention. Chapter 6 examines that kind of causal question in detail. The point here is earlier and simpler. Holding the fact is not the same as understanding what it means, and the decision depends on the understanding.
The honest limits of individual understanding
It would be easy to draw an unhelpful conclusion from all this: that we should understand everything we rely on. Nobody can. In
The Knowledge Illusion

, published in 2017, Steven Sloman and Philip Fernbach argue that human intelligence is fundamentally collective. We live successfully among technologies, institutions and bodies of expertise that no individual understands in full. We flush toilets without understanding plumbing and take medicines without understanding pharmacology, and that is not a failure. It is what allows a complex society to work at all.

I find this argument persuasive, and it changes what the lesson of this chapter should be. The goal is not complete understanding. It is accurate awareness of where our own understanding stops and where we are relying on others. The illusion of explanatory depth is a problem not because we depend on knowledge held elsewhere but because we often fail to notice that we are doing so. We treat borrowed understanding as if it were our own, and then we make confident judgments in areas where we hold only the label.

Seen this way, the useful skill is a kind of honest self-mapping. For any belief that is about to carry weight, it helps to know which of three positions you are in. You may understand the matter yourself, well enough to explain and predict. You may be relying on someone else’s understanding, in which case the important questions concern whom you are trusting and why, and Chapter 10 takes those up. Or you may hold only information, a fact or a name, without either your own understanding or a trusted source behind it. The third position is the most common and the least noticed. It is also where the most avoidable mistakes are made.
The student’s illusion

The same confusion appears wherever people learn. Consider, as a hypothetical, a student preparing for an examination by rereading her notes for the third time. Each pass feels easier than the last. The material looks familiar, the arguments seem obvious, and her confidence rises. What has grown is her familiarity with the page. Whether she understands it is a different question, and rereading cannot answer it. The test is to close the notes and try to explain the material, or to answer a question she has not seen before. The gap between how ready she feels and how ready she is usually appears at that moment, and it is far better that it appears at her desk than in the examination hall.

Any clear explanation can produce the same effect, whether it comes from a textbook, a lecture or, as Chapter 13 discusses, a machine. A good explanation lends its clarity to the reader, and the reader can mistake that borrowed clarity for their own.
Three practical tests
The research in this chapter suggests a few simple ways to check whether we understand something before we rely on it. None is new, but all are underused.
The first is to
explain the mechanism

. Not the reasons for a view, but how the thing works: what leads to what. Try to do it in writing or aloud to someone willing to keep asking “and then what?” Where the explanation becomes vague, understanding has run out.
The second is to
predict a change

. If you understand a situation, you should be able to say what would happen if one element changed: if prices rose, if a key person left, if a dose were doubled. Predictions expose shallow understanding because shallow knowledge describes what is, not what would be.
The third is to
find the boundary

. Ask under what conditions the rule or fact you rely on would stop holding. If you cannot name any, you may be holding a rule without understanding it, because almost every useful rule has limits and people who understand a rule usually know where they are.
These tests take a few minutes, and most conclusions do not need them. They are worth using when a belief is about to support a decision that will be costly to reverse.
What the distinction is for
In Plato’s
Apology

, Socrates describes his surprise at being called the wisest man in Athens. After questioning people with a reputation for wisdom, he concluded that his advantage was a small one. They believed they knew things they did not. He did not believe he knew what he did not know. The passage is often quoted as praise of humility, but I think its real point is more precise. Socrates was not claiming to know nothing. He was claiming to have an accurate sense of where his knowledge ended.

That is the distinction that matters most for judgment. The difference between knowing and understanding is not mainly a difference in how much a person holds. It is a difference in what they can do with it, and in whether they can tell when they have reached its edge. If this chapter has one thing to leave behind, it is that familiarity and understanding feel the same from the inside and are not the same at all. Familiarity comes from having met something often. Understanding shows itself only when we try to explain, predict or find the edge, which is why the most reliable sign of it is not a feeling but a test.

sections.title: Why We Believe What We Believe
sections.label: 2. Why We Believe What We Believe

runs.text: How experience, familiarity, authority, emotion and evidence shape beliefs.

In 1877 the English mathematician William Kingdon Clifford published an essay called “The Ethics of Belief”. It opens with a story. A shipowner is about to send an emigrant ship to sea. He knows the ship is old and was not especially well built, and he has been told it may need repairs. These doubts trouble him. But he reminds himself that the ship has survived many voyages, that providence is unlikely to abandon the families aboard, and that the builders and contractors are honest people. Gradually he talks himself into a sincere and comfortable belief that the vessel is safe. He watches it leave port with a light heart. It sinks in mid-ocean, and he collects the insurance.

Clifford’s verdict is that the shipowner is guilty of the deaths, and not because he lied. He genuinely believed the ship was safe. He is guilty because he had no right to believe it on the evidence before him. His belief was formed not by investigation but by stifling his doubts. Clifford then adds a twist that makes the argument sharper. Suppose the ship had arrived safely after all. The shipowner would be no less guilty, because the wrongness lay in how he came to believe, not in whether the belief turned out true. The essay ends with a sentence that has been quoted and argued over ever since: “It is wrong always, everywhere, and for anyone, to believe anything upon insufficient evidence.”

I will come back to whether Clifford was right. What interests me first is the story itself, because it describes something most of us do and rarely notice. The shipowner did not decide to believe the ship was safe. He arrived there by a sequence of small reassurances, each of which felt reasonable: past experience, trust in other people, a hopeful mood. By the end he held a belief whose real origins had vanished from view. All he could see was the belief.

This chapter is about that disappearance. It asks how beliefs actually form, which is often quite different from how we would justify them if asked, and what it would take to keep the route visible long enough to judge whether it can be trusted.
Causes and reasons

Every belief has two kinds of history. It has a causal history: the sequence of experiences, conversations and feelings that actually produced it. And it may have a justification: the reasons that would support it if someone asked us to defend it. Ideally the two coincide. We believe something because we encountered good evidence, and the evidence is also our justification.

Often they do not coincide. A person may believe that a colleague is unreliable because of one memorable failure, and then justify the belief by pointing to a pattern they noticed only afterwards. Another may believe that a diet works because a friend they admire swears by it, and then justify the belief by citing a study they found when they went looking. The justification can be perfectly sincere. It is still not the reason the belief exists.

The gap matters because the strength of a belief tends to reflect its causal history, while our confidence in it tends to reflect the justification we can produce. A belief that arrived through a weak route can feel well supported once we have gathered reasons for it. That is the shipowner’s situation in miniature, and it is probably more common than outright self-deception.
Peirce and the settling of doubt
In the same year that Clifford published his essay, the American philosopher Charles Sanders Peirce published “The Fixation of Belief” in
Popular Science Monthly

. Peirce started from a psychological observation. Doubt, he argued, is an uneasy state that we struggle to escape, and belief is the calm state we reach when doubt is settled. Inquiry is the struggle. The question is how the struggle ends.
Peirce described four methods. The method of
tenacity
settles doubt by holding on to whatever we already believe and turning away from anything that might disturb it. The method of
authority
settles doubt by accepting what an institution or community teaches. The
a priori
method settles doubt by adopting whatever seems agreeable to reason, what feels intuitively right. And the method of
science
settles doubt by appeal to something outside our own preferences: observations and tests that others could repeat and that might prove us wrong.

Peirce’s point was not that the first three methods are stupid. He acknowledged that tenacity brings peace of mind and that authority has kept whole societies stable. His point was that only the fourth method has a way of correcting itself. Tenacity cannot correct itself because it refuses contrary evidence. Authority cannot correct itself unless the authority does. The a priori method changes only when fashions in what seems reasonable change. Only a method that lets the world push back can, over time, bring beliefs closer to the way things are.

I find Peirce’s framing more useful than Clifford’s in one respect. It treats belief formation as something that happens to us under the pressure of doubt, rather than as a series of deliberate choices. That is closer to how most beliefs form. We do not usually sit down and choose a method. A method is chosen for us by circumstance, temperament and habit, and we discover which one we used, if at all, only by looking back.
Five routes to a belief

Peirce’s four methods were philosophical categories. Modern psychology lets us describe the routes more concretely. Most everyday beliefs arrive by one or more of five routes: personal experience, familiarity, authority, emotion and evidence. None is inherently bad. Each is reliable under some conditions and misleading under others. The discipline this chapter recommends is not to avoid any of them but to notice which one produced a given belief, and to ask whether its conditions held.
Experience

What we have seen for ourselves carries special weight, and often it should. Direct experience is hard to fake and rich in detail. A mechanic who has repaired hundreds of engines knows things no manual contains.

But personal experience is also a small and unrepresentative sample of the world. It overweights what is recent, vivid and close to us. In 1973 Amos Tversky and Daniel Kahneman described what they called the availability heuristic: people judge how frequent or likely something is by how easily examples come to mind. Ease of recall is a reasonable cue, because common things are usually easier to remember. It fails when ease of recall is driven by something other than frequency, such as how dramatic an event was, how recently it happened, or how much attention it received.

Experience is most trustworthy when it is extensive, when it comes with clear and quick feedback, and when the situations we encountered resemble the one we are now judging. It is least trustworthy when it consists of a few memorable cases, when we never learned how things turned out, or when the present situation differs in ways we have not noticed. A manager who once hired an excellent candidate from a particular university may come to believe that graduates of that university are excellent. The belief rests on a sample of one, but the experience that produced it was vivid and personal, and vividness is easily mistaken for weight.
Familiarity

Some beliefs form simply because we have encountered a claim many times. In 1977 Lynn Hasher, David Goldstein and Thomas Toppino asked students to rate the truth of plausible but obscure statements on three occasions, two weeks apart. Some statements were repeated across sessions; others were not. Repeated statements were rated as more likely to be true at each session, whether they were actually true or false. Repetition alone increased belief. The finding, now called the illusory truth effect, has been replicated many times. These studies mostly use obscure trivia rated in a laboratory, so they show that repetition can tip belief when other grounds are weak, not that repetition can make people believe anything. The inference I would draw for everyday life is a modest one: when a claim feels obviously true, it is worth asking whether I have evidence for it or have simply met it often.

It would be comforting to think that knowledge protects us. A study published in 2015 by Lisa Fazio, Nadia Brashier, Keith Payne and Elizabeth Marsh suggests it does not, at least not reliably. Repetition increased belief in false statements even when participants demonstrably knew the correct answer. The authors called this knowledge neglect: when a statement feels easy to process, people sometimes go with that feeling instead of consulting what they know.

Why would the mind work this way? Probably because familiarity can sometimes be a useful cue. We often encounter reliable information repeatedly, from people, institutions and experiences we have learned to trust. But repetition does not establish truth. A false claim may spread widely because it is emotionally appealing, because influential people repeat it, or because many sources copy the same original account. A claim seen in ten places may still have only one origin. Familiarity can explain why we believe something without providing adequate grounds for believing it.
Authority

The great majority of what any of us believes was learned from other people. Most of us believe that the Earth orbits the Sun, that our blood type is whatever a laboratory reported, and that countries we have never visited exist. None of these beliefs rests on our own investigation. They rest on testimony, and that is not a weakness. A person who refused to believe anything they had not personally verified would know almost nothing.

Authority becomes a problem not when we rely on it but when we stop noticing that we are relying on it, or when we rely on a source for something outside the area where its reliability was earned. A respected physician speaking about medicine is one kind of authority. The same physician speaking about economic policy is another. The tone of authority carries over between the two. The reliability may not. Chapter 10 examines in detail how to judge whom to trust. Here the point is about origins: many beliefs that feel like our own conclusions are, on inspection, someone else’s conclusions that we adopted without registering the moment of adoption.
Emotion

Feelings shape beliefs more directly than we tend to admit. Paul Slovic and colleagues have described an affect heuristic, in which people consult their overall positive or negative feeling about something when judging its risks and benefits. In a study published in 2000, Melissa Finucane, Ali Alhakami, Paul Slovic and Stephen Johnson found that people tend to judge activities they feel good about as both low in risk and high in benefit, and activities they feel bad about as the reverse. In reality, risk and benefit are often unrelated or even move together: something can be both very risky and very useful. The inverse relationship in people’s judgments grew stronger under time pressure, when there was less opportunity for analysis. Telling people about an activity’s benefits also lowered their estimates of its risks, as if the information had simply shifted their feeling about it. A well-powered replication by Emir Efendić and colleagues, published online in 2021, confirmed the central finding: a strong inverse relationship between how risky and how beneficial people judge an activity to be.

Emotion is not the enemy of good belief. Fear can be an accurate response to danger, and unease about a deal can reflect something we have noticed but not yet named. The difficulty is that emotion is a summary, and a summary hides its inputs. When a belief arrives with strong feeling attached, it helps to ask what the feeling is responding to. Sometimes the answer is a real feature of the situation. Sometimes it is a feature of a different situation, or of our mood that day, or of how the matter was presented.
Evidence

The fifth route is the one the other four imitate. Evidence, in the sense this book uses the word, means observations and information whose connection to the claim can be examined and, in principle, checked by someone else. Part II is devoted to what evidence can and cannot establish. For now, it is enough to notice that evidence is rarely the only route at work. Even when we have good evidence for a belief, we usually also have an emotional relationship to it, a history of hearing it repeated, and some trusted figure who holds it too. The routes combine, and the strength of the evidence can be hard to separate from the strength of everything else.
How origins disappear

If beliefs simply carried labels showing how they were formed, examining them would be easy. They do not. Psychologists who study memory distinguish between remembering a piece of information and remembering where it came from. In a 1993 review, Marcia Johnson, Shahin Hashtroudi and Stephen Lindsay set out what they called the source monitoring framework, describing how people attribute memories to their origins and how often they get those attributions wrong. We may remember a claim clearly and have no idea whether we read it in a reliable report, heard it from a friend, or imagined it while thinking about something else.

This has a quiet but important consequence. Over time, a belief detaches from its source and starts to feel like plain knowledge, simply the way things are. The colleague’s offhand remark becomes “something everyone knows”. The headline glimpsed years ago becomes a fact. Once that happens, the belief no longer feels like something that could be examined. It feels like something we see.

I suspect this is why the most consequential beliefs are often the hardest to question. They are not necessarily the ones held with the most emotion or defended most loudly. They are the ones that have been held longest and examined least, until they have hardened into the background against which everything else is judged. Chapter 3 follows that process one step further, into the assumptions we no longer recognize as beliefs at all.
Was Clifford right?

Clifford’s principle is admirable and, taken literally, impossible to live by. Nobody has sufficient evidence for most of what they believe, if sufficient means evidence they have personally gathered and assessed. We believe our doctors, our encyclopaedias and the people who build bridges. The philosopher William James answered Clifford in an 1896 lecture called “The Will to Believe”. James argued that some questions cannot be settled by evidence in advance, yet still demand an answer, because refusing to decide is itself a decision. For questions of that kind, which he described as live, forced and momentous, he thought it was legitimate to let something other than evidence tip the balance.

The debate between Clifford and James is not over, and I do not think this book needs to settle it. What both of them share is more useful than where they differ. Both treat belief as something we are responsible for. Both recognize that belief leads to action, and that action affects other people. And both, in different ways, ask us to be honest about the basis on which we hold what we hold. Clifford’s shipowner fails not because he believed without perfect evidence, which everyone does, but because he had real reasons for doubt and chose to make them go away instead of investigating them. James would not have defended him either.

This suggests a more workable standard than Clifford’s. The question is not whether we have sufficient evidence for everything we believe. It is whether, for the beliefs that are about to carry weight, the route that produced them is one we would trust if we could see it clearly, and whether we have dismissed doubts that deserved investigation.
Bringing the route into view
Practically, this comes down to a few questions that can be asked of any belief before it is used to justify a significant decision.
The first is simply:
How did I come to believe this?

Not why I think it is true, which invites a search for supporting reasons, but how it actually arrived. Was it a single experience, something I have heard many times, something a respected person told me, a feeling that grew over time, or evidence I looked at and could describe? Often the honest answer is “I am not sure”, and that is useful to know.
The second is:
Under what conditions is that route reliable, and did they hold here?

Experience is reliable when it is broad and comes with feedback. Familiarity is reliable when repetitions are independent. Authority is reliable within the domain where it was earned. Emotion is reliable when it is responding to the situation at hand rather than to something else. If the conditions did not hold, the belief may still be true, but its confidence should be lower than it feels.
The third is the shipowner’s question:
Did I have doubts that I resolved by reassurance rather than by investigation?

This is the hardest to answer honestly, because reassurance feels like resolution. But it is often the most important, because a doubt that was suppressed rather than examined is still there, waiting.

None of this requires suspicion of everything we believe. It requires something more modest: the habit of remembering that beliefs have origins, that those origins vary in quality, and that a belief can feel completely solid long after the route that produced it has been forgotten. The shipowner’s problem was not that he trusted. It was that, by the time the ship left port, he could no longer see that trust was all he had.

sections.title: The Assumptions We Never Question
sections.label: 3. The Assumptions We Never Question

runs.text: How hidden premises influence conclusions and decisions.

On 23 September 1999, NASA’s Mars Climate Orbiter fired its main engine to enter orbit around Mars, passed behind the planet as planned, and was never heard from again. The spacecraft had travelled for more than nine months. When it arrived, its trajectory was roughly 170 kilometres lower than intended, deep enough in the Martian atmosphere that it was almost certainly destroyed.

The Mishap Investigation Board reported its findings that November. The root cause was a ground software file that produced data about the spacecraft’s thruster firings in English units, pound-force seconds, while the navigation software that used the data assumed metric units, newton-seconds. One pound-force is about 4.45 newtons. Every small correction that the navigation team calculated during the long cruise was based on figures that were off by that factor. No single error was dramatic. Together they added up to the loss of the mission.

It is tempting to read this as a story about carelessness. The Board’s report suggests something more instructive. The project had an interface specification stating which units should be used. The error survived because nobody checked whether that agreement had been honoured, and because the people using the data had no reason to question it. Each team was working competently within its own picture of the system. The assumption that the numbers arriving from the other team were in the expected units was so basic that it did not register as an assumption at all. It was simply part of what the numbers meant.
That is what makes hidden assumptions different from ordinary errors. An ordinary error is a mistake in something we are thinking about. A hidden assumption is a mistake in something we are thinking
with
What an assumption is

Every conclusion rests on premises. Some premises are stated: the evidence we point to, the reasons we give. Others are unstated but necessary. If any of them is false, the conclusion does not follow, however strong the stated reasons look.

Consider an everyday piece of reasoning, offered here as a hypothetical. A team leader notices that a new hire has missed two deadlines and concludes that the person is not suited to the role. The stated evidence is the two missed deadlines. The unstated premises are numerous. That the deadlines were reasonable. That the new hire understood them. That the work was within their control. That two instances indicate a pattern rather than a rough start. That the deadlines reflect what the role actually requires. That nobody else was responsible for the inputs the work depended on. Each of these is plausible. Any one of them might be false. The conclusion depends on all of them, yet the team leader is aware of only the evidence. The cost of an error here is not abstract. If the conclusion is wrong, a capable person may be managed out of a job in their first months, the team loses someone it spent time and money recruiting, and the actual cause, perhaps an unrealistic schedule or a missing input, remains in place for the next hire.

Assumptions of this kind are not failures of reasoning. They are what make reasoning possible. Nobody can state every premise of every conclusion, and nobody needs to. Most assumptions are true most of the time, which is why they become assumptions in the first place. The trouble begins when an assumption that is doing a great deal of work in a conclusion is also one we cannot see.
Why some premises become invisible
Assumptions do not hide at random. They tend to disappear for a few identifiable reasons, and knowing those reasons helps in finding them.
They are shared.

An assumption held by everyone in a room is rarely spoken, because there is nobody to disagree with it. Shared assumptions feel like facts about the world rather than beliefs about it. The Mars Climate Orbiter teams shared an expectation that the agreed units were being used. Nobody had cause to mention it.
They have worked before.
An assumption that has never failed gains authority with every success. This is the mechanism the sociologist Diane Vaughan described in her 1996 study
The Challenger Launch Decision

. Before the space shuttle Challenger was lost in January 1986, engineers had repeatedly observed erosion of the rubber O-rings that sealed joints in the solid rocket boosters. Each flight that returned safely despite erosion made the next instance easier to accept. What began as an anomaly became, through a series of reasonable-seeming judgments, an expected and acceptable condition. Vaughan called this the normalization of deviance. Her research in the archives led her to argue that the decision to launch was not, as it first appeared, simply a case of managers knowingly overriding engineers. Within the culture and procedures of the time, the people involved believed it was safe to fly. The assumption that past survival indicated an acceptable margin had become part of the frame through which the evidence was read.
They are built into tools and categories.

Many assumptions live inside the instruments we use to think: the units in a data file, the definitions in a report, the categories on a form, the metric on a dashboard. A spreadsheet that measures employee productivity in tickets closed per week carries an assumption about what productive work looks like. People who use the spreadsheet every day may never consider that assumption, because they encounter it as a column heading rather than as a claim.
They are flattering or convenient.

Some assumptions persist because questioning them would be uncomfortable. It is pleasanter to assume that a project failed because of external conditions than because of the plan, or that a customer left because of price rather than because of how they were treated. Such assumptions are not exactly hidden. We simply do not look in their direction.
Assumptions inside every test
The physicist and philosopher Pierre Duhem made an observation in the early twentieth century that is worth carrying beyond science. In
The Aim and Structure of Physical Theory

, published in 1906, he pointed out that a scientific hypothesis is never tested in isolation. A prediction depends on the hypothesis together with a set of auxiliary assumptions: that the instruments work, that background conditions are as believed, that other known theories hold. When a prediction fails, the failure shows that something in the whole set is wrong, but it does not, by itself, tell us what.

The practical version of Duhem’s point is this. Whenever we test an idea against experience, we are also testing our assumptions, whether we know it or not. If a marketing campaign fails, the failure might mean the message was wrong. It might also mean the audience was not the one assumed, the channel did not reach them, the timing was off, or the measure of success was poorly chosen. People who see only their stated hypothesis will draw a conclusion about it. People who can see their assumptions will know that several conclusions are possible, and will ask which one the evidence actually supports.

The reverse is equally important. A test can appear to succeed because an assumption failed in a lucky direction. Teams that do not know what they assumed cannot tell a real success from a fortunate accident, and they will carry the accident forward as a lesson.
The deepest assumptions
Some assumptions are so fundamental that they shape which questions can be asked at all. The philosopher R. G. Collingwood, in
An Essay on Metaphysics
(1940), called these absolute presuppositions. They are not answers to questions within an inquiry. They are what decide which questions the inquiry thinks to ask.

Organizations have presuppositions of this kind. A company may presuppose that growth is the measure of health, that its competitors are the firms in its own industry, or that its customers are the people who pay. These presuppositions are rarely wrong in a simple sense. They are frames, and frames determine what a team notices. A firm that assumes its competitors are other firms like itself may not see a threat coming from a different kind of product that solves the same problem. The threat is not invisible because it is subtle. It is invisible because it falls outside the frame.
Ludwig Wittgenstein, in the notes published after his death as
On Certainty

(1969), made a related point from the other direction. He observed that doubt itself depends on certain things not being doubted. The questions we raise rest on some propositions that are, in his image, like hinges on which the questions turn. If the hinges moved, the door could not open. This is a necessary corrective to any book that encourages questioning. We cannot question everything at once, and attempting to would not make us more rational. It would leave us unable to reason at all.

The lesson I take from Collingwood and Wittgenstein together is that the goal is not to eliminate assumptions but to know which ones are carrying the weight of a particular decision, and to examine those.
Load-bearing and fragile

A useful way to sort assumptions is along two dimensions. The first is how much the conclusion depends on the assumption: whether the conclusion would collapse if it were false, or merely shift a little. The second is how likely the assumption is to be false in this particular situation, given what we know.

An assumption that is both load-bearing and fragile deserves attention before the decision is made. An assumption that is load-bearing but robust, such as the assumption that a reputable bank will still exist next month, can usually be accepted. An assumption that is fragile but not load-bearing can be noted and left alone. The mistake is to spend effort questioning assumptions that do not matter while the ones that matter go unexamined, which is what tends to happen when people question whatever is easiest to see rather than whatever is most important.

In practice, the most dangerous assumptions are often those that were once robust and have quietly become fragile. Conditions change. Markets shift, technologies improve, teams turn over, regulations are amended. An assumption that was entirely safe five years ago can become a weak point without anyone noticing, precisely because it was safe for so long that people stopped checking it. This is the normalization of deviance in reverse: not an anomaly becoming normal, but a normal becoming anomalous while still being treated as normal.

Households face the same pattern. Consider a hypothetical couple choosing how large a mortgage to take on. The calculation that says they can afford it rests on assumptions they may never state: that both incomes will continue, that the interest rate will stay near its current level, that no large repair or illness will arrive in the first few years. Several of these are load-bearing, and at least one, a variable interest rate, may be more fragile than it was when they first did the sums. Naming them does not settle the decision. It tells them which assumptions to test, and which risks to protect against, before they sign.
Bringing assumptions into view
Since hidden assumptions are by definition hard to see, finding them requires deliberate methods. The following are specific to uncovering premises. Chapter 4 deals with questioning more generally.
Reconstruct the argument.

Write the conclusion at the bottom of a page and the stated evidence above it. Then ask what else would have to be true for the evidence to lead to the conclusion. The gaps between evidence and conclusion are where the assumptions sit. In the team-leader example, the gap between “missed two deadlines” and “not suited to the role” contains a whole set of unstated premises about fairness, control, understanding and pattern.
Reverse the conclusion.

Imagine that the conclusion turns out to be wrong, and ask what would most likely explain that. The answers tend to point directly at the assumptions that were doing the most work. If the new hire turns out to be excellent, the most likely explanation might be that the deadlines were unrealistic or that their inputs arrived late. Those are the premises worth checking now.
Examine the instruments.

Look at the measures, units, definitions and categories that the reasoning relies on, and ask what each one assumes. What does this metric count, and what does it leave out? What does this category include, and who decided? Assumptions embedded in tools are the ones least likely to be spoken and most likely to be shared.
Look for the newcomer’s view.

People who are new to a team, a field or a country often notice assumptions that insiders cannot, because the assumptions are not yet part of how they see things. Their questions can sound naive. They are often the most valuable questions in the room. The same effect can be produced deliberately by asking how someone from a different discipline, a different organization or a different culture would view the same situation.
Ask what has changed.

For any assumption that has been reliable for a long time, ask whether the conditions that made it reliable still hold. This is especially important for assumptions about customers, technology, competitors and people, all of which change more than our pictures of them do.
A shared responsibility

There is one more feature of hidden assumptions that deserves emphasis. In both the Mars Climate Orbiter and Challenger cases, the assumptions that mattered were not held by any one careless person. They were held across teams and embedded in procedures. Nobody owned them, which meant nobody was responsible for checking them.

This is a general pattern. In organizations, the most consequential assumptions usually sit at the boundaries between groups: between engineering and operations, between design and sales, between the people who build a measure and the people who use it. Each side assumes the other has checked. In families and relationships, something similar happens. Each person assumes the other understands an arrangement in the same way, until the moment it becomes clear that they never did.

The practical implication is that assumption-checking cannot be left entirely to individual vigilance. It has to be built into how work is done: in the reviews that ask what a plan depends on, in the interfaces where one group’s output becomes another group’s input, and in the habit of saying aloud what everyone thinks goes without saying. That habit can feel awkward, even slightly insulting, as if one were doubting colleagues’ competence. It is better understood as respect for how easily competent people can share an error.
Conclusions rest on what we do not say

In the Mars Climate Orbiter case the assumption was technical and, once found, easy to state. Most assumptions are not like that. They are woven into how we describe a situation, what we treat as relevant, and what we never think to measure. They are rarely wrong in an obvious way. More often they were right once, or right in a different context, or right for most cases but not for this one.

Much of good judgment, then, consists in the unglamorous work of making the unstated visible: not every assumption, which is impossible, but the few that a particular conclusion cannot survive without. That work rarely produces a dramatic discovery. More often it produces a modest adjustment in confidence, a question asked of the right person, or a check run before rather than after. Its value lies mostly in the mistakes that do not happen, which is why it is so easy to undervalue. From the outside, a decision whose premises were examined looks exactly like one whose premises were not. The difference appears only when the world tests them.

sections.title: The Discipline of Asking Better Questions
sections.label: 4. The Discipline of Asking Better Questions

runs.text: How questions shape investigation, reveal overlooked possibilities and improve reasoning.

Every inquiry starts as a question, and the question decides much of what the inquiry can find. This is easy to agree with and easy to forget, because questions feel like neutral containers. We imagine that we ask, the world answers, and the answer depends on the world. In practice, the form of a question shapes which answers are available, which evidence seems relevant, and when the search will feel finished. A poorly framed question can be answered with great care and still lead somewhere useless. A well-framed question can make a difficult problem tractable before any information has been gathered.

The previous chapter was about the assumptions beneath our conclusions. This one is about the questions in front of them. The two are related, since every question carries assumptions, but the practical skill is different. Finding assumptions means looking backwards at reasoning already done. Asking better questions means shaping reasoning before it starts.
How a question changes what we find

In 1974 Elizabeth Loftus and John Palmer showed students short films of traffic accidents and then asked them how fast the cars had been going. The only thing that varied between groups was the verb. Some were asked how fast the cars were going when they “smashed into” each other; others heard “collided”, “bumped”, “hit” or “contacted”. Estimates rose with the intensity of the verb, from an average of about 32 miles per hour for “contacted” to about 41 for “smashed”. In a second experiment, students were asked a week later whether they had seen any broken glass. There had been none. Of those who had originally been asked the “smashed” question, 16 out of 50 said they had seen broken glass, compared with 7 out of 50 of those asked the “hit” question.

The second finding is the more unsettling. The wording of a question did not merely bias an estimate in the moment. It appears to have altered what people later remembered seeing. A question is not only a request for information. It is also a piece of information, and the mind incorporates it.

This matters well beyond eyewitness testimony. Any time we ask ourselves or others about a situation, the words we choose carry implications about what happened and what matters. “Why did the project fail?” presupposes that it failed and invites a search for a cause. “What happened with the project?” leaves more open. “Who dropped the ball?” invites a search for a person. Each question will produce a sincere, coherent answer, and the answers will differ, not because the facts differ but because each question selects different facts.
The frame inside the question
In a well-known study published in
Science

in 1981, Amos Tversky and Daniel Kahneman asked people to imagine that a country was preparing for an unusual disease expected to kill 600 people. One group chose between two programmes: under the first, 200 people would be saved; under the second, there was a one-in-three chance that all 600 would be saved and a two-in-three chance that nobody would be. Seventy-two per cent chose the certain option. A second group was given the same choice described in terms of deaths: under one programme, 400 people would die; under the other, there was a one-in-three chance that nobody would die and a two-in-three chance that all 600 would. Now 78 per cent chose the gamble.

The programmes were identical. Only the description changed, from lives saved to lives lost, and with it the majority preference reversed. Tversky and Kahneman called this a framing effect, and it has been studied extensively since.

Framing is usually discussed as something done to us by others, such as advertisers or negotiators. It is just as often something we do to ourselves through the questions we ask. A manager who asks “How much will we lose if we cancel this project?” has framed the decision around loss and will tend to feel the weight of what has already been spent. A manager who asks “If we were starting today, would we choose to invest in this?” has framed the same decision around a fresh choice. Neither question is dishonest. But they will tend to produce different answers, and the person asking may never notice that the question, rather than the evidence, made the difference.
Answering an easier question

One of the most common failures of questioning is invisible because it happens automatically. Faced with a hard question, the mind often answers an easier one without noticing the swap. Daniel Kahneman and Shane Frederick described this in 2002 as attribute substitution. Asked “How likely is this candidate to succeed as a manager?”, which is difficult, we may answer “How much did I like this candidate in the interview?”, which is easy. Asked “Is this investment sound?”, we may answer “Does this company feel exciting?”

The substituted answer arrives with all the confidence of a real one, because we did answer a question, just not the one that mattered. The defence is simple to describe and requires discipline to use: state the real question explicitly, in words, before trying to answer it, and then check afterwards whether the answer actually addresses it. When the answer comes very quickly to a question that should be hard, it is worth suspecting that a substitution has occurred.
Questions that close too early

Many decisions are posed as a choice between doing something and not doing it. Should we launch the product? Should I accept the job? Should we hire this person? These yes-or-no questions are natural, and they quietly exclude every option except one.

The management researcher Paul Nutt spent two decades studying decisions in organizations. In a 1999 paper he reported that about half of the 356 decisions he examined in medium and large organizations failed, and he traced many failures to managers who imposed a solution early and limited the search for alternatives. Chip and Dan Heath, drawing on Nutt’s data in their book
Decisive

(2013), report that decisions framed as “whether or not” failed 52 per cent of the time over the long term, against 32 per cent for decisions in which two or more alternatives were considered. Nutt’s research is observational, and it is possible that harder problems were both more likely to be framed narrowly and more likely to fail. But the pattern fits a straightforward logic. A question that admits only two answers cannot discover a third.

The remedy is often a change of grammar. “Should we launch the product?” can become “What are the different ways we could get this product to customers, and what would each require?” “Should I accept this job?” can become “What am I hoping this job will give me, and what are the various ways I could get that?” The new questions are slower to answer. They are also much more likely to reveal an option nobody had considered.
The question behind the question
John Dewey, in
Logic: The Theory of Inquiry

(1938), repeated what he called a familiar and significant saying: that a problem well put is half solved. Dewey’s point was that the formulation of a problem is not a preliminary to inquiry but part of it. Until we know what we are trying to find out, we cannot know what counts as relevant, and we will gather information that answers nothing in particular.
In practice, putting a problem well often means separating questions that have been run together. Three are especially easy to confuse.
What is happening?
is a question about facts.
Why is it happening?
is a question about causes.
What should we do?

is a question about action. A meeting that tries to answer all three at once tends to answer none of them well, because people jump to proposals before the facts are clear, or argue about causes when they agree on what to do. Taking them in order, and noticing when a discussion has jumped ahead, is one of the simplest ways to improve collective reasoning.
A fourth question often hides among them:
Who is to blame?

It is not always an illegitimate question, since accountability matters. But it tends to crowd out the others. Once the conversation turns to blame, people defend themselves, information becomes guarded, and the questions about what happened and why become harder to answer honestly. Sidney Dekker, a researcher in safety and human error, has argued in
The Field Guide to Understanding Human Error

that investigations learn far more when they ask why people’s actions made sense to them at the time than when they ask who made the mistake. The useful question concerns what people knew and the pressures they faced. The first question leads to understanding the conditions that produce errors. The second tends to stop at a name.
The limits of asking “why” repeatedly

One popular technique for getting beneath the surface of a problem is to ask “why” several times in succession. It is associated with Taiichi Ohno, who described it in his account of the Toyota Production System as a way of reaching a root cause by repeating the question about five times. A machine stops; why? A fuse blew; why? The bearing was not lubricated; why? And so on, until a fixable cause appears.

The technique has genuine value. It discourages stopping at the first and most obvious cause, and it pushes inquiry towards conditions rather than symptoms. But its limits are worth understanding, because they reveal something general about questions. Alan Card, writing in
BMJ Quality & Safety

in 2017, criticized the uncritical use of “five whys” in healthcare. He argued that it tends to produce a single linear chain when most real failures have several interacting causes, and that the chain depends heavily on what the person asking already knows and expects. Two people asking “why” about the same incident can follow different branches and reach different root causes, each feeling they have found the answer.

The lesson is not that the technique is useless, but that any fixed sequence of questions inherits the assumptions of the person asking. A question is a probe, and a probe finds what lies along its path. To see more of the terrain, it helps to ask from more than one starting point, and to ask with people who would naturally follow different branches.
What makes a question good
It is easier to recognize bad questions than to define good ones, but several features recur in questions that improve reasoning.
A good question serves a decision.

It is clear what would be done differently depending on the answer. Questions that would change nothing, however interesting, can wait. When a team is gathering information without being able to say how it will be used, it is often avoiding a decision rather than preparing for one.
A good question is open where openness matters.
It does not presuppose its answer or limit the options more than necessary. “How might we reduce customer churn?” invites more possibilities than “Should we cut prices to reduce churn?”
A good question is neutral in its wording.

It avoids terms that carry the asker’s conclusion. “What happened during the handover?” will get a more accurate account than “What went wrong during the handover?”, which in turn will get a more accurate account than “Why did the night shift mess up the handover?”
A good question asks about mechanism, not only verdict.

“Is this plan good?” invites an opinion. “How exactly will this plan produce the result we want, step by step?” invites an explanation, and, as Chapter 1 showed, the attempt to explain is one of the most reliable ways of discovering what we do not understand.
A good question can tell possibilities apart.

The most useful questions are those whose answers would differ depending on which of several possibilities is true. If two explanations for a problem would both predict the same answer to a question, asking it will not help choose between them. Chapter 7 develops this idea in detail. Here it is enough to notice that a question’s value lies not in how much information it gathers but in how much it reduces uncertainty about what matters.
A good question specifies what an answer would look like.

“Is the new process working?” can be argued about forever. “Has the average time to resolve a complaint fallen since the new process started, and by how much?” can be answered, and the answer can be checked.
Asking other people

Much of the information we rely on comes from asking others, and the quality of what we receive depends heavily on how we ask. The lessons from the Loftus and Palmer study apply in every meeting, interview and conversation. Leading questions get agreeable answers. Questions that reveal what the asker hopes to hear tend to receive it, especially when the asker has more power than the person being asked.

Consider a hypothetical manager who wants to know whether a new policy is causing problems. If she asks her team “The new policy is working well, isn’t it?”, she has told them the answer she prefers, and most people will give it. If she asks “What has the new policy made harder?”, she has signalled that problems are expected and that reporting them is welcome. The second question will not guarantee honesty, but it removes one of the main obstacles to it. The difference matters because the cost of the first question is delayed. The manager hears that all is well, and the problems the policy created surface months later, as a resignation, a missed target or a customer complaint, by which time they are harder and more expensive to fix.
The Socratic dialogues offer an older model. In Plato’s
Euthyphro

, Socrates questions a man who is confident he knows what piety is. Socrates does not argue against him directly. He asks him to define the term, then asks questions that test each definition against cases, until Euthyphro sees that his confident understanding does not hold together. The dialogue ends without a satisfactory definition, which can seem like a failure. But the questions have done their work: they have replaced false confidence with an accurate sense of what remains unknown.

That is what good questions can do that answers cannot. An answer adds to what we know. A good question can show us the shape of what we do not know, which is often more useful when a decision is approaching.
When to stop asking

There is a tension in all of this that should not be hidden. Questions can improve reasoning, but they can also be used to avoid commitment. A person or organization that never stops asking questions may be avoiding the discomfort of deciding. More research, another analysis and further consultation can all become forms of procrastination dressed as diligence. Dewey, who valued inquiry as highly as anyone, insisted that its purpose was to resolve a problematic situation, to reach what he called a warranted judgment. Inquiry that never reaches judgment has not finished its work.

This is the third of the book’s questions in its plainest form: when should examination stop and action begin? I do not think there is a formula. What helps is to ask, alongside every investigative question, a second question about the investigation itself: what would we need to learn for this decision to change, and is it realistic to learn it in the time we have? If the honest answer is that nothing we could plausibly learn would change the decision, the questioning has done its job, and the time has come to conclude. If the answer is that one specific piece of information would change everything, the next question is obvious. And if nobody can say what would change the decision, that is itself a sign that the right question has not yet been asked.

Questioning can also do harm in a quieter way. In a team, every question carries a social message as well as a request for information, and a leader who interrogates every decision can teach people to stop making them. Questions asked after a decision is irreversible can feed regret without improving anything. And in a situation that a skilled person has seen many times, questioning their routine judgment may replace a well-calibrated intuition with a slower and worse analysis. Good questioning is aimed at the decisions where an answer could still change something, and at the parts of a judgment where experience offers no reliable guide.

sections.title: Reasoning in an Uncertain World
sections.label: Part II — Reasoning in an Uncertain World

runs.text: Part I was about the material we reason with. Part II is about the world that material is meant to describe, and about the evidence that connects the two.
