Chapter 5 asks what an observation can actually justify, and finds that evidence gains its force only in comparison with the alternatives. That raises the question of which comparisons we routinely fail to make. Chapter 6 takes the most common one, the leap from two things happening together to one causing the other. Chapter 7 asks why the alternative explanations that would test our first story so rarely come to mind, and what happens when they are kept in view. Chapter 8 asks why numbers, which seem to settle such questions, can mislead even when every figure in them is correct.

The common thread is that evidence never interprets itself. The same observation, association or statistic can support very different conclusions depending on what it is compared with. Reasoning well in an uncertain world is largely a matter of supplying the right comparison before reaching a conclusion. That raises an awkward question, which Part III takes up: if the right comparisons are so useful, why do intelligent people so often fail to make them?

sections.title: What Does the Evidence Really Tell Us?
sections.label: 5. What Does the Evidence Really Tell Us?

runs.text: Distinguishing observations, interpretations, claims and justified conclusions.

In the early 1900s, a retired Berlin schoolteacher named Wilhelm von Osten began exhibiting a horse he called Hans. Asked to add, subtract, multiply or tell the date, Hans tapped out the answer with his hoof, and he was usually right. Von Osten charged no admission and appears to have been entirely sincere. The case attracted so much attention that in 1904 a commission of thirteen people, organized by the psychologist Carl Stumpf and including a zoo director, a circus manager and a cavalry officer, examined the horse. They concluded that no trickery was involved.

They were right about that. There was no trick. But Stumpf’s student Oskar Pfungst continued the investigation, and in a study published in 1907 he showed what was actually happening. Pfungst varied the conditions systematically. He used questioners other than von Osten, put blinders on the horse so it could not see the questioner, and, crucially, arranged for some questioners to ask questions to which they themselves did not know the answer. Hans’s accuracy collapsed whenever he could not see the questioner, or the questioner did not know the answer. The horse had learned to read tiny, involuntary changes in posture and expression: a slight lean forward as he began tapping, a slight relaxation when he reached the right number. Pfungst found that he produced these cues himself, even when he was trying not to.

The Clever Hans case is usually told as a story about animals or about unconscious cues. I think it is better understood as a story about evidence. Everything the commission observed was real. The horse did tap the correct number. No one was signalling deliberately. The error lay in a single step of inference: from “there is no fraud” to “the horse can do arithmetic”. The observation was sound. The interpretation was one of several that fitted it, and the commission had not designed any test that could tell the interpretations apart. Pfungst did.
Four things that look alike
When people say “the evidence shows”, they usually run together four different things.
An
observation
is what was actually seen, measured or recorded: Hans tapped eight times after being asked what three plus five is. Observations can be mistaken, but they are the closest we come to raw material.
An
interpretation
is what the observation is taken to mean: Hans understood the question and computed the answer. Interpretations go beyond what was seen. They connect it to a story about why it happened.
A
claim

is a statement put forward as true, often by someone else, and often packaged with its interpretation already attached: “This horse can do arithmetic.” Most of the evidence we encounter in daily life arrives in the form of claims. We rarely see the observations behind them.
A
justified conclusion

is a belief that the observations actually support, held with confidence proportionate to that support, after other interpretations have been considered. It is the end point that the first three are supposed to lead to, and often do not.

The distance between observation and justified conclusion is where most reasoning goes wrong. That distance is easy to cross without noticing, because interpretations do not feel like additions. When we see a colleague arrive late to three meetings, we do not experience ourselves as observing three late arrivals and then adding an interpretation. We experience ourselves as seeing someone who does not respect other people’s time. The interpretation is fused with the perception. Separating them takes deliberate effort.
What makes an observation evidence
An observation becomes evidence for a claim only in relation to other possibilities. This is the central idea of the chapter, and it is less obvious than it sounds.

An observation supports a claim to the extent that it would be more likely to occur if the claim were true than if it were false. If an observation is just as likely either way, it is not evidence for the claim at all, however closely it seems to relate to it. Statisticians express this precisely through ratios of likelihoods, but the idea does not require mathematics. It requires asking one question:
How likely would I be to see this if I were wrong?

Hans tapping the correct answer was very likely if he could do arithmetic. It was also very likely if he was reading cues from a questioner who knew the answer. So the observation, impressive as it was, did almost nothing to distinguish between the two. The observation that would have distinguished them, correct answers when the questioner did not know, was the one the commission had not made. When Pfungst made it, the answers stopped being correct.

The same logic applies to ordinary judgments. Consider a hypothetical job interview in which a candidate speaks fluently and confidently about their past achievements. It feels like evidence of competence. But fluent, confident self-presentation is also what we would expect from a candidate who has practised interviewing, or who is simply extroverted, whether or not they are competent. The observation is real. Its power to distinguish competent from incompetent candidates may be modest. A better piece of evidence would be one that competent and incompetent candidates would be unlikely to produce equally, such as a work sample in the actual task.

This way of thinking changes what counts as strong evidence. Strong evidence is not evidence that is vivid, abundant or emotionally compelling. It is evidence that would be surprising if the claim were false.
Absence of evidence
The same logic clarifies an old argument. Is absence of evidence evidence of absence? The answer depends on whether we would expect to find evidence if the thing were there.

If I search my desk for my keys and do not find them, that is good evidence that they are not on my desk, because I would very probably have seen them if they were. If I search my house for a single missing earring and do not find it, the absence tells me much less, because earrings are small and houses are large. The question is always about the power of the search: how likely would it have been to turn something up if there were something to find?

This matters in serious decisions. A safety review that finds no problems is reassuring only if it was capable of finding the problems that matter. A clinical trial that finds no side effects is reassuring about common side effects but may say little about rare ones, simply because it did not include enough people for a rare event to appear. An internal audit that finds no misconduct is reassuring only if the people who would have engaged in misconduct had no influence over what the auditors were shown. In each case, “we found nothing” is a claim about the search as much as about the world.
How observations are collected
Even an accurate observation can mislead if we do not know how it was collected. Three questions are especially useful.
Who or what was counted, and who or what was left out?

A collection of customer testimonials is a real set of observations about real customers. It is also a sample selected for enthusiasm. Customers who were indifferent or disappointed are not represented, and the selection may be entirely innocent. The observations are accurate. What they cannot do is tell us how typical they are.
How was it measured?

Measurements embody choices about what to record and how. A survey that asks employees whether they are “satisfied” with their manager measures something, but what it measures depends on the wording, on who chose to respond, and on whether employees believed their answers were anonymous.
Are the observations independent?

This connects to Chapter 2’s discussion of familiarity. Ten observations that share a single source are not ten pieces of evidence. If ten news reports all rely on one press release, they provide roughly the evidential weight of the press release. If ten colleagues all say a project is going well because they all heard it from the project lead, their agreement adds very little to the project lead’s own view. Before counting how much evidence there is, it helps to ask how many independent routes it took to reach us.
Anecdotes and systematic evidence

It has become common to dismiss anecdotes as worthless. I think that is a mistake, though an understandable one. An anecdote is a real observation. Someone took a medicine and recovered. A company adopted a practice and prospered. These things happened.

The problem with anecdotes is not that they are false. It is that we usually do not know how they were selected or what the comparison would have shown. We do not know how many people took the medicine and did not recover, or how many would have recovered anyway. We do not know how many companies adopted the practice and failed. An anecdote is a single observation with no denominator and no comparison, and those are precisely the things needed to turn an observation into evidence for a general claim.

Anecdotes have real uses. They can suggest hypotheses worth testing. They can reveal possibilities that systematic data missed. A single well-documented case can disprove a claim that something never happens. What they cannot do, on their own, is establish how often something happens or what causes it. Systematic evidence, collected in a way designed to answer a specific question and with an appropriate comparison, can do those things, within its own limits.

Medicine has formalized this into what is often called a hierarchy of evidence, with randomized controlled trials and systematic reviews near the top and case reports and expert opinion near the bottom. The hierarchy is useful as a rough guide, but it should not be applied mechanically. A poorly conducted trial can be less informative than a careful observational study, and some questions cannot ethically or practically be answered by experiments at all. The more durable lesson is the one behind the hierarchy: evidence is stronger when the way it was collected rules out more of the alternative explanations.
Proportioning belief
In
An Enquiry Concerning Human Understanding

, published in 1748, David Hume wrote that “a wise man, therefore, proportions his belief to the evidence.” The sentence is often quoted as though it were a simple instruction. It is actually a demanding one, because it implies that belief should come in degrees.

Most everyday thinking treats belief as a switch. Something is true or not; we believe it or we do not. But the evidence for most claims of practical importance supports some degree of confidence rather than certainty. A justified conclusion is not just a claim we accept. It is a claim we accept to a particular extent, an extent that would change if the evidence changed.

This has two practical consequences. The first is that the same evidence can justify acting in one situation and not in another, depending on what is at stake. Moderate evidence that a supplier is unreliable might be enough to add a second supplier but not enough to end a long relationship. Chapter 14 develops this connection between confidence and action. The second consequence is that how much evidence is needed depends partly on how plausible the claim was to begin with. A claim that fits well with everything else we know needs less support than one that would overturn it. Carl Sagan popularized a version of this principle when he said that extraordinary claims require extraordinary evidence. A horse that understands arithmetic would have been an extraordinary discovery. The commission’s evidence was ordinary.
Objections worth taking seriously
There are two reasonable objections to the approach described here.

The first is that it seems to demand more evidence than everyday life can supply. Most decisions must be made quickly, on partial information, by people who are not trained in research methods. If every belief required systematic evidence and a consideration of alternatives, nobody would get anything done. This is true, and it is why the approach should be applied selectively. The habits in this chapter are for conclusions that will carry real weight. For the rest, rough judgment is fine.

The second objection is subtler. Some of what experienced people know cannot easily be reduced to observations and interpretations. A seasoned engineer may sense that a design is fragile. A teacher may sense that a student is struggling before any grade falls. These judgments are often correct, and demanding that they be justified in explicit terms can lead to their being dismissed. I think the right response is not to dismiss such judgments but to treat them as a particular kind of evidence: observations made by a well-trained instrument whose workings are not fully visible. Like any instrument, it can be calibrated. We can ask how often such judgments have been right in the past, in situations like this one. Chapters 11 and 15 return to the question of when intuition can be trusted.
The question that evidence cannot answer for us

The Hans commission did not lack intelligence, expertise or honesty. Its members were experienced and careful within the limits of what they set out to check. What they did not do was ask how their observations would have looked if the most interesting interpretation were false. That question, which Pfungst asked, turned an unexplained marvel into an understood phenomenon.

Evidence never interprets itself. It can tell us what happened, under what conditions, and how often. It cannot tell us which story about it to believe until we have set the stories side by side and asked which observations each one predicts. The most useful habit this chapter can offer is simple to state: before treating an observation as support for a conclusion, ask what you would have expected to see if the conclusion were wrong. If the answer is “much the same thing”, the observation has not yet told you very much, however convincing it feels.

sections.title: When Two Things Happen Together
sections.label: 6. When Two Things Happen Together

runs.text: Correlation, causation, coincidence and misleading causal explanations.

For several decades, a large body of observational research suggested that postmenopausal women who took hormone therapy had substantially lower rates of coronary heart disease than women who did not. The reductions reported were in the range of 40 to 50 per cent. There was a plausible biological story to go with the numbers, and many physicians prescribed hormone therapy partly in the hope of protecting their patients’ hearts.

Then came the Women’s Health Initiative, a large randomized controlled trial in the United States. In the arm testing combined oestrogen and progestin, 16,608 postmenopausal women aged 50 to 79 were randomly assigned to take either the hormones or a placebo. In May 2002, after an average of 5.2 years, the trial’s monitoring board recommended stopping it early. The results, published in
JAMA

that July, showed no heart protection. Women taking the hormones had a higher rate of coronary heart disease than women taking the placebo, with an estimated hazard ratio of 1.29, along with increased rates of stroke, blood clots in the lungs and invasive breast cancer.

How could so many studies point one way and a single trial point the other? The leading explanation is not that the earlier researchers were careless. It is that the women who chose to take hormone therapy differed from those who did not in ways that also affected their heart health. They tended to be wealthier, better educated, more likely to see doctors regularly, and healthier in other respects. The hormones were associated with healthier hearts because healthier women were more likely to take the hormones. The association was real. The causal story attached to it was not, at least not for the women and the regimen the trial tested. Researchers continue to debate whether the timing of therapy relative to menopause changes the picture, which is a reminder that even a large trial answers a specific question rather than every question.
This chapter is about the gap between two things happening together and one of them causing the other. It is the most familiar warning in all of statistics, and one of the least consistently heeded.
Why causation is so tempting

The mind is built to find causes. David Hume argued in the eighteenth century that we never directly observe causation at all. We observe one event regularly followed by another, and the mind supplies the sense of necessary connection. Whatever one thinks of Hume’s philosophy, his psychological point has held up well. When two things occur together, a causal explanation tends to arrive unbidden, and it arrives feeling like an observation rather than an inference.

This is usually useful. Most of the time, things that reliably occur together are causally connected in some way, and acting as though they are is a reasonable bet. The trouble is that “connected in some way” covers several quite different possibilities, and the one that first comes to mind is not always right. Getting causation wrong matters because decisions are interventions. We do something in the hope that it will change something else. An association that is not causal can be perfectly accurate as a description and still give exactly the wrong advice about what to do.
Five ways two things go together
When two things are associated, there are at least five broad explanations worth considering.
The first causes the second.
This is the explanation that usually comes to mind, and sometimes it is correct.
The second causes the first.

Causation can run in the opposite direction from the one assumed. People who use walking aids fall more often than people who do not, but walking aids do not cause falls. Unsteadiness causes both. A company that spends heavily on marketing may grow faster than its rivals, but it may also be the case that growing companies have more money to spend on marketing. Reverse causation is easy to miss because the direction we first assume quickly comes to feel like part of the observation.
Something else causes both.

This is confounding, and it is what the hormone therapy story illustrates. A third factor, in that case general health and the advantages that go with it, influences both the supposed cause and the supposed effect. In 2012 the cardiologist Franz Messerli published a deliberately playful note in the
New England Journal of Medicine

showing a strong correlation, across 23 countries, between chocolate consumption per person and Nobel laureates per ten million people. Nobody seriously believes that chocolate wins Nobel prizes. National wealth is an obvious candidate for a common cause of both, since wealthy countries can afford both more chocolate and more research. The example is useful because it is absurd. In real decisions, the confounder is rarely so easy to spot.
Chance.
If enough pairs of measurements are compared, some will be correlated by coincidence. Tyler Vigen’s book
Spurious Correlations

(2015) collects striking examples, such as series of unrelated annual figures that rise and fall together for years. These are entertaining, but the underlying problem is serious. In any large dataset, a determined search will find associations that mean nothing, and the more variables are examined, the more such associations will appear. An association found by searching through many possibilities deserves much more suspicion than one that was predicted in advance and then observed.
Selection.

Sometimes an association is produced by the way cases were chosen for examination. Consider a hypothetical company that hires only applicants whose combined score on a written test and an interview exceeds a threshold. Among the people it hires, written-test scores and interview scores may appear to be negatively related: those who did brilliantly in the interview often scraped through the test, and vice versa. This pattern can arise even if the two scores are unrelated, or positively related, among all applicants. It is created by the selection, because anyone who did poorly on both was never hired and so is not in the data. The statistician Joseph Berkson described a version of this effect among hospital patients in 1946, and it is now often called Berkson’s paradox. It is worth suspecting whenever the data come only from people or cases that passed some filter.

The five explanations are not only for researchers. Consider a hypothetical parent who notices that in the weeks her daughter does homework at the kitchen table rather than in her bedroom, her marks are better. Perhaps the kitchen helps, with fewer distractions and help close at hand. Perhaps the direction runs the other way: in weeks when the material is easy and going well, the daughter is happy to work where others can see. Perhaps something else drives both, such as the weeks when a parent gets home early, which bring both company at the kitchen table and help with the hardest problems. Perhaps it is chance, since a handful of weeks is a small sample. And perhaps it is selection: if the parent only looks at the marks in weeks when she happens to check, the weeks she remembers may not be typical. Moving the desk to the kitchen is cheap, so it may be worth trying anyway. But if the decision were expensive, each of these possibilities would deserve a moment’s thought before it was made.
A special case: regression to the mean
One pattern deserves separate attention because it produces convincing causal stories out of pure statistics. Daniel Kahneman describes in
Thinking, Fast and Slow

(2011) an exchange with flight instructors in the Israeli Air Force. He had been explaining that rewarding good performance is more effective than punishing poor performance. A senior instructor disagreed. In his experience, when he praised a cadet for an excellent manoeuvre, the next attempt was usually worse. When he shouted at a cadet for a poor one, the next attempt was usually better. Praise seemed to hurt and criticism seemed to help.

Kahneman realized that the instructor’s observations were accurate and his conclusion was wrong. Performance on any single attempt reflects both skill and luck. An unusually good attempt was probably helped by luck, and the next attempt would likely be closer to the cadet’s average, whatever the instructor said. An unusually poor attempt was probably partly bad luck, and the next would likely be better. The instructor praised after good attempts and criticized after bad ones, so he saw deterioration after praise and improvement after criticism. He had attached a causal story to a statistical inevitability.

Regression to the mean appears wherever extreme results are followed up. A team that had a record quarter will probably do less well next quarter. A school whose test scores were the worst in the region will probably improve somewhat next year, whatever the intervention. A treatment given to people at their sickest will often appear to work, because many people improve from their worst point regardless. Any intervention aimed at extremes will appear to succeed or fail partly because of regression, and the only reliable way to separate the effect of the intervention from regression is to compare with similar cases that did not receive it.
How causation can be established
If associations can mislead in so many ways, how do we ever learn what causes what? There are several routes, of different strengths.
The most powerful is a well-conducted
randomized experiment

. If people are assigned to receive an intervention or not by chance, then on average the two groups will be similar in every other respect, including respects nobody thought to measure. Any substantial difference in outcomes can then be attributed to the intervention with much greater confidence. This is why the Women’s Health Initiative could overturn decades of observational findings. Randomization did what no amount of statistical adjustment could fully do: it broke the link between who chose the hormones and who was healthy.
When experiments are impossible,
natural experiments

can sometimes take their place. The physician John Snow provided a classic example during the London cholera epidemic of 1854. Two water companies supplied overlapping parts of south London, with pipes from both running down the same streets. One company, Southwark and Vauxhall, drew its water from a stretch of the Thames contaminated with sewage. The other, Lambeth, had moved its intake upstream. Snow argued that the households supplied by the two companies were otherwise similar, rich and poor alike, so the choice of supplier acted almost like a random assignment. His figures, published in 1855, showed about 315 cholera deaths per 10,000 houses supplied by Southwark and Vauxhall, compared with 37 per 10,000 supplied by Lambeth. The comparison was hard to explain away, because the obvious confounders were roughly balanced by the accident of which company happened to lay pipes to which house.
Where neither experiment nor natural experiment is available, causal conclusions must be built from
converging lines of evidence

. In a 1965 lecture to the Royal Society of Medicine, the epidemiologist Austin Bradford Hill set out nine considerations to weigh when deciding whether an association reflects causation. They included the strength of the association, its consistency across studies, whether the supposed cause came before the effect, whether more exposure led to more effect, and whether the relationship made sense in light of other knowledge. Hill was explicit that these were viewpoints rather than rules: none could prove or disprove causation on its own, and none was strictly necessary. His considerations are still widely used, and still widely misused as a checklist, against his own advice.
The question that matters for decisions
The computer scientist Judea Pearl, in
The Book of Why

(2018, written with Dana Mackenzie), describes a ladder of causal reasoning. The bottom rung is association: seeing that two things go together. The second rung is intervention: knowing what would happen if we changed one of them. The third is counterfactual reasoning: knowing what would have happened if things had been different.

The value of this framing for everyday judgment is that it clarifies what a decision actually requires. Most decisions are questions on the second rung. We want to know what will happen if we do something. Most data, by contrast, sit on the first rung: they tell us what tends to go together when nobody has intervened. The gap between those rungs is exactly where the hormone therapy story, the flight instructor’s error and the chocolate correlation all fall. In each case, an association was read as though it answered a question about intervention.

A useful discipline, then, is to rephrase a causal belief as a prediction about intervention. Not “customers who use this feature renew more often”, but “if we persuade more customers to use this feature, more of them will renew”. The second sentence makes clear what we are assuming, and it invites the obvious question: what else might differ between customers who use the feature and those who do not?
When the demand for proof goes too far

It would be easy to conclude that only randomized experiments can establish causation, and that every other kind of evidence should be distrusted. That conclusion is itself a mistake. In 2003 Gordon Smith and Jill Pell published a satirical article in the
BMJ

reporting a systematic review of randomized controlled trials of parachutes. They found none, and noted with mock seriousness that the effectiveness of parachutes had never been rigorously evaluated. The joke made a serious point. Some causal relationships are so strong, so immediate and so well understood that demanding experimental proof would be absurd, and in some cases unethical.

Many important causal conclusions, including the link between smoking and lung cancer that Bradford Hill helped establish, were reached largely through observational evidence, carefully assembled and tested against alternatives. The lesson is not that observation is useless. It is that observation must be interrogated: by asking what else could produce the association, by looking for evidence that would distinguish those possibilities, and by proportioning confidence to how many alternatives have been ruled out. Chapter 7 takes up that process of comparing explanations directly.
A decision that rests on an association

Consider, as a hypothetical, a company deciding whether to expand a voluntary wellness programme. An internal report shows that employees who joined it took about a third fewer sick days the following year. The finance director wants to make it compulsory. The questions in this chapter turn that single number into a decision that can actually be examined.

The first is whether the relationship could run the other way, or have a common cause. People who already feel healthy and energetic are more likely to sign up for a wellness programme, so the healthier group may have chosen the programme rather than been made healthier by it. The second is how the association was found. If the report’s authors examined twenty outcomes and highlighted the one that looked good, the finding deserves less weight than one predicted in advance. The third is who is missing. If people who dropped out of the programme were excluded from the analysis, the remaining group has been filtered for the most committed. The fourth is whether anyone was selected because they were extreme: if the programme was first offered to staff with the worst sickness records, some improvement would have followed whatever was offered.

The last question matters most for the decision itself: what would happen if we intervened? Making the programme compulsory would put into it exactly the people who had chosen not to join. The association, even if partly causal, says little about them. A small trial, offered to a randomly chosen group, would answer the real question for a modest cost.
The comparison we never see

Every causal claim is, underneath, a claim about something we cannot observe: what would have happened otherwise. The cadet would have regressed without the shouting. The healthy women would have stayed healthy without the hormones. A business that grew after a new strategy might have grown anyway. We see one version of events and must infer the other. This is the causal form of the question Chapter 5 drew from the story of Clever Hans: what would we expect to see if our explanation were wrong?

This is what makes causal reasoning genuinely hard, rather than merely technical. It requires imagination disciplined by evidence: picturing the world in which the supposed cause was absent, and then looking for the best available stand-in for that world, whether a randomized control group, a natural experiment or a carefully chosen comparison. When we skip that step, we are not reasoning about causes at all. We are telling a story about two things that happened together, and trusting the story because it feels like an explanation.

sections.title: The Explanations We Fail to Consider
sections.label: 7. The Explanations We Fail to Consider

runs.text: Alternative hypotheses, competing explanations and the evidence that distinguishes them.

Women about to give birth in Vienna in the 1840s begged not to be admitted to the First Division of the city’s General Hospital. They had good reason. The hospital had two maternity divisions, and women who gave birth in the First Division died of puerperal fever, also called childbed fever, at a far higher rate than women in the Second Division. In 1844, according to the account later given by the philosopher Carl Hempel, 260 of the 3,157 women delivered in the First Division died of the disease, 8.2 per cent, against 2.3 per cent in the Second. The divisions were in the same hospital, in the same city, admitting women on alternate days. The difference was well known, and nobody could explain it.
The young physician Ignaz Semmelweis set out to explain it. Hempel’s
Philosophy of Natural Science

(1966) uses his investigation as its opening example of scientific inquiry, and the reason is clear. Semmelweis did not begin with the right answer. He began with a list of possibilities and worked through them.

One popular explanation blamed “epidemic influences”, vague atmospheric changes spreading through the city. But such influences should have affected both divisions, and women who gave birth on the way to the hospital, in the street, had lower rates than those delivered in the First Division. Another explanation blamed overcrowding, but the Second Division was more crowded. Another pointed to rough examination by medical students, who trained in the First Division; but reducing the number of students and their examinations made no lasting difference. Another blamed fear: a priest bringing the last rites to dying women had to walk through the First Division’s wards, preceded by an attendant ringing a bell. Semmelweis persuaded the priest to take a different route, silently. The deaths continued. Women in the First Division gave birth lying on their backs; in the Second, on their sides. Semmelweis changed the position. Nothing changed.

The decisive clue came in 1847, when his colleague Jakob Kolletschka was cut by a student’s scalpel during an autopsy and died of an illness resembling the one killing the mothers. Semmelweis reasoned that something from the cadavers, which he called cadaveric matter, had entered Kolletschka’s blood, and that physicians and students coming directly from the dissecting room to examine women in labour carried the same material on their hands. The midwives in the Second Division did not perform autopsies. He ordered everyone to wash their hands in a solution of chlorinated lime before examining patients, and mortality in the First Division fell to roughly the level of the Second.

The story is usually told for its ending. I find its middle more instructive. Most of the explanations Semmelweis tested were plausible. Several were widely believed. Each one fitted some of the facts. What made his inquiry valuable was not that he had a brilliant idea but that he kept several ideas alive at once and looked for evidence that would separate them.
The problem of the first good story

The ordinary way of explaining something is to find an explanation that fits and stop. This is efficient. Most of the time the first plausible explanation is good enough, and searching for others would waste effort. Herbert Simon called this kind of strategy satisficing: accepting the first option that meets a threshold rather than searching for the best.

The cost of satisficing in explanation is that a story which fits the facts we have looked at can feel complete even when other stories would fit them equally well. Once we have an explanation, it organizes how we see everything else. New information is read in its light. Evidence that fits is noticed; evidence that does not is explained away or simply not seen.

This effect is not confined to novices. Experts may be especially susceptible, because their experience supplies a familiar explanation quickly and with great confidence. Psychologists call this the Einstellung effect, a German term meaning roughly “set” or “attitude”. In a study published in 2008, Merim Bilalić, Peter McLeod and Fernand Gobet gave expert chess players positions that contained a familiar winning plan and a shorter, less familiar one. Many failed to find the better solution. The players said they were looking for alternatives, but eye-tracking showed that their gaze kept returning to the squares relevant to the solution they had already found. The first idea was steering their attention even while they believed they were searching freely.

In medicine, the corresponding error has a name: premature closure, the failure to keep considering reasonable alternatives once an initial diagnosis has been reached. In a 2005 study of 100 cases of diagnostic error in internal medicine, Mark Graber, Nancy Franklin and Ruthanna Gordon found that cases typically involved several contributing factors, both cognitive and system-related, and premature closure was among the most common of the cognitive ones. The clinicians involved were not ignorant. They had reached an explanation and stopped looking.

The same pattern runs through ordinary life. Suppose, as a hypothetical, that a colleague who usually replies within hours has not answered any of your messages for a week. The first explanation to arrive may be personal: they are annoyed about something you said in last week’s meeting. Once that story is in place, the silence starts to look like evidence for it, and a brief reply when one finally comes looks cold. Yet several other explanations fit the same silence. They may be on leave, ill, overloaded by a deadline, or receiving your messages in a folder they never check. These alternatives are not hard to think of. They simply do not come to mind once a story that feels complete has arrived. Each of them also predicts something checkable, such as an automatic out-of-office reply, or whether other people have heard from them, and checking takes a minute. Chapter 9 looks at the harder case, in which the first explanation is also the one we would prefer to be true.
Multiple working hypotheses
In 1890 the American geologist Thomas Chrowder Chamberlin published a short paper in
Science
called “The Method of Multiple Working Hypotheses”. It remains one of the clearest descriptions of the problem and its remedy.

Chamberlin described three stages in the development of explanation. In the first, a person adopts a single explanation and becomes attached to it, a condition he called the ruling theory. The theory becomes, in his memorable image, something like a favoured child: the investigator looks on it with parental affection, notices the facts that support it, and passes over those that do not. In the second stage, a more careful investigator treats the explanation as a working hypothesis, something to be tested rather than defended. Chamberlin thought this was better but still dangerous, because a single working hypothesis can quietly turn back into a ruling theory.

The third stage was his recommendation: to develop several hypotheses at once, each a serious candidate, and to test them against each other. The advantage is partly logical and partly psychological. Logically, evidence is most informative when it distinguishes between explanations, and that is only possible if more than one explanation is in view. Psychologically, holding several hypotheses divides one’s affection among them, so that no single explanation can command loyalty before the evidence is in.
In 1964 the biophysicist John Platt developed the idea further in a
Science

article called “Strong Inference”. He argued that the fastest-moving fields in science were those that systematically devised alternative hypotheses, designed experiments whose outcomes would exclude one or more of them, carried out the experiments, and then repeated the cycle. The key move, for Platt, was the crucial experiment: a test designed not to confirm an idea but to eliminate a rival.
Evidence that distinguishes

Chapter 5 argued that an observation is evidence for a claim only to the extent that it would be more likely if the claim were true than if it were false. When several explanations are in play, this principle becomes a practical tool.
The intelligence analyst Richards Heuer, in
Psychology of Intelligence Analysis

, published by the CIA’s Center for the Study of Intelligence in 1999, described a method he called Analysis of Competing Hypotheses. The analyst lists all reasonable hypotheses, then lists the significant items of evidence, and asks for each item how consistent it is with each hypothesis. Heuer’s crucial observation was that evidence consistent with every hypothesis has no diagnostic value, however much of it there is and however strongly it seems to support the analyst’s favoured view. The useful evidence is the evidence that is consistent with some hypotheses and inconsistent with others. He also recommended focusing on trying to disprove hypotheses rather than confirm them, because a single strong inconsistency can eliminate an explanation, while any number of consistencies cannot prove one.

Semmelweis’s investigation follows this logic closely. The observation that more women died in the First Division was consistent with almost every hypothesis on his list, and so could not choose between them. The observation that women who gave birth in the street fared better was inconsistent with the epidemic hypothesis. The unchanged death rate after the priest changed his route was inconsistent with the fear hypothesis. Each test was designed so that one explanation predicted a change and the others did not.

The same logic applies in a hypothetical business case. Suppose a company’s sales have fallen in one region. Possible explanations include a new competitor, a change in the regional sales team, a pricing change, a shift in customer needs and a problem with distribution. The fall in sales is consistent with all of them and so cannot distinguish them. But each explanation predicts different patterns in other data. A competitor should affect products that compete directly more than others. A sales-team change should show up in the timing of the decline and in the accounts that team managed. A distribution problem should show in delivery times and stock levels. Listing what each explanation predicts, and then looking for the patterns that would separate them, can turn a vague argument into a short investigation.
When a whole institution forgets the alternatives
Failing to consider alternatives is not only an individual error. Organizations can build it in.

In March 2005, the Commission on the Intelligence Capabilities of the United States Regarding Weapons of Mass Destruction, usually known by the names of its co-chairs as the Robb-Silberman Commission, reported on the intelligence assessments that preceded the 2003 invasion of Iraq. Its conclusion was that the intelligence community had been wrong in almost all of its pre-war judgments about Iraq’s weapons programmes. The commission found many causes, including thin and unreliable sources. But it attributed the failure in large part to analytical shortcomings: analysts had been too attached to their assumptions about the regime’s intentions, and had been insufficiently rigorous in questioning those assumptions and in considering alternatives. The hypothesis that Iraq had weapons programmes was, the commission acknowledged, reasonable given the regime’s past behaviour. The failure lay in allowing a reasonable hypothesis to harden into a conclusion that new evidence could not move.

The point I take from this case is not about any particular agency. It is that the alternative which turned out to be correct, that the regime had largely abandoned its programmes but behaved as though it had not, was available. It was not exotic or unthinkable. It was simply not developed with the same seriousness as the favoured hypothesis, and so the evidence that might have supported it was never organized in its favour. An alternative that nobody is assigned to take seriously tends to lose by default.
Generating alternatives deliberately
If the first good story tends to crowd out others, alternatives must be generated on purpose. A few methods help.
Ask what else would produce the same observations.
For any explanation, ask what other process could have led to exactly what was seen. This is the most direct method, and the one most often skipped because the first explanation feels sufficient.
Consider the opposite.

In a 1984 study, Charles Lord, Mark Lepper and Elizabeth Preston found that asking people to consider whether they would have evaluated evidence the same way if it had pointed in the opposite direction reduced the bias in their evaluations more effectively than simply asking them to be fair and unbiased. Instructions to be objective are weak. A concrete mental operation, imagining the reverse case, is stronger.
Assign the alternatives to people.

In groups, an explanation without an advocate tends to lose. Assigning someone to develop the strongest version of each serious alternative, and to look for evidence in its favour, gives alternatives a fair hearing. The practice is sometimes called red-teaming. It works best when the role is respected rather than treated as an obstacle, and when the people assigned are allowed to change the conclusion rather than merely decorate it with objections.
Widen the categories.

Alternatives often come from categories of explanation that were not considered at all. If every hypothesis on the list is about people, add some about systems. If every hypothesis is about the internal causes of a problem, add some about external ones. If every hypothesis assumes the data are accurate, add one in which they are not.
Include the boring explanations.

Some of the most important alternatives are mundane: measurement error, chance, a change in how something was recorded, a single unusual case. They are easy to overlook precisely because they are uninteresting, and they explain a surprising share of puzzling results.
Not every alternative deserves equal weight

There is a risk in all of this that should be named. Treating every conceivable alternative as a serious possibility is not open-mindedness. It is a failure to use what we know. Some explanations are much more plausible than others from the start, and evidence that would slightly favour an implausible explanation is rarely enough to overturn a well-supported one. The aim is not to generate as many alternatives as possible, but to make sure that the plausible ones have been considered and that the evidence has been asked to choose between them.

The practical test is whether the alternatives under consideration are ones that a knowledgeable, fair-minded person might actually hold. A list padded with far-fetched possibilities can be a way of appearing thorough while protecting the favoured explanation, since the alternatives are easy to dismiss. A shorter list of serious rivals is more demanding and more useful.
Being right is not enough

Semmelweis’s story has a sad epilogue. His findings were largely rejected by the medical establishment of his time. Historians have offered several reasons: the absence of a germ theory to explain why handwashing worked, professional resistance to the suggestion that doctors themselves were carrying disease, and Semmelweis’s own reluctance to publish his findings fully until many years later, combined with an often combative manner. He died in 1865. Within a few decades, the work of Louis Pasteur, Robert Koch and Joseph Lister had established the role of microorganisms in infection, and Semmelweis came to be celebrated.

I mention this not to add a moral about persistence but because it reveals an unresolved tension in the discipline this chapter describes. Considering alternative explanations is uncomfortable, and it is socially costly. It slows decisions, questions the competence of those who reached the first explanation, and often implicates the people doing the explaining. Semmelweis’s correct explanation implied that his colleagues had been killing their patients. The Robb-Silberman Commission’s findings implied that experienced analysts had let a reasonable assumption become a fixed belief. No method for generating and testing alternatives will work if the people who must use it pay a price for the answers it gives.

The method of multiple working hypotheses is therefore not only an intellectual technique. It is also a social arrangement, one that requires organizations, teams and families to make it safe to say “there might be another explanation” and to take that statement seriously before the evidence forces them to. Whether that arrangement exists in any particular place is a question the technique itself cannot answer.

sections.title: The Numbers That Mislead Us
sections.label: 8. The Numbers That Mislead Us

runs.text: Rates, denominators, averages, percentages, comparisons and missing context.

Imagine, as a hypothetical, a woman in her forties who has a routine screening mammogram. The result is positive. She asks her doctor what this means. The doctor knows three numbers about this screening programme. About 1 per cent of women in her age group who are screened have breast cancer. If a woman has breast cancer, the test will detect it about 80 per cent of the time. If she does not, the test will still come back positive about 9.6 per cent of the time. Given those numbers, how likely is it that this woman actually has cancer?

These are close to the figures used in a well-known problem studied by the physician David Eddy in the early 1980s. As the psychologist Gerd Gigerenzer has described it, Eddy reported that 95 of 100 physicians he asked estimated the probability at around 75 per cent. The correct answer, given those numbers, is under 8 per cent. In later studies, Gigerenzer and his colleague Ulrich Hoffrage found that physicians’ estimates for similar problems ranged widely, from as low as 1 per cent to as high as 90 per cent.

The numbers in the problem are accurate, and there is nothing tricky about them. Yet most people, including most of the professionals who use such tests, misread them. The reason is not a lack of intelligence or training. It is that the numbers are presented in a form that hides the most important fact, which is how few women in the screened group have cancer in the first place.

The same information can be restated in a different form. Picture 1,000 women in this age group being screened. About 10 of them have breast cancer. Of those 10, about 8 will test positive. Of the 990 who do not have cancer, about 95 will also test positive. So roughly 103 women will receive a positive result, and only about 8 of them have cancer. Eight out of 103 is a little under 8 per cent.
Put this way, the answer is almost obvious. In a 1995 paper in
Psychological Review

, Gigerenzer and Hoffrage showed that presenting this kind of problem in what they called natural frequencies, counts of people rather than conditional probabilities, substantially improved people’s reasoning. The underlying mathematics had not changed. Only the representation had.

This chapter is about numbers that are correct and still mislead. The problem is rarely the arithmetic. It is that every number comes with a shape: a denominator, a comparison, a reference group, a way of being expressed. Those choices can make accurate information point in an inaccurate direction.
Forgetting the base rate

The mammography problem is an example of what psychologists call base-rate neglect. The base rate is how common something is before we have any specific information: how many screened women have cancer, how many job applicants turn out to be excellent, how many transactions are fraudulent. When new information arrives, such as a test result, a strong interview or an alert from a fraud system, it is natural to focus on how well that information distinguishes the cases we care about and to forget how rare those cases were to begin with.

The consequence is predictable. When the thing being looked for is rare, even a fairly accurate test will produce many more false alarms than true detections, simply because there are so many more cases in which it can raise a false alarm. A fraud-detection system that correctly flags 99 per cent of fraudulent transactions and wrongly flags only 1 per cent of legitimate ones sounds excellent. But if only one transaction in 10,000 is fraudulent, then for every genuine fraud it catches it will flag roughly a hundred legitimate transactions. The people reviewing its alerts will spend most of their time on innocent customers, and if they do not understand why, they may come to distrust a system that is working exactly as designed.

The same arithmetic explains a familiar habit. When a car alarm sounds in a street, few passers-by look round expecting to see a thief. Alarms are designed to sound when a car is broken into, but break-ins are rare, while bumps, gusts of wind and heavy lorries passing are common, so most of the alarms anyone hears are false. People who ignore them are not reasoning carelessly. Without ever naming it, they have taken the base rate into account. The difficulty arises in less familiar settings, such as a medical test or a fraud alert, where we have no such everyday experience of how often an alarm turns out to be false.

The practical remedy is to translate. When a probability depends on a base rate, rewrite it as counts of people or cases out of a round number, such as 1,000 or 10,000, and follow them through. It takes a minute, and it makes the size of the error visible before anyone acts on it.
Relative and absolute risk

In October 1995, the United Kingdom’s Committee on Safety of Medicines warned that certain newer contraceptive pills, the so-called third-generation pills, were associated with about twice the risk of venous thromboembolism, a type of blood clot, compared with older pills. The warning was widely reported, and many women stopped taking the pill.
What the phrase “twice the risk” did not convey was how small the risk was to begin with. Figures from the British National Formulary, cited in a 2001
BMJ

editorial by the obstetrician J. O. Drife, put the annual risk of deep venous thrombosis among young women without other risk factors at about 5 per 100,000. For users of older pills it was about 15 per 100,000, and for users of the newer ones about 25. A doubling of a small number is still a small number. In 2011 Emilia Del Bono, Marco Francesconi and Nicky Best published an economic analysis of the scare as a University of Essex discussion paper. Using a regression discontinuity design, they estimated that conception rates rose by about 7 per cent and abortion rates by about 9 per cent after the warning. That pattern is consistent with many women abandoning contraception without switching to an alternative. The scientific question of how much greater the risk of the newer pills really is has been debated since, with different studies reaching different estimates.

The case illustrates the difference between relative risk, which says how much a risk changes, and absolute risk, which says how large it is. Both are accurate descriptions of the same facts. But they answer different questions, and the question a person actually needs answered when making a decision is usually about absolute risk: how likely is this to happen to me, and how does that compare with the risks of the alternatives? A doubling of a one-in-a-million risk and a doubling of a one-in-ten risk are described by the same phrase and mean entirely different things.
Whenever a risk is described as a percentage change, it is worth asking: a change from what to what? If the answer is not given, the number cannot yet be interpreted.
Percentages and percentage points

A related confusion arises between percentage changes and percentage-point changes. If the share of customers who renew a subscription rises from 10 per cent to 15 per cent, that is an increase of 5 percentage points. It is also an increase of 50 per cent. Both descriptions are correct. The first sounds modest, the second dramatic, and a writer can choose whichever suits the point they want to make.

Small starting numbers make this especially misleading. A product line that grew from two sales to six has grown by 200 per cent. A crime category that went from one case to three has tripled. These are true statements about tiny quantities, and they can be presented in ways that make them sound like trends. Percentage changes from small bases should always be read alongside the actual counts. The error has real costs. A hypothetical manager who reads a product’s growth from two sales to six as “200 per cent growth” and hires staff to support the trend has committed salaries on the strength of four extra sales.
How the denominator disappears

In a study published in 1997, the psychologist Kimihiko Yamagishi asked people to rate the riskiness of various causes of death described in different ways. Participants rated cancer as more dangerous when it was described as killing 1,286 out of 10,000 people than when it was described as killing 24.14 out of 100. The first figure is about 13 per cent; the second is about 24 per cent. People responded to the size of the numerator, 1,286 people, and paid too little attention to the denominator.

This tendency, sometimes called ratio bias or denominator neglect, is easy to exploit. A large absolute number of incidents can be made to sound alarming without mentioning that it occurred in an enormous population. A small number can be made to sound reassuring without mentioning that it occurred in a tiny one. Neither the count nor the rate alone is sufficient. Understanding requires both, and the comparison that matters is usually between rates.
What an average hides
Averages compress many numbers into one, and in doing so they discard information that is sometimes the most important thing about the data.

The most familiar example is the difference between the mean and the median. Consider a hypothetical company with ten employees each earning a modest salary and an owner who pays herself many times as much. The mean salary, the total divided by eleven, may be several times what any of the ten employees earns. The median, the salary of the person in the middle, describes the typical employee far better. When a distribution is skewed, as incomes, house prices, company sizes and many other quantities are, the mean can describe almost nobody.

Averages also hide variation. Two treatments may produce the same average improvement, one by helping everyone a little and the other by helping some people a lot and harming others. Two investment funds may have the same average return with very different chances of a catastrophic year. Two teams may have the same average delivery time, with one consistently on schedule and the other alternating between early and very late. The question “what is the average?” should usually be followed by “how much does it vary, and what do the extremes look like?”
When the whole contradicts the parts

In the autumn of 1973, the graduate division of the University of California, Berkeley, received applications from 8,442 men and 4,321 women. About 44 per cent of the men were admitted and about 35 per cent of the women. The gap was large enough to raise concern about discrimination, and the statistician Peter Bickel, with Eugene Hammel and J. W. O’Connell, examined the data. Their analysis, published in
Science
in 1975, found that when admissions were looked at department by department, most departments showed no significant bias, and the overall pattern, if anything, slightly favoured women.

The apparent contradiction had a straightforward cause. Women had applied in larger proportions to departments that were more competitive and admitted a smaller share of all applicants, whatever their sex. Men had applied in larger proportions to departments that admitted a larger share. When all the departments were pooled, the difference in where people applied produced a difference in overall admission rates that did not reflect how any individual department treated applicants.

This pattern, in which a relationship in combined data reverses or disappears when the data are separated into groups, is known as Simpson’s paradox, after the statistician Edward Simpson, who described it in 1951. It is not a curiosity. It can arise whenever groups of different sizes or compositions are pooled: hospitals that treat patients of different severity, schools that serve students from different backgrounds, sales regions with different product mixes. None of this means that pooled data are always misleading or that subgroup data are always correct. The Berkeley analysis itself raised a further question, about why women were applying in greater numbers to the more competitive fields, which concerns a different stage of the process. What it does mean is that a comparison between totals should not be trusted until we know whether the groups being compared differ in composition in ways that affect the outcome.
The data we never see

Some numbers mislead because of what has been left out of them before anyone looks. During the Second World War, the statistician Abraham Wald, working with the Statistical Research Group at Columbia University, developed methods for estimating aircraft vulnerability from the damage observed on planes that returned from missions. The essential insight was that the returning planes were a biased sample. Damage that brought a plane down was, by definition, rarely seen on the planes available for inspection. Areas that showed little damage on survivors might be exactly the areas where hits were most dangerous.

The popular version of this story, often illustrated with a diagram of a bomber covered in red dots, has been simplified and embellished over the years. Wald’s actual memoranda, later reprinted by the Center for Naval Analyses in 1980, are technical work on estimating survival probabilities. But the principle the story illustrates, now usually called survivorship bias, is sound and widely applicable. Studies of successful companies, long-lived investment funds, best-selling authors or people who reached the top of a profession examine only those who survived some filter. Whatever they have in common may also be common among those who failed and are no longer visible. Without looking at the failures, it is impossible to know whether a shared trait contributed to success or was simply widespread. Survivorship bias is a close relative of the selection effect described in Chapter 6: in both, the filter that decided which cases we see has shaped the pattern we find in them.
When a number decides a life

The most consequential misuses of numbers combine several of these problems at once. In 1999 the English solicitor Sally Clark was convicted of murdering her two infant sons, who had died suddenly some fourteen months apart. A prominent paediatrician testified that, for a family like hers, the chance of a single sudden infant death was about 1 in 8,543, and that the chance of two such deaths was therefore about 1 in 73 million, obtained by multiplying the first figure by itself.

The Royal Statistical Society issued a statement in 2001 and wrote to the Lord Chancellor in 2002 to say that the calculation had no statistical basis. Multiplying the probabilities assumed that the two deaths were independent events, which would be true only if nothing about a family, such as genetic or environmental factors, affected the risk of both. There was good reason to think such factors existed. A second, equally serious error lay in how the figure could be understood. Even a correct estimate of the probability of two natural deaths is not the probability that the mother is innocent. That requires comparing the probability of two natural deaths with the probability of two murders, both of which are extremely rare. Treating the rarity of the innocent explanation as if it were the probability of innocence is a reasoning error common enough to have a name: the prosecutor’s fallacy.

Clark’s convictions were overturned on a second appeal in January 2003, after it emerged that medical evidence relevant to one of the deaths had not been disclosed. The statistical evidence was not the only issue in the case. But it shows how a number that sounds precise and authoritative can carry assumptions that, once stated, are clearly unjustified, and how a figure can answer a different question from the one being decided.
Questions to ask of any number
Numbers deserve neither automatic trust nor automatic suspicion. They deserve a few questions.
Out of how many?
Every count needs a denominator, and every rate needs to say what it is a rate of.
Compared with what?
A number on its own is rarely informative. The relevant comparison might be the same measure at an earlier time, in a different group or under an alternative course of action.
How common was this to begin with?
When a test or signal is involved, the base rate often matters more than the test’s accuracy.
Relative or absolute?
If a change is described as a percentage, find out what it is a percentage of.
What does the average hide?
Ask about the median, the spread and the extremes.
Who is in the data, and who is missing?
Ask whether the cases were filtered before they were counted, and whether groups of different composition have been pooled.
What assumptions produced this figure?
Especially for estimates and projections, the assumptions are often more important than the arithmetic.
Accurate is not the same as informative

A number can be accurate, in the sense that it correctly reports what was measured, without being informative about the question we need answered. The 9.6 per cent false-positive rate, the doubled risk of thrombosis, the 44 and 35 per cent admission rates and the 1 in 73 million figure all reported something real or claimed to. Each, read without its context, pointed towards a mistaken conclusion.

Numbers have a particular authority because they look like facts with the interpretation removed. In practice, every number arrives with interpretation built in: in its denominator, its comparison, its choice of unit and its selection of what to count. Reading numbers well mostly means making those choices visible, and then asking whether they match the question we are actually trying to answer.

That suggests a test worth applying before any number is allowed to settle a decision. Can you say what it is out of, what it is being compared with, and who is missing from it? If you cannot answer all three, you have not yet read the number. You have only seen it.

sections.title: The Human Mind and Its Blind Spots
sections.label: Part III — The Human Mind and Its Blind Spots

runs.text: Parts I and II treated reasoning as though it happened in calm conditions, with time to examine assumptions and compare explanations. Part III turns to the forces that make that calm rare.

Chapter 9 asks why people who examine evidence carefully can still reach the conclusions they started with, and finds the answer in uneven scrutiny rather than in ignoring evidence. If our own scrutiny is uneven, we need others to check us, which raises the question of Chapter 10: whom should we trust, and on what grounds? Chapter 11 asks what happens to all of this when there is no time, when emotion runs high or when the group has already decided. Chapter 12 asks the hardest question of the part: when the evidence does tell us we were wrong, what does it take to change our minds, and when should we not?

What connects these chapters is that the obstacles they describe are not failures of intelligence. They are features of how people think among other people, under pressure, with commitments and identities at stake. That is why the remedies they suggest are as often social and structural as they are individual. All of them, however, assume a world in which claims come from people, and in which producing a convincing claim costs effort. Part IV asks what happens when that assumption no longer holds.

sections.title: Why We Prefer Evidence That Agrees With Us
sections.label: 9. Why We Prefer Evidence That Agrees With Us

runs.text: Confirmation bias, motivated reasoning and selective interpretation.

Two people can read the same report and come away more certain of opposite conclusions. This is one of the more unsettling facts about human reasoning, because it means that more information does not reliably bring people closer together. Sometimes it pushes them apart.

In a study published in 1979, Charles Lord, Lee Ross and Mark Lepper recruited students who held strong views on capital punishment, some in favour and some opposed. Each student read descriptions of two studies on whether the death penalty deters crime. One study appeared to support deterrence; the other appeared to undermine it. The studies were fictitious, and their designs were balanced so that each side had one study in its favour and one against. The evidence, taken as a whole, was mixed.

The students did not respond to it as mixed. Supporters of capital punishment judged the study that favoured deterrence to be more convincing and better conducted, and found methodological flaws in the other. Opponents did the reverse. Both groups reported that their views had become stronger after reading the evidence. The same pair of studies left each side more convinced that it had been right. Lord, Ross and Lepper called the pattern biased assimilation, and the resulting divergence attitude polarization.

The participants were a small group of American university students, and later research has found the biased evaluation of evidence more consistently than the strengthening of attitudes, a point this chapter returns to below. What makes this study so instructive is that the students were not ignoring evidence. They read both studies carefully and evaluated them critically. The bias lay in where their critical attention went. Each group scrutinized the study it disliked and accepted the study it liked. That asymmetry, rather than any outright refusal to look, is the subject of this chapter.
Two different problems with one name
The phrase “confirmation bias” is used for several things, and it helps to separate two of them.

The first is a cognitive tendency that operates even when we have no stake in the answer. In 1960 the psychologist Peter Wason gave people a sequence of three numbers, 2, 4, 6, and told them it followed a rule he had in mind. Their task was to discover the rule by proposing other sequences; he would say whether each one fitted. Most people formed a hypothesis quickly, such as “even numbers increasing by two”, and then proposed sequences that fitted their hypothesis, such as 8, 10, 12. Each received a yes, and they announced their rule with confidence. The actual rule was simply “any three increasing numbers”. People rarely discovered it, because they rarely proposed a sequence that their own hypothesis predicted would fail, such as 1, 2, 3 or 3, 2, 1. They tested their idea only in ways that could confirm it.

Later work by Joshua Klayman and Young-Won Ha, published in 1987, argued that this positive test strategy is not always irrational. In many real situations, testing cases where you expect something to happen is an efficient way to learn. The problem arises in a specific kind of situation, the kind Wason designed, where the true rule is broader than the hypothesis, so that confirmations keep arriving even though the hypothesis is wrong. The lesson is not that confirming tests are useless but that they cannot reveal an error of over-specificity. Only a test that might fail can do that.
The second problem is different in kind. It concerns conclusions we want to reach. The psychologist Ziva Kunda, in an influential 1990 review in
Psychological Bulletin

, described motivated reasoning: the tendency for people’s goals to influence how they search for, evaluate and interpret information. Kunda’s important observation was that motivated reasoning is constrained. People do not simply believe whatever they like. They try to reach their preferred conclusion while maintaining an illusion of objectivity, and they can do so only to the extent that they can construct a justification a reasonable person might accept. The bias works through the reasoning, not around it.
Chapter 2 examined how beliefs originate. This chapter is about what happens afterwards, when a belief we already hold, or a conclusion we would like to reach, shapes how new evidence is received.
Different standards for welcome and unwelcome evidence
The psychologist Thomas Gilovich, in
How We Know What Isn’t So

(1991), described the asymmetry with a useful pair of questions. When we encounter evidence for something we want to believe, we tend to ask, in effect, “Can I believe this?” We look for some reason to accept it, and usually we find one. When we encounter evidence for something we do not want to believe, we ask “Must I believe this?” We look for some reason to reject it, and usually we find one of those too. Both questions feel like critical thinking. The difference lies in which side bears the burden of proof.

Peter Ditto and David Lopez demonstrated this asymmetry experimentally in a study published in 1992. Participants took what they were told was a medical test for an enzyme deficiency, using a strip of paper that would change colour in contact with saliva. Some were told that a colour change indicated a healthy result; others were told it indicated a problem. In fact the strip never changed colour. Participants who believed that no change meant bad news waited longer before deciding the test was complete, were more likely to retest, and rated the test as less accurate. Those who believed no change was good news accepted the result readily. The evidence was identical. The scrutiny was not. The study concerned a medical test, but my reading is that it describes something most of us do at work every week. When a project we proposed runs late, we look for the special circumstances; when a rival’s project runs late, we look for the flaw in the plan. The same asymmetry operates at home. In a disagreement with a partner about who said what, each person tends to search their memory carefully for the remarks that support their own account and to treat the other person’s recollection as the one that needs checking.

This pattern, a higher evidential bar for unwelcome conclusions, appears across many domains. It shows up in how managers evaluate projects they championed, how investors read news about stocks they own, how scientists assess studies that challenge their theories, and how people interpret the behaviour of others they already like or dislike. Its effect is gradual but powerful. If one set of conclusions faces a higher standard than another, then over time beliefs will drift towards the favoured set, even if every individual judgment seems careful.
Where selection happens
The preference for agreeable evidence can enter reasoning at several points, each of which is easier to overlook than the last.
What we look for.

We tend to search for information in places where we expect to find support, and we tend to ask questions framed in ways that invite agreement. Chapter 4 discussed how questions shape answers. Here the point is that the motive behind the question shapes the question.
What we notice.

In a busy information environment, attention is selective by necessity. Information that fits an existing belief is easier to process and more likely to register. Information that does not fit is more easily overlooked, especially when it is ambiguous.
How hard we examine it.

As the Lord, Ross and Lepper study showed, the most consequential selection may be in scrutiny. Disagreeable evidence is examined closely enough that flaws are found, as flaws can usually be found in any study or report. Agreeable evidence passes with lighter inspection.
How we interpret it.

Ambiguous information can usually be read more than one way. A colleague’s silence in a meeting can be read as disagreement, distraction or quiet assent. A dip in sales can be read as noise or as a trend. Existing beliefs supply the default reading.
What we remember.

Over time, memory tends to retain what fitted the story and lose what did not. Months later, the record of evidence we carry in our heads may be considerably more one-sided than the evidence we actually encountered.
Intelligence is not a cure
It would be reassuring if more skilled reasoners were less susceptible to these effects. The evidence suggests that, in some circumstances, the opposite can be true.
In a study published in
Behavioural Public Policy

in 2017, Dan Kahan, Ellen Peters, Erica Cantrell Dawson and Paul Slovic gave participants a difficult problem that required interpreting the results of a study presented in a table. For some participants the study concerned a new skin cream. For others the same numbers described the effects of a ban on carrying concealed handguns, a politically charged topic in the United States. When the problem concerned skin cream, participants with higher numeracy, meaning greater skill and comfort with quantitative information, got the right answer more often, as expected. When the problem concerned gun control, responses became polarized along political lines, and the polarization did not shrink among the most numerate participants. It grew. The authors interpreted this as evidence that more numerate people used their quantitative skill selectively, applying it more effectively when it led to a conclusion consistent with their political outlook.

This finding has a sobering implication. Skill at reasoning is a tool, and a tool can be used to reach a destination chosen in advance. The person best equipped to find the flaw in an unwelcome study is also best equipped to overlook the flaw in a welcome one. Being clever helps only if the cleverness is applied evenly.
A note of caution about the research itself

It is easy to overstate how resistant people are to evidence, and a book about examining beliefs should be careful not to do so. In 2010 the political scientists Brendan Nyhan and Jason Reifler published an influential paper reporting that factual corrections of political misperceptions could sometimes make people hold the misperception more strongly, an effect they called backfire. The idea spread widely, in part because it seemed to capture something about political life.
Later research has not supported the idea that backfire is common. In a paper published in
Political Behavior

in 2019, Thomas Wood and Ethan Porter reported five experiments with more than 10,100 participants, testing corrections on 52 issues where backfire might be expected.
