They found no corrections that reliably triggered it. By and large, people moved at least somewhat towards accurate information, even when it challenged their political commitments. Nyhan himself reviewed this literature in 2021 and concluded that corrections are typically at least somewhat effective. The more serious problem, he argued, is that their effects often fade or are overwhelmed by the cues people keep receiving from their own side.

The more accurate picture, then, is not that people reject evidence that contradicts their beliefs. It is that they update less than they should, scrutinize unequally, and interpret ambiguity in their own favour. These are quieter effects than backfire, but they operate constantly, which may make them more important.
When asymmetric scrutiny is justified
There is a complication that deserves attention, because it is often missed in discussions of confirmation bias. Not all asymmetric scrutiny is a bias.

If I have strong, well-founded reasons to believe something, and a single new study contradicts it, it is reasonable for me to examine that study more carefully than I would examine one that agreed with everything else I know. A surprising result is more likely than an unsurprising one to contain an error, simply because it disagrees with a large body of prior evidence. Chapter 5 noted that how much evidence a claim requires depends on how plausible it was to begin with. Scrutinizing surprising evidence more closely is consistent with that principle, not a violation of it.
The difference between legitimate and illegitimate asymmetry lies in its source. Asymmetric scrutiny based on how
plausible
a conclusion is, given everything else we know, is sound reasoning. Asymmetric scrutiny based on how
desirable

a conclusion is, given what we want, is motivated reasoning. In practice the two are hard to separate, because what we want to believe often feels plausible to us. But the distinction suggests a useful test. If I find myself scrutinizing a piece of evidence closely, I can ask whether I would apply the same scrutiny to equally strong evidence pointing in the direction I prefer. If not, plausibility is probably not what is driving my scepticism.
Why reasoning might work this way
The cognitive scientists Hugo Mercier and Dan Sperber have proposed an explanation for these patterns that changes how we might respond to them. In a 2011 article in
Behavioral and Brain Sciences
and later in
The Enigma of Reason

(2017), they argued that human reasoning did not evolve primarily to help individuals reach true beliefs on their own. It evolved to help people produce arguments to persuade others and to evaluate the arguments others present. On this view, the tendency to generate reasons for one’s own side is not a malfunction. It is what a system designed for argument would be expected to do.

Mercier and Sperber also emphasized a hopeful corollary. People tend to be much better at spotting weaknesses in others’ arguments than in their own. That suggests that the remedy for myside reasoning is often social rather than individual. A group in which people with different views genuinely examine each other’s arguments can reason better than any of its members alone, provided the group is not so homogeneous that everyone’s arguments point the same way, and provided disagreement is welcomed rather than punished.

The theory is debated, and I do not want to present it as settled. But its practical implication seems sound whether or not the evolutionary account is correct. If we are poor judges of our own reasoning and good judges of other people’s, then one of the most effective things we can do is to expose our reasoning to people who will judge it, and listen when they do.
Practices that help
No technique eliminates the preference for agreeable evidence. Some practices reduce its effects.
Apply the symmetry test.

Before rejecting a piece of evidence because of a flaw, ask whether you would have rejected it if it had supported your view. Before accepting a piece of evidence, ask whether you would have accepted it if it had challenged your view. This is the most direct check on selective scrutiny.
Decide on standards before seeing results.

Scientists increasingly use pre-registration, committing in advance to how a study will be analysed and what will count as support for a hypothesis. The same idea applies to everyday decisions. Deciding, before a pilot project starts, what results would count as success makes it much harder to reinterpret disappointing results as encouraging ones afterwards.
Seek out the strongest version of the opposing case.

Not the weakest version, which is easy to dismiss and often the one most readily available, but the version that a thoughtful advocate would make. If you cannot state the opposing view in a way its holders would recognize as fair, you are not yet in a position to reject it.
Notice when a belief has become part of identity.

Kahan’s research suggests that motivated reasoning is strongest when beliefs signal membership in a group we care about. When a question starts to feel like a question about who we are, rather than about what is true, it helps to recognize that the stakes have changed and that our reasoning is likely to be affected.
Let others check your reasoning.

Share your conclusions and the evidence for them with people who are likely to disagree, and treat their objections as information rather than opposition. This is uncomfortable, which is a sign that it is doing something.
The bias is in how hard we look

The students in the capital punishment study did not refuse to look at the evidence. They looked at all of it, carefully. What differed was how hard they looked at each piece, and in which direction their scepticism pointed. That is why the preference for agreeable evidence is so difficult to detect from the inside. It does not feel like bias. It feels like being rigorous about the evidence that deserves rigour.

The practical consequence is that the feeling of having been careful is not a reliable sign of having been fair. A person can examine evidence with great diligence and still reach a conclusion that was set before the examination began. What protects against this is not more effort but more even effort: the discipline of asking, each time we find a reason to doubt something, whether we would have looked for that reason if the evidence had told us what we wanted to hear.

sections.title: Whom Should We Trust?
sections.label: 10. Whom Should We Trust?

runs.text: Expertise, authority, credibility, incentives and independent verification.

There is a contradiction at the centre of how anyone comes to know anything. On one hand, we cannot avoid trusting others. Nobody can personally verify the safety of the medicines they take, the structural soundness of the buildings they enter, the history they were taught or the science behind the weather forecast. A person who insisted on checking everything for themselves would end up knowing very little. On the other hand, trust is where a great many errors enter our thinking. Many of the mistaken beliefs described in this book arrived through someone we trusted: a respected physician, a confident colleague, a prestigious journal, a familiar voice.
The philosopher John Hardwig addressed the first half of this contradiction directly in a 1985 paper in the
Journal of Philosophy

titled “Epistemic Dependence”. He argued that a layperson who defers to a genuine expert is often behaving more rationally than one who insists on thinking the matter through alone, because the expert has evidence and training the layperson lacks. Rationality, on this view, sometimes consists precisely in recognizing that someone else is better placed to judge. Hardwig’s argument removes any easy assumption that independent thinking means believing only what one has checked. In a complex society, independent thinking must include thinking well about whom to rely on.
This chapter is about that second-order skill. It does not ask whether to trust others, since we have no choice. It asks how to decide whom to trust, about what, and how much.
What expert track records show
It would simplify matters if expertise were a reliable guarantee of good judgment. The evidence is mixed in an instructive way.

Between the mid-1980s and 2003, the psychologist Philip Tetlock asked 284 people who made their living commenting on or advising about political and economic trends to make forecasts about future events, eventually collecting around 28,000 predictions. He reported the results in
Expert Political Judgment

(2005). On many long-range questions, the average expert did only slightly better than simple rules of thumb or chance. Experts who were confident in a single overarching theory, whom Tetlock called hedgehogs after an old line from the Greek poet Archilochus popularized by Isaiah Berlin, tended to do worse than those who drew on many ideas and adjusted readily, whom he called foxes. And experts with prominent media profiles tended to be somewhat less accurate than their less visible colleagues.

It would be a mistake to conclude from Tetlock’s work that expertise is worthless. His experts were forecasting complex political events years ahead, a task in which the world provides little regularity and slow, ambiguous feedback. In other domains the picture is very different. In 2009 Daniel Kahneman and the psychologist Gary Klein, who had long disagreed about the value of expert intuition, published a joint article in
American Psychologist

setting out the conditions under which they agreed it could be trusted. Expert judgment tends to be reliable, they argued, when the environment is regular enough to be predictable and when practitioners have had extensive practice with timely, clear feedback on their judgments. Firefighters, experienced nurses and chess players often meet these conditions. Long-range political and economic forecasters usually do not.

This gives the first and most useful question to ask of any expert: does this person work in a domain where expertise can actually develop? Credentials and experience indicate that someone has spent time in a field. They do not by themselves indicate that the field rewards accurate judgment with clear feedback.
Signals of credibility and signals of reliability

When we decide whom to trust, we usually rely on cues: how confident someone sounds, how fluently they speak, what titles they hold, how often we have seen them, and whether they say things that fit with what we already believe. These are signals of credibility. They make a source seem trustworthy. Some of them are weakly related to reliability. Some are unrelated or even inversely related.

Confidence is a striking example. People tend to trust confident advisers more than hesitant ones, and research on advice-taking suggests that this preference persists even when confidence is a poor predictor of accuracy. Tetlock’s finding that media prominence went with lower accuracy may partly reflect the same pattern: confident, simple predictions make better television than hedged, complicated ones, so the forecasters most visible to the public may be selected for the very trait that makes them less reliable. Chapter 13 returns to this problem in a newer form, where the confident voice belongs to a machine.

Reliability is harder to observe, but it has its own signals. A reliable source tends to have a record of being right on questions like this one, and of saying how confident it is in a way that matches how often it turns out to be right. It works in a domain where its methods have been tested. It explains its reasoning and its evidence, so that others can check them. It acknowledges uncertainty and limits. It has no strong incentive to reach one particular answer, or discloses the incentives it has. And other qualified sources, working independently, reach similar conclusions.
The gap between these two sets of signals is where many errors of trust occur. We are drawn to credibility and need reliability, and the two are only loosely connected.
A framework from philosophy

The philosopher Alvin Goldman, in a 2001 paper titled “Experts: Which Ones Should You Trust?”, considered the problem of a non-expert faced with two apparent experts who disagree. He identified five kinds of evidence a novice can use without becoming an expert. His list remains a useful practical guide.
The first is the
arguments

each expert offers. A non-expert often cannot evaluate the technical content, but can sometimes notice whether one expert responds directly to the other’s evidence while the other evades it, or whether one can explain why the other’s view seems persuasive and where it goes wrong.
The second is the
agreement of other experts

. A view shared by many qualified people is, other things equal, more likely to be correct. But Goldman stressed that numbers count only to the extent that the agreeing experts reached their views independently. If many experts believe something because they all deferred to one influential figure, their agreement is not much more informative than that figure’s view alone. This is the problem of echoes, discussed in Chapter 5, in a different setting.
The third is
appraisals by meta-experts
: credentials, peer review, professional standing. These carry information, but they measure what institutions recognize, which is not always the same as accuracy on a particular question.
The fourth is
evidence of interests and biases
: whether an expert stands to gain from a particular conclusion, or has a strong prior commitment to it.
The fifth, and in Goldman’s view the most promising, is
track record
: how often the expert has been right in the past on questions where the answer later became clear.
These five sources rarely settle a question on their own. Together, they turn an impression of whom to trust into something closer to an assessment.
Incentives
Incentives deserve particular attention because they are easy to overlook and powerful in effect.
In 2016 Cristin Kearns, Laura Schmidt and Stanton Glantz published an analysis in
JAMA Internal Medicine

of internal documents from the Sugar Research Foundation, an industry group. The documents showed that in 1965 the foundation funded a literature review by researchers at Harvard, which was published in the
New England Journal of Medicine

in 1967. The review downplayed evidence linking sugar to coronary heart disease and emphasized dietary fat and cholesterol. The industry funding was not disclosed in the publication. The authors of the 2016 analysis argued that the review helped shape decades of scientific and public discussion about diet and heart disease. They did not claim that the review’s conclusions were entirely wrong; their concern was that an undisclosed interest had influenced how the evidence was presented.

The case illustrates something general. Incentives rarely produce outright fabrication. More often they shape emphasis: which studies are highlighted, which weaknesses are mentioned, which questions are asked in the first place, and how uncertainties are described. A source with an incentive can be entirely accurate about every fact it states and still leave a misleading overall impression.

The same applies closer to home. Consider a hypothetical financial adviser who is paid a commission on the products she recommends. Everything she says about a particular fund may be true: its past returns, its manager’s experience, its popularity. What may be missing is a comparison with a cheaper fund that pays her nothing. The useful response is not to assume she is dishonest. It is to ask how she is paid, and to check her recommendation against a source that has no stake in the answer.

It does not follow that every interested source should be dismissed. Almost everyone has some interest in the conclusions they reach, and an expert’s livelihood depends on being right often enough to keep their reputation. The useful question is not whether a source has an incentive, but whether the incentive points strongly in one direction on this particular question, whether it has been disclosed, and whether independent sources without the same incentive reach similar conclusions.
When institutions correct themselves

Science as an institution deserves trust not because individual scientists are always right but because the institution has mechanisms for discovering when they are wrong. Those mechanisms are imperfect, and it is worth knowing how imperfect.
In 2015 a group of 270 researchers organized as the Open Science Collaboration published in
Science

the results of an attempt to replicate 100 studies from three prominent psychology journals. Ninety-seven per cent of the original studies had reported statistically significant results. Only 36 per cent of the replications did, and the average size of the effects found in the replications was about half that of the originals. Similar projects have since examined other fields, with varying results.

These findings are often cited as reasons to distrust science. I think they point to a more precise conclusion. They show that a single published study, especially a surprising one, is weaker evidence than its publication might suggest. They also show the institution doing what it is supposed to do: testing its own claims and reporting when they fail. The appropriate response is not to stop trusting research but to trust bodies of evidence more than individual findings, replicated results more than novel ones, and conclusions that have survived serious attempts to overturn them more than conclusions that have simply not yet been tested.
Experts outside their field

One of the most common errors of trust is extending an expert’s authority beyond the area in which it was earned. The philosopher Nathan Ballantyne has called this epistemic trespassing: experts drawing conclusions in fields where they lack the relevant competence, often without noticing that they have crossed a boundary. A distinguished physicist speaking about economics, a successful entrepreneur speaking about medicine, or a celebrated doctor speaking about history may be no better informed than any careful non-expert, while sounding considerably more authoritative.

The same applies within fields. A cardiologist is an expert on hearts, not necessarily on nutrition research methods. A software engineer is an expert on building software, not necessarily on how it will affect employment. Before relying on someone’s expertise, it helps to state precisely what question you are asking and whether their expertise bears on that specific question.
What a non-expert can check
Even without specialist knowledge, a non-expert can examine several features of a claim and its source.
Provenance.
Where did this claim originate? Is the source the person who did the work, or someone reporting on it, or someone reporting on a report? Each step adds distance and room for distortion.
Specificity.
Does the source say exactly what it claims, with numbers, conditions and limits? Vague claims are harder to check and easier to defend whatever happens.
Acknowledged uncertainty.

Does the source say what it does not know, or under what conditions its conclusion would change? Sources that never express uncertainty are either working on unusually simple questions or overstating their confidence.
Independent agreement.
Do other qualified sources, without the same incentives or influences, reach similar conclusions?
Consistency over time.
Has the source changed its view when evidence changed, and does it acknowledge past errors? Both are signs of reliability, though in public life they are often treated as weakness.
The opposite mistake
All of this could be read as an invitation to distrust expertise generally. That would be a serious error, and in my judgment a more common one now than excessive deference.

People who reject expert consensus rarely replace it with their own independent investigation. More often, they replace one authority with another: a different commentator, a dissenting voice, a community that shares their scepticism. The new authority is usually less accountable than the one it replaces, with no track record, no peer review and no mechanism for correction. Rejecting experts because experts sometimes err is not independent thinking. It is a change of trusted source, often to a worse one.

The better course is calibrated trust: greater deference where expertise is real, the question falls within its domain, the experts agree independently and the incentives are not distorting; less deference where any of those conditions fails. That is more demanding than either blanket trust or blanket suspicion, because it requires attention to particulars. It is also the only position that takes seriously both halves of the contradiction this chapter began with.
Trust as a revisable judgment

The practical implication of this chapter is that trust should be treated less like a feeling and more like an ongoing judgment that can be revised. We usually experience trust as an attitude towards a person or an institution: we trust our doctor, or we do not. A more useful approach treats trust as specific to a domain and responsive to evidence. I may trust my doctor on diagnosis and not on nutrition. I may trust a newspaper’s reporting and not its forecasts.
I may trust a research field’s well-replicated findings and hold its newest claims more loosely.

Such trust can grow or shrink as track records accumulate. When a source turns out to have been right on something difficult, it earns a little more trust on similar questions. When it turns out to have been wrong, especially if it does not acknowledge the error, it earns a little less. Nothing about this is complicated. What makes it difficult is that it requires us to keep paying attention after we have decided whom to believe, which is exactly when attention tends to lapse.

There is a tension here that this chapter cannot resolve. The sources most worth checking are often the ones we are least able to check: the specialist whose field we do not understand, the institution whose data we cannot see. Track records help, but most of us never see the track record. In the end, much of our knowledge rests on trust that we cannot fully audit. The aim is not to escape that dependence, which is impossible, but to choose where to place it with our eyes open.

sections.title: Thinking Under Pressure
sections.label: 11. Thinking Under Pressure

runs.text: How urgency, emotion, social influence and limited attention affect judgment.

On 27 March 1977, two Boeing 747s collided on a fog-bound runway at Los Rodeos airport on the island of Tenerife. Both had been diverted there after a bomb exploded at their intended destination, Gran Canaria, and the small airport was crowded with diverted traffic. The crew of the KLM aircraft had been delayed for hours. Strict Dutch rules on crew duty time meant that if they did not depart soon, the flight might have to be cancelled, with hotels needed for hundreds of passengers on a congested island. The weather was closing in. Visibility on the runway was falling.

The KLM aircraft was positioned at the end of the runway. A Pan Am 747 was still taxiing along the same runway in the fog, looking for its exit. The KLM crew received a route clearance from the tower, which described the path they would fly after take-off but did not clear them to take off. The captain began the take-off roll. During it, the flight engineer, who had heard a radio exchange suggesting that the Pan Am aircraft was still on the runway, asked whether it was clear. According to the investigation’s account of the cockpit recording, the captain replied emphatically that it was. Seconds later the KLM aircraft struck the Pan Am 747. In all, 583 people died. It remains the deadliest accident in the history of aviation.

The Spanish investigation identified the KLM captain’s decision to take off without clearance as the fundamental cause, and it described the pressures acting on him: the accumulating delays, the duty-time rules, the worsening weather, and a growing sense of tension as problems piled up. The captain was among the airline’s most senior and respected pilots. The question the accident raises is not why an incompetent person made a mistake. It is how an experienced and careful professional came to act on a conclusion he had not checked, while a colleague beside him held the information that would have changed it.
What pressure does to the interval

Pressure does not mainly introduce new errors. It removes the interval in which ordinary errors would have been caught. That changes the remedy: if pressure created special biases, we could learn about them, but because it takes away the time to check, the checking has to be built into situations before the pressure arrives.
Four kinds of pressure are especially common: urgency, emotional arousal, social influence and limited attention. They often arrive together, as they did at Tenerife.
Urgency

In a study published in 1973, the psychologists John Darley and Daniel Batson asked students at Princeton Theological Seminary to prepare a short talk, some of them on the parable of the Good Samaritan, and then sent them to another building to record it. Some were told they had time to spare, some that they were expected now, and some that they were already late. On the way, each student passed a man slumped in a doorway, coughing and groaning. Of those who believed they had time, 63 per cent stopped to offer help. Of those who believed they were late, 10 per cent did. Whether they had just been thinking about the Good Samaritan made no significant difference. Being in a hurry did.

The study was small, and its participants were seminary students in a single American setting, so the precise percentages should not be generalized. Darley and Batson were also studying helping, not reasoning, but their finding illustrates something broader about urgency. Under time pressure, attention narrows to the task in front of us. Information outside that task, even important information, is less likely to be noticed or acted upon. The seminarians who hurried past were not, presumably, people who would have endorsed ignoring someone in distress. Hurry changed what registered as relevant.

In decision-making, the same narrowing tends to reduce the number of options considered and the care with which they are compared. In 1987 the psychologist Giora Keinan reported an experiment in which participants solved decision problems while some were exposed to the threat of electric shocks. Those under threat were more likely to offer a solution before considering all the available alternatives, and to scan the alternatives in a disorganized way. Their solutions were less often correct. Keinan argued that much of the damage stress does to decisions comes from this failure to consider options systematically.

Urgency is sometimes real and sometimes manufactured. Negotiators, salespeople and fraudsters all know that a deadline, especially an artificial one, discourages the careful comparison of alternatives. A useful habit is to ask, whenever a decision feels urgent, whether the urgency is a feature of the situation or a feature of how the situation has been presented.
Emotion and arousal

Strong emotion is a form of pressure in its own right. Fear, anger, excitement and anxiety tend to focus attention on whatever provoked them and to push towards action. Chapter 2 described the affect heuristic, in which feelings about something stand in for an assessment of its risks and benefits, and noted that the effect grew stronger under time pressure. Under emotional arousal, people rely more heavily on whatever conclusion feels right and less on deliberate analysis.

This is not always harmful. Emotions often carry real information, and in a genuine emergency a strong response may be exactly what is needed. The difficulty is that emotion makes it harder to tell whether the conclusion it supports was reached for good reasons. A decision made in anger feels justified in the moment because the anger supplies its own justification. Only later, when the feeling has passed, does it become possible to see whether the reasons would have been sufficient without it.

One practical implication is simple and widely ignored: where possible, separate the moment of emotional reaction from the moment of decision. An angry message drafted and not sent, a resignation letter written and kept overnight, an investment decision delayed until after the market has calmed: these delays cost little and protect the interval that emotion would otherwise close.
Social influence

In experiments carried out in the early 1950s, the psychologist Solomon Asch asked participants to judge which of three lines matched the length of a reference line. The task was easy; tested alone, people almost never made mistakes. But each real participant sat in a group with several others who were secretly working with the experimenter and who, on certain trials, unanimously gave the same wrong answer. Across these critical trials, participants went along with the group’s incorrect answer roughly a third of the time, and about three-quarters of them conformed on at least one trial. These were American students in the 1950s, and the level of conformity is not a constant of human nature. A 1996 meta-analysis by Rod Bond and Peter Smith, covering 133 Asch-type studies from 17 countries, found that conformity in American studies had declined since the 1950s and tended to be higher in more collectivist cultures.

Two further findings from Asch’s work are, I think, more useful than the headline result. When just one other person in the group gave the correct answer, breaking the unanimity, conformity fell sharply. And when participants could write their answers privately rather than announcing them aloud, they rarely went along with the group. The pressure came not from doubt about the lines but from the social cost of standing alone in public. Asch did not study meetings, but this is the finding I would most want a chairperson to know. The number of people who disagree matters less than whether even one of them is visible.

Tenerife adds a further dimension: hierarchy. The flight engineer had the crucial information and voiced it as a question. When the captain answered firmly, the engineer did not press further. In cultures and organizations where seniority carries great weight, a junior person’s doubt is easily expressed too softly to stop a senior person’s conclusion. The airline industry’s response to this and other accidents was crew resource management training, which teaches cockpit crews to share information, voice concerns clearly and treat challenges from junior members as a normal part of operations rather than a breach of authority.
The psychologist Irving Janis, in
Victims of Groupthink

(1972), argued that cohesive groups under pressure can come to value agreement over critical evaluation, suppressing doubts and overestimating their own judgment. His concept has been very influential, though later research has found mixed support for it as a precise theory. The broader observation it captured is well supported: groups under pressure to reach consensus tend to examine alternatives less and dissent less than the situation warrants.
Limited attention

The fourth form of pressure is the least dramatic and the most constant. Attention is limited. Fatigue, multitasking, interruption and simple overload all reduce the capacity available for the deliberate checking this book recommends. A person who is juggling many tasks may make a judgment on one of them with only a fraction of their attention, and the judgment will feel just as confident as one made with full attention.

This is important because it means that the conditions of ordinary working life often amount to a mild version of the pressures described above. An inbox full of messages, a day of back-to-back meetings or the end of a long shift can all shrink the interval in which conclusions are examined. Few of these conditions feel like pressure, so their effects are easy to miss.
When pressure helps

It would be wrong to suggest that pressure always degrades judgment. The psychologist Gary Klein spent years studying people who make high-stakes decisions under extreme time pressure, including firefighters, military commanders and intensive-care nurses. In
Sources of Power

(1998) he described what he called recognition-primed decision-making. Experienced practitioners in such settings often do not compare options at all. They recognize the situation as a familiar type, an appropriate course of action comes to mind, and they evaluate it by quickly imagining how it would play out. If it seems workable, they act; if not, they adjust or consider the next option.

This kind of decision-making can be remarkably effective. As Chapter 10 noted, however, Klein and Kahneman later agreed that it works where the environment is regular and practitioners have had extensive feedback. A firefighter’s intuition about a burning building is trained by thousands of similar situations. Experience can prepare people for pressure, but only for the situations it actually resembles. Fog, a crowded diversion airport, a runway shared with taxiing traffic and an expiring duty-time limit, all at once, is not a combination that anyone practises often.

The practical lesson is that pressure is most dangerous when it combines with novelty: when the situation is unfamiliar, so that intuition has no reliable pattern to match, and the time available is too short for deliberate analysis. Those are the situations most worth preparing for in advance.

The opposite error is also real. In familiar, fast-moving situations, slowing down can itself be the mistake. A driver who stops to deliberate at a junction, a nurse who postpones a routine response to a deteriorating patient in order to reconsider it, or a team that convenes a meeting where an experienced person could have acted, has paid for the pause in time that the situation did not have. The aim is not to resist pressure at all times. It is to know which situations one’s experience genuinely covers, act quickly within them, and reserve the interval for the ones it does not.
Building the interval in advance

If pressure removes the opportunity to think carefully at the moment of decision, the thinking has to happen earlier, and the conditions of decision have to be arranged so that the thinking carries over.
Decide the rules before the pressure.

Many high-stakes fields use explicit rules for exactly the situations in which judgment is most likely to fail: a pilot does not take off without clearance, whatever the delay; a surgeon does not proceed without confirming the patient’s identity and the site of the operation. Such rules can seem rigid or even insulting to expertise. Their value lies precisely in the fact that they do not depend on the judgment of the person under pressure.
Make challenge easy and expected.

Asch’s finding that a single dissenter breaks the force of unanimity suggests that groups should make dissent structurally normal. Asking the most junior person to speak first, collecting written views before discussion, or assigning someone to raise objections can all help preserve the information that hierarchy and consensus tend to suppress.
Distinguish real deadlines from presented ones.

Ask what would actually happen if the decision were delayed by an hour, a day or a week. Often, very little would happen. Consider, as a hypothetical, a job offer that must be accepted by the end of the day. The deadline makes the decision feel urgent, but the urgency belongs to the employer, and the cost of accepting the wrong job, months or years in a poor fit, is far larger than the cost of asking for two more days. Many such deadlines turn out to be negotiable once someone asks.
Pause where pauses are cheap.

For decisions that can wait even briefly, the cost of a pause is usually small compared with its value. A short delay between reaction and decision, or between drafting and sending, gives emotion time to subside and attention time to return.
Protect attention for the decisions that matter.

Not every judgment needs full attention, but the important ones should not be made in the gaps between other tasks. Scheduling consequential decisions for times when attention is available is a mundane form of good judgment, and an effective one.
The decision before the decision

Tenerife is now taught as a case study across aviation and beyond, and much of what changed afterwards concerned communication: standard phrasing to prevent route clearances being mistaken for take-off clearances, and training that encourages any crew member to challenge a decision that seems unsafe. What strikes me most about the accident is that every piece of information needed to avoid it was present in the cockpit. What was missing was a few seconds of examination, and a social arrangement in which the person who had doubts felt able to insist on them.

The deeper point is that judgment under pressure is largely determined before the pressure arrives. It depends on the rules that have been decided in advance, the habits that have been practised, and the norms that make it acceptable to stop and check. By the time the pressure is felt, it is usually too late to build any of these. The examination we want to happen in the moment has to be designed into the moment beforehand, because the moment itself will not leave room for it.

sections.title: The Courage to Change Your Mind
sections.label: 12. The Courage to Change Your Mind

runs.text: Intellectual humility, belief revision and the willingness to reconsider conclusions.

In the autobiographical sketch he wrote late in life for his family, published after his death in 1887, Charles Darwin described a habit he had kept for many years. Whenever he came across a published fact, a new observation or a thought that ran against his general conclusions, he made a note of it immediately. He explained why. He had found by experience that such facts and thoughts were far more likely to slip from memory than favourable ones. He called this practice a golden rule, and he credited it with helping him anticipate many of the objections later raised against his theory.

Darwin’s rule is remarkable for what it assumes. It does not assume that he was unusually open-minded, or that he welcomed contrary evidence. It assumes the opposite: that his memory, like everyone’s, would quietly discard what he did not want to keep, and that only a deliberate habit could prevent it. The rule was not an expression of intellectual virtue. It was a device for compensating for its absence.

This chapter is about changing one’s mind for good reasons. Chapter 9 examined why we tend to prefer evidence that agrees with us. Here the question is what justified revision of a belief looks like, why it is so hard even when we recognize it is warranted, and what practices make it more likely.
Why revision feels like loss

Changing one’s mind is often described as a purely intellectual act: new evidence arrives, and a rational person updates. In practice, revising a significant belief usually carries costs that have little to do with evidence.
There is the cost to
consistency
. Most people value being seen, and seeing themselves, as consistent. A changed view can look like an admission that one was careless or foolish before.
There is the cost to
commitment

. Once we have acted on a belief, by investing in it, defending it publicly or building plans around it, abandoning it means acknowledging that those actions may have been mistaken. In a 1976 study titled “Knee-deep in the big muddy”, the organizational psychologist Barry Staw found that people who felt personally responsible for an earlier decision that had gone badly tended to commit more resources to it, not fewer. The effect, now called escalation of commitment, reflects the difficulty of separating a decision from the person who made it.
There is the cost to
identity and belonging
. Some beliefs mark membership in a group, a profession or a community. Revising them can feel like leaving, and others may treat it that way.
And there is the cost to
authority

. For people in positions of leadership or expertise, a changed view can appear to undermine the confidence others place in them. Research by the economists Pierre Azoulay, Christian Fons-Rosen and Joshua Graff Zivin, published in the
American Economic Review

in 2019, examined what happened to research fields in the life sciences when a prominent scientist died unexpectedly. Contributions from the scientist’s collaborators declined, while contributions from outsiders to the field rose, and the new work was disproportionately likely to be highly cited. The authors concluded that outsiders appeared reluctant to challenge a field’s leadership while the leading figure was alive. Their title borrowed a line often attributed to the physicist Max Planck: “Does Science Advance One Funeral at a Time?” Their findings suggest that eminence can slow not only the eminent person’s own revisions but those of everyone around them.
None of these costs is imaginary. That is why changing one’s mind can take courage. It is not only a matter of seeing that a belief is wrong. It is a matter of accepting the costs of saying so.
Not every change is an improvement

It would be easy to write a chapter that praised changing one’s mind without qualification. That would be a mistake. A person who changes their views with every new argument or every shift in the mood of the people around them is not displaying intellectual humility. They are displaying a different failure, one that leaves them as unreliable as a person who never changes at all.

The question is not whether to change one’s mind but how much, in response to what. Statisticians and philosophers have a precise framework for this, associated with the eighteenth-century minister and mathematician Thomas Bayes. Its core idea can be expressed without equations. How much a belief should move in response to new evidence depends on two things: how confident we were before, and how strongly the new evidence distinguishes between the possibilities. Strong evidence should move a weakly held belief a long way. Weak evidence should move a strongly supported belief only a little. A belief built on many independent observations should not collapse because of one contrary report, but neither should it be immune to an accumulation of them.
This framework identifies two opposite errors. One is
under-reaction
: failing to update enough when evidence arrives, often because the evidence is unwelcome or because the prior belief has become part of identity. The other is
over-reaction

: updating too much on a single vivid piece of evidence, a dramatic anecdote, a recent event or a persuasive speaker. Both errors are common, and the same person can show one in some areas and the other in others.
What good updating looks like

Chapter 10 described Tetlock’s finding that experts who adjusted readily outperformed those committed to a single theory. His later forecasting research with Barbara Mellers provides unusually direct evidence about what good belief revision looks like in practice. In the Good Judgment Project, thousands of volunteers made probabilistic forecasts about hundreds of geopolitical questions during a multi-year tournament sponsored by the United States intelligence community’s research agency. Their forecasts could be scored precisely once the outcomes were known.

In a 2020 study drawing on more than 400,000 forecasts across almost 500 questions, Pavel Atanasov and colleagues, including Mellers and Tetlock, found that the most accurate forecasters tended to make frequent, small updates. They revised their estimates often, but each revision was modest. Forecasters who rarely updated tended to be less accurate, and so did those who made large swings. Tetlock and Dan Gardner, in
Superforecasting
(2015), described the best forecasters as treating their beliefs as hypotheses to be tested rather than treasures to be guarded.

The pattern of frequent, small revisions is worth dwelling on, because it is quite different from how changing one’s mind is usually imagined. The usual picture is a conversion: a moment of realization, after which one view is abandoned and another adopted. The forecasting evidence suggests that good revision more often looks like continual adjustment. Confidence rises a little here, falls a little there. Beliefs remain stable when evidence is stable and move when it moves. There is rarely a single dramatic moment at which one admits to having been wrong, because one has never claimed to be more certain than the evidence warranted.
Never certain enough to be immovable

In 1650, Oliver Cromwell wrote to the General Assembly of the Church of Scotland urging them to reconsider their position. His letter contains a sentence that has outlived its political context: “I beseech you, in the bowels of Christ, think it possible you may be mistaken.” Centuries later the statistician Dennis Lindley gave the name Cromwell’s rule to a principle in probability theory: one should avoid assigning a probability of exactly zero or exactly one to any proposition about the world that is not a matter of logic. The reason is mathematical as much as moral. If a belief is held with absolute certainty, no evidence, however strong, can change it.

Cromwell’s rule is a useful discipline for everyday beliefs. Holding a view with very high confidence is often entirely reasonable. Holding it with literal certainty, as something that no possible evidence could disturb, closes the door to revision before any evidence has a chance to knock. A practical test is to ask whether there is anything that could change your mind. If nothing could, the belief has moved outside the reach of evidence, and you should at least know that it has.
A case of justified resistance and justified change

The history of continental drift illustrates both halves of good belief revision. In 1912 the German meteorologist Alfred Wegener proposed that the continents had once been joined and had slowly moved apart. He pointed to the matching shapes of coastlines, similar fossils on continents now separated by oceans, and geological formations that seemed to continue across them. Many geologists rejected the idea for decades.

It is tempting to tell this as a simple story of closed minds. The reality was more complicated. Wegener’s evidence for past connection was suggestive, but he could not offer a convincing mechanism for how continents could plough through the ocean floor, and the forces he proposed were judged inadequate by physicists. Scepticism about a claim with no plausible mechanism was not unreasonable in itself. What changed the consensus, in the 1950s and 1960s, was new evidence of a different kind: studies of magnetism preserved in ancient rocks, and then the discovery of symmetrical magnetic patterns on either side of mid-ocean ridges. The interpretation of those patterns was published by Fred Vine and Drummond Matthews in 1963 and proposed independently by Lawrence Morley. These findings supported the idea that new ocean floor was being created and spreading outward. Within a few years, plate tectonics had become the organizing framework of the earth sciences.

The lesson I draw is not that the early sceptics were simply wrong to resist. Some of their objections were legitimate, and the theory that was eventually accepted differed in important ways from Wegener’s. The lesson is that the field changed its mind when the right kind of evidence arrived, and did so relatively quickly once it did. Justified resistance and justified revision are not opposites. They are two expressions of the same commitment: letting beliefs follow the strength of the evidence.
A small example of revision

A modest illustration is close at hand. A line often attributed to the economist John Maynard Keynes runs: “When the facts change, I change my mind. What do you do, sir?” It appears in countless speeches, articles and books about changing one’s mind. But the researcher Garson O’Toole, who runs the Quote Investigator website, has reported finding no direct evidence that Keynes said it. The earliest version he located was a recollection by the economist Paul Samuelson, from 1970, of Keynes saying something like “When my information changes, I alter my conclusions.” Samuelson could not himself have been present for the remark he described. The attribution may be roughly right in spirit. As a documented quotation, it does not hold up.

The example is small, but the pattern is general. A familiar, satisfying belief arrived with the authority of repetition. Checking its origin required a few minutes and revealed that the confidence it carried was borrowed. The appropriate response was not to abandon the idea, which is sound whoever expressed it, but to stop presenting it as something it was not.
Intellectual humility

Psychologists have recently begun studying intellectual humility as a measurable trait: the recognition that one’s beliefs might be wrong, together with attention to the limits of one’s evidence and reasoning. In a 2017 paper in
Personality and Social Psychology Bulletin

, Mark Leary and colleagues reported that people who scored higher on intellectual humility were more attentive to the strength of persuasive arguments, and less inclined to regard politicians who changed their positions as flip-floppers. The research is still young, and measures of the trait are debated. But the findings fit a plausible picture. Intellectual humility does not mean having weak opinions. It means holding opinions in a way that remains responsive to how good the reasons for them actually are.

Intellectual humility is also easy to fake, sometimes even to ourselves. A person can speak tentatively about everything while changing their mind about nothing. The test is not how a person talks about their beliefs but how their beliefs behave when good evidence arrives.
Practices that make revision easier
Because the costs of revision are real, it helps to arrange things so that revision is cheaper and more routine.
Say in advance what would change your mind.

For any important belief, identify the evidence that would lead you to revise it, before such evidence appears. This makes it harder to explain the evidence away when it arrives, and it reveals beliefs for which no possible evidence would count.
Hold beliefs as degrees of confidence.

Instead of believing that a project will succeed, believe that it is likely to succeed, and try to say roughly how likely. Changing a 70 per cent belief to 55 per cent is much easier, psychologically and socially, than reversing a belief one has stated as certain.
Keep a record.

Darwin’s golden rule generalizes. Write down important predictions and the reasoning behind them, and note contrary evidence as it arrives. Memory edits the past to make our earlier selves look wiser. A written record does not.
Separate the belief from the person.
Wherever possible, discuss a view as a hypothesis under examination rather than as a position someone owns. “The plan assumes” invites revision more readily than “you said”.
Make revision normal and visible.

In teams and organizations, leaders who openly revise their views when evidence warrants, and say why, make it easier for everyone else to do the same. The reverse is also true: an environment that punishes changed minds will produce people who stop admitting to having them.
Distinguish core beliefs from peripheral ones.

Not every belief deserves the same treatment. Peripheral beliefs, about which little depends, can be revised quickly. Core beliefs, which many other beliefs and actions rest on, deserve more careful scrutiny before revision, but they also deserve more careful scrutiny before they harden into certainty.
The readiness to change

The title of this chapter speaks of courage, and I want to be precise about where the courage lies. It does not lie mainly in the dramatic moment of changing one’s mind, though such moments can be difficult. It lies in maintaining, over time, a relationship with one’s own beliefs that keeps them revisable: noticing contrary evidence instead of letting it slip away, stating confidence honestly instead of inflating it, and accepting in advance that some of what one now believes will turn out to be wrong.

Darwin did not wait for his theory to be challenged before recording the facts against it. He built the expectation of challenge into his daily practice, and in doing so made his eventual conclusions stronger. That is the distinction worth keeping. The aim is not to be someone who has changed their mind, which anyone can claim, but to remain someone whose mind could still be changed by good evidence, which is much harder to sustain.

It is worth ending with a question that only the reader can answer. Think of one belief you hold firmly about your work, a person close to you or a public question you care about. What evidence, if you met it, would lead you to change it? If you can name something, you hold the belief in the way this chapter has argued for. If you cannot, it may be worth asking whether the belief is still answering to evidence, or whether it has become something you would defend whatever the evidence said.

sections.title: Thinking in the Age of AI
sections.label: Part IV — Thinking in the Age of AI

runs.text: The first three parts of this book assumed, mostly without saying so, that the claims we evaluate come from people and documents whose polish cost someone effort. Part IV asks what happens to the earlier principles when that assumption fails.

None of them becomes obsolete, but several change their weight. Chapter 1’s distinction between recognizing and understanding matters more when clear explanations arrive on demand. Chapter 2’s question about where a belief came from becomes harder to answer when the source is a system that cannot show its sources. The demand for independent confirmation, from Chapters 5 and 10, becomes the central safeguard. Chapter 13 works through those changes for AI-generated answers. Chapter 14 then asks what to do when examination has gone as far as it usefully can and a decision still has to be made. Chapter 15 asks the practical question the whole book leads to: how does any of this become something we actually do, rather than something we know?
The thread running through Part IV is that the more easily conclusions can be produced, the more the quality of judgment depends on what happens before we accept them.

sections.title: When Machines Sound More Certain Than They Are
sections.label: 13. When Machines Sound More Certain Than They Are

runs.text: AI-generated answers, apparent authority, verification, and the difference between fluent explanation and established knowledge.

In March 2023, lawyers representing a passenger in a personal injury suit against the airline Avianca filed a brief in a federal court in New York. The brief cited a number of earlier court decisions in support of its argument. When the airline’s lawyers tried to find them, they could not. Neither could the judge. The cases did not exist. They had been produced by ChatGPT, which one of the lawyers had used for legal research, complete with plausible case names, docket numbers, judges and quotations.

On 22 June 2023, Judge P. Kevin Castel of the Southern District of New York sanctioned the two lawyers and their firm, imposing a fine of $5,000. His written opinion found that they had acted in bad faith, not merely because they submitted fictitious citations but because they continued to stand by them after their existence was questioned. At a hearing, one of the lawyers testified that he had been operating under the false perception that the tool could not possibly be fabricating cases on its own.

The case is now widely cited, and it is worth being clear about why. The details belong to a particular moment in the development of a particular technology, and they will date. The tools have changed since 2023 and will keep changing. The underlying lesson will not. An experienced professional received an answer that looked exactly like the kind of answer he expected. It had the form of legal authority. It had the specificity that usually indicates real research. It was fluent, confident and well organized. What it lacked was any connection to the documents it described, and nothing in its appearance revealed that.

This chapter is about that gap between how an answer sounds and what it rests on. It concerns AI-generated information specifically, because such systems produce the gap more often and more convincingly than most earlier sources. But the principles it develops are not about any product. They are about how to treat a claim whose fluency has become cheap.
When fluency was expensive

For most of history, a fluent, detailed and well-organized explanation was a reasonably good sign that someone knew something. Producing it took effort. A person had to gather information, understand it well enough to organize it, and take the time to write it clearly. A legal brief that cited specific cases with page numbers usually meant that someone had found those cases. A confident technical explanation usually meant that its author had studied the subject. Fluency was costly to produce, and costly signals tend to be informative.

That was never perfectly true. Confident nonsense has always existed, and Chapter 10 examined how credibility and reliability can come apart in human experts. But there was a rough correlation between the polish of an explanation and the work behind it, and people learned, reasonably, to treat polish as evidence.

Generative AI systems break that correlation. Large language models are trained to produce text that resembles the text they learned from. They can generate fluent, specific, well-structured prose on almost any subject, and they do so with the same surface quality whether the content is accurate or not. Researchers often call inaccurate but plausible output “hallucination”, a term surveyed by Ziwei Ji and colleagues in
ACM Computing Surveys
in 2023. The term is imperfect, but the phenomenon is well documented. A model can produce a citation, a statistic or a quotation that has every formal feature of a real one and no source at all.

When fluency becomes cheap, it stops carrying information about whether the content is true. That is the central change this chapter is concerned with. The cue that people have long used to judge explanations, how knowledgeable they sound, no longer distinguishes reliable answers from unreliable ones.
Why fluent answers persuade
The problem would be smaller if people could simply decide to ignore fluency. Psychological research suggests that is difficult.

In 1999 the psychologists Rolf Reber and Norbert Schwarz showed participants statements printed in colours that made them easier or harder to read against the background. Statements that were easier to read were more likely to be judged true. Chapter 2 described a related finding: repeated statements are rated as more likely to be true, even when people know better, because repetition makes them easier to process. The common thread is that a feeling of ease is taken as a signal of truth. Fluently generated text produces exactly that feeling.

There is a further effect, specific to answers produced on demand. Chapter 1 showed that a clear explanation can produce a feeling of understanding that the reader has not earned. A generated answer removes the friction that once came from consulting several sources, so the feeling can arrive with even less work behind it. The reader comes away informed in feeling but not in fact.
A third effect concerns tools in general. In a 2010 review in
Human Factors

, Raja Parasuraman and Dietrich Manzey examined research on automation bias: the tendency of people using automated decision aids to accept their output without sufficient checking, both by following incorrect recommendations and by failing to notice problems the aid did not flag. They found that the effect appeared in experts as well as novices and was not easily removed by training or instructions alone. Their review predates current language models, but its findings describe a general relationship between people and systems that seem competent. When a tool usually performs well, people tend to stop checking it, and the checking stops precisely when it would be most valuable.
Output and knowledge
The most important distinction in this chapter is between generated output and independently established knowledge.

Knowledge, in the practical sense this book has used, is information connected to evidence that could, in principle, be checked: observations someone made, documents that exist, measurements that were taken, arguments whose steps can be followed. When a reliable reference work states a fact, it does so because someone established it, and the chain from the claim back to its basis can usually be traced.

Generated output is text produced by a system that has learned patterns from a vast body of other text. Sometimes that output accurately reflects established knowledge, because the patterns it learned reflect it. Sometimes it does not. Crucially, the output does not usually carry its own provenance. It arrives without a reliable trail back to the evidence behind it, and in many cases there is no single piece of evidence behind it at all. Even when a system provides citations or links, those must themselves be checked, since a citation can be misattributed or a linked source may not say what the summary claims.

This does not make generated output worthless. It can be extremely useful for drafting, summarizing, explaining, brainstorming and suggesting where to look. The point is that its usefulness lies in what it helps us do next, not in its standing as an authority. An AI-generated answer is best treated as a well-informed suggestion from a source whose reliability on the specific question is unknown until checked.
Provenance
The concept that does the most work in evaluating AI-generated information is provenance: where a claim ultimately comes from, and whether that origin can be identified and examined.

For any claim that matters, the useful question is not “Does this sound right?” but “Can I trace this to something outside the system that produced it?” A statistic should lead to the study or dataset that reports it. A quotation should lead to the text in which it appears. A legal citation should lead to the decision. A factual claim about a person, an event or a policy should lead to a primary or authoritative source. If the trail cannot be found, the claim has not been established, however plausible it seems.

This is not a new standard. It is the same standard that careful researchers, journalists and lawyers have always applied to secondary sources. What has changed is how often it needs to be applied. When most fluent claims had some trail behind them, spot-checking was often enough. When fluent claims can be generated without any trail, every important one needs to be traced.
Asking the system is not checking

One tempting shortcut is to ask the same system whether its answer is correct. In the Avianca case, the lawyer’s own filings showed that he had asked the chatbot whether one of the cases was real, and had been told that it was. A system that generated an inaccurate claim may also generate an inaccurate confirmation of it, for the same reasons.

This is the problem of echoes from Chapters 5 and 10 in a new form. A confirmation that comes from the source being checked is not independent evidence. The same applies, to a lesser degree, to checking one AI system against another, since systems trained on similar data and with similar methods may share similar errors. Independent verification means verification through a route that does not depend on the original source: a primary document, a reputable reference, a person with direct knowledge, or a test against reality.

Related research has identified a tendency in some language models to agree with the views their users express, sometimes at the expense of accuracy. A 2023 study by Mrinank Sharma and colleagues described this as sycophancy and found it across several models of that time. The specific models will change, and developers have worked to reduce the tendency. The general lesson holds: a system designed to be helpful may be more inclined to tell you what fits your question than to tell you that your question rests on a mistake. Questions that reveal what answer you hope for are, as Chapter 4 argued, a poor way to find out what is true, whether you are asking a person or a machine.
Expressed confidence and actual reliability

Human experts can be poorly calibrated, as Chapter 10 discussed, but they usually signal uncertainty in some way: by hedging, by saying they would need to check, by declining to answer. Generated text can be uniformly confident in tone whether the content is well supported or not. Research on whether language models can estimate their own accuracy, such as work published in 2022 by Saurav Kadavath and colleagues, has found some ability to do so under certain conditions. But the tone of a particular answer is not a reliable guide to its accuracy, and a user typically has no way to tell from the text alone which kind of answer they have received.

This means the burden of calibration shifts to the user. Since the answer will not reliably indicate how much it should be trusted, the person relying on it has to decide independently, based on the stakes, the kind of question and the ease of checking.
Verification in proportion

Not every AI-generated answer needs to be verified. Doing so would remove most of the value these tools provide. The skill is to verify in proportion to what is at stake and to what can be checked. This is the book’s second question, how much examination is enough, in the setting where it now arises most often.
Consider the consequences of being wrong.

A suggested synonym, a draft paragraph or a list of ideas to consider carries little risk, because the user will evaluate it directly. A medical dosage, a legal citation, a financial figure, a factual claim in a published document or a statement about a real person carries much more. The higher the cost of error, the more important independent verification becomes.
Check the checkable.

Specific claims such as names, dates, numbers, quotations and citations are both the most likely to be fabricated and the easiest to check. They are also the elements that give an answer its appearance of authority. Checking them is often quick, and a single failed check is a strong signal that the rest of the answer needs scrutiny too.
Separate generation from verification.

A useful working pattern is to use AI systems to generate possibilities, drafts and leads, and then to verify through independent sources before relying on any specific claim. The two activities require different attitudes. Generation benefits from openness. Verification benefits from scepticism. Mixing them, by treating generated output as already verified, is where most errors occur.
Notice when you are learning and when you are borrowing.

If the purpose is to understand something, apply the test from Chapter 1. If you could not explain the answer without it in front of you, you have borrowed it, and your confidence should reflect that.
Responsibility does not transfer

In February 2024, a tribunal in British Columbia decided a small claim brought by a customer against Air Canada. The customer had used a chatbot on the airline’s website, which said the customer could apply retroactively for a reduced bereavement fare after travelling. The airline’s actual policy did not allow this, and it refused the refund. The tribunal, in
Moffatt v. Air Canada

, found the airline liable for negligent misrepresentation and awarded the customer the difference in fare, about C$650. The tribunal rejected the airline’s suggestion that it should not be held responsible for information provided by its chatbot, and noted that the company had not taken reasonable care to ensure the chatbot’s accuracy.

The amount involved was small, and the decision was made by a small-claims tribunal rather than a high court. Its interest lies in the principle it illustrates, which is the same principle at stake in the Avianca case. In both, a party tried, in effect, to place responsibility for an inaccurate claim on the system that generated it. In both, the decision-maker held that the person or organization that relied on the system, and presented its output to others, remained responsible for it.

This is what I mean by epistemic responsibility in an age of generated answers. The use of a tool does not reduce our responsibility for the beliefs we form and the claims we pass on. If anything, it increases it, because the tool removes the friction that once forced a certain amount of checking. A lawyer who copied a citation from a colleague’s memo would once have been expected to read the case. A lawyer who copies one from a chatbot should be expected to do the same.
What remains when fluency is free

The arrival of systems that can explain anything fluently does not make human judgment less important. It changes where judgment is needed. Producing a plausible answer is no longer the scarce skill. Evaluating one is. The capacities this book has described, knowing whether one understands, tracing beliefs to their sources, examining assumptions, asking what evidence would distinguish one claim from another, deciding whom and what to trust, are precisely the capacities that generated answers cannot supply for themselves.

The practical rule I would offer is this. Treat a fluent answer as a starting point, not an endpoint, and let the effort you spend checking it rise with the consequences of being wrong. Fluency is now free. Provenance is not, and it is provenance, not fluency, that tells us whether a claim deserves to carry weight.

sections.title: Making Decisions Without Knowing Everything
sections.label: 14. Making Decisions Without Knowing Everything

runs.text: Uncertainty, risk, reversibility, trade-offs and proportionate action.

Most important decisions have to be made before the evidence is complete. Whether to accept a job, launch a product, start a treatment, move a family, invest savings or change a policy: in each case, the information that would settle the question will arrive only after the decision has been made, and sometimes not even then. Waiting for certainty is rarely an option. Waiting is itself a decision, with consequences of its own.

Much of this book has been about examining beliefs before reaching conclusions. This chapter is about what happens when examination has done what it can and uncertainty remains. The question is no longer “What is true?” but “Given that I cannot know what is true, what should I do?” That question needs its own discipline, because the habits that make for careful belief can, if applied without adjustment, make for paralysed action. In the terms of the Introduction, this chapter is about the third move: how to close the interval and act.
Risk and uncertainty
In
Risk, Uncertainty and Profit

, published in 1921, the economist Frank Knight drew a distinction that remains useful. He used “risk” for situations in which the possible outcomes and their probabilities can be measured, as with a fair die, an insurance table or a well-studied medical procedure. He used “uncertainty” for situations in which they cannot, because the situation is new, the relevant factors are unknown, or the future depends on choices other people have not yet made.

Most decision advice is written as if every situation were a matter of risk: list the outcomes, estimate their probabilities, weigh their values and choose the option with the best expected result. That approach works well where it applies, and it is worth using where the numbers are genuinely available. But many of the decisions people find hardest fall closer to Knight’s uncertainty. The economists John Kay and Mervyn King, in
Radical Uncertainty
(2020), argued that in such situations the pretence of precise probabilities can do more harm than good, and that the more useful starting question is simply: what is going on here?

The practical implication is not to abandon estimation. Rough estimates are better than none, and Chapter 12 showed that people who think in degrees of confidence tend to judge better than those who think in certainties. The implication is to treat estimates under uncertainty as rough, to avoid decisions that depend on their precision, and to prefer actions that would turn out acceptably across a range of possibilities rather than optimally under one.
A worked example

It will help to have a case in view. Consider, as a hypothetical, a woman who runs a small, profitable bakery and is weighing whether to open a second location across town. She has a lease offer for a site she likes. The new location might double her business. It might also stretch her finances and attention so thin that both shops suffer. She has some evidence: her current customers, a rough sense of the new neighbourhood, a projection her accountant has prepared. She does not know how the neighbourhood will respond, whether she can find a reliable manager, or whether costs will rise. No amount of further thinking will tell her those things in advance.
I will return to this example through the chapter. Its details are invented. Its structure is common to many decisions in business, careers and family life.
How reversible is it?
Before anything else, it is worth asking how easily a decision under uncertainty can be undone.

In his 2015 letter to Amazon shareholders, Jeff Bezos distinguished between two kinds of decisions. Some are consequential and irreversible or nearly so, like one-way doors: once through, you cannot easily come back. These, he argued, should be made slowly and carefully. Most decisions, however, are reversible, like two-way doors: if the result is disappointing, you can step back through. Those should be made quickly, by individuals or small groups, without heavy process. His warning was that organizations, as they grow, tend to apply the slow, careful process to every decision, including the reversible ones, and so become slow and timid. In his 2016 letter he added that most decisions should probably be made with somewhere around 70 per cent of the information one wishes one had, because waiting for more usually costs more than it gains.

The framework is useful precisely because it applies in both directions. Treating a reversible decision as irreversible wastes time and opportunity, and it usually means less is learned, since much of what matters can only be discovered by trying. Treating an irreversible decision as reversible is the more dangerous error, because by the time the mistake is visible, it can no longer be corrected.

For the baker, the decision has both kinds of elements. A ten-year lease with heavy fit-out costs is close to a one-way door. A six-month pop-up, a shared kitchen arrangement or a wholesale partnership with a café in the new neighbourhood is much closer to a two-way door. Often the most valuable move in a decision under uncertainty is not choosing between the options as first presented, but finding a version of the decision that is more reversible.
Asymmetric outcomes

The second question is what happens in the bad cases. Expected values average over good and bad outcomes, which makes sense when there will be many similar decisions and the good and bad results will balance out over time. It makes much less sense when a bad outcome would be catastrophic, permanent, or would prevent any future recovery.

A useful way to look at this is to ask, separately, how good the best realistic outcome is and how bad the worst realistic outcome is, and whether the worst could be survived. An option with a modest expected gain and a small chance of ruin may be worse than an option with a smaller expected gain and no chance of ruin. The baker can survive a second shop that breaks even for a year. She may not survive one that fails in a way that takes the first shop with it.

This concern underlies what is often called the precautionary principle. Its best-known statement, Principle 15 of the 1992 Rio Declaration on Environment and Development, holds that where there are threats of serious or irreversible damage, lack of full scientific certainty should not be used as a reason for postponing cost-effective measures to prevent environmental degradation. The principle captures something important: when harms are severe and irreversible, waiting for certainty can mean waiting too long. But critics, among them the legal scholar Cass Sunstein in
Laws of Fear

(2005), have pointed out that a strong version of the principle can become incoherent, because inaction carries risks too, and precaution against one danger can create another. The useful core is narrower: give extra weight to outcomes that are severe and cannot be undone, on every side of the decision, including the side of doing nothing.
What would more information be worth?

The third question is whether it is worth waiting to learn more. Additional information has value only if it could change the decision. If the baker would open the shop whatever a further month of research revealed, the research is not worth a month. If one particular uncertainty, say whether she can hire a capable manager, would by itself determine whether the second shop succeeds, then resolving that uncertainty before signing anything is worth a great deal.

This suggests a practical approach to uncertainty that avoids both rushing and endless delay. List the uncertainties that matter. For each, ask whether it could be reduced before deciding, at what cost, and whether resolving it would change the decision. Pursue the ones that are cheap to resolve and decisive if resolved. Accept the rest as uncertainties to be managed rather than eliminated.

There is also a less obvious reason to stop gathering information: beyond a certain point, more of it can make judgment worse while making it feel better. In a study published in 1965, Stuart Oskamp gave clinical psychologists and students a case study in four stages and asked them, after each stage, to answer questions about the person described and to rate their confidence. As they read more, their confidence rose steadily, while the accuracy of their answers did not improve significantly. By the end, almost all of them were overconfident. The study was small, and it concerned one kind of judgment, but its lesson extends naturally to decisions: information that does not bear on the outcome can still increase certainty, and certainty is not the same as being better informed.

Some uncertainties can only be resolved by acting. Whether customers in the new neighbourhood will come cannot be fully known from a desk. It can be learned from a small, reversible test. This is the point where decision-making and inquiry meet: when information cannot be obtained by thinking, it can sometimes be obtained by doing something small and watching what happens.
Proportionate action
