The principle that ties these questions together is proportionate action: the size and irreversibility of a commitment should match the strength of the evidence behind it.

When confidence is low, the most appropriate actions are usually small, reversible and informative. Pilots, trials, staged investments, options to expand later and arrangements that preserve the ability to change course are all ways of acting without betting everything on an uncertain judgment. As confidence grows, commitments can grow with it. This is not timidity. It is a way of letting evidence and action reinforce each other, so that each step is justified by what the previous step revealed.

The opposite pattern, a large irreversible commitment made on thin evidence, is common, especially when a decision has acquired momentum or when someone senior has become attached to it. Chapter 12 described how commitment can escalate after a decision goes badly. Proportionate action is partly a defence against reaching that point, by ensuring that early commitments are small enough to abandon without loss of face.

Proportion also works in the other direction. When the evidence is strong and the cost of delay is high, hesitation can be its own error. A person who requires overwhelming evidence before every decision will often act too late. The goal is not caution as such but a match between confidence and commitment.
Imagining failure in advance

One simple technique helps surface the risks that optimism tends to hide. In 1989 Deborah Mitchell, J. Edward Russo and Nancy Pennington published research on what they called prospective hindsight. People asked to imagine that an event had already happened, and to explain why, generated more reasons than people asked merely to consider why it might happen. The psychologist Gary Klein, writing in
Harvard Business Review
in 2007, cited their finding that prospective hindsight increased the ability to identify reasons for future outcomes by about 30 per cent, and built on it a method he called the premortem.

In a premortem, a team that has tentatively agreed on a plan imagines that it is some time in the future and the plan has failed badly. Each person writes down, independently, the most likely reasons for the failure. The reasons are then shared and discussed. The exercise works partly because it changes the social situation. Raising doubts about a plan the group has just agreed on can feel disloyal. Explaining why a hypothetical failure occurred is simply the task. In the terms of Chapter 7, a premortem is a way of generating alternative explanations for a failure before it happens rather than after.

For the baker, a premortem might reveal that the most plausible failure is not lack of customers but exhaustion: running two shops without a trusted manager. That insight points to a specific condition for proceeding, finding the manager first, which is more useful than a general feeling of risk.
Judging decisions without hindsight

Decisions under uncertainty create a particular problem when we look back on them. Good decisions sometimes turn out badly, and bad decisions sometimes turn out well, because outcomes depend partly on luck. Yet people tend to judge decisions by their results. In a study published in 1988, Jonathan Baron and John Hershey found that undergraduate participants rated the same medical decision as better reasoned when it was followed by a good outcome than when it was followed by a bad one. The decision-maker had no more information in one case than in the other, and many participants said they believed outcomes should not affect such ratings, yet their ratings were affected all the same. They called this outcome bias. The former professional poker player Annie Duke, in
Thinking in Bets
(2018), uses the word “resulting” for the same habit.

Outcome bias matters for two reasons. It is unfair to people who made sound decisions that happened to go wrong, and it can discourage the reasonable risk-taking that good decisions under uncertainty sometimes require. It also teaches the wrong lessons. A reckless decision that happened to succeed will be repeated. A careful decision that happened to fail will be abandoned. Over time, an organization or a person that judges by outcomes alone will drift towards luckier rather than better decision-making.

The remedy is to evaluate a decision by what was known and knowable when it was made: whether the options were considered, the uncertainties identified, the reversibility assessed and the commitment proportionate. Recording the reasoning at the time, as Chapter 12 recommended for beliefs, makes this possible. Without such a record, hindsight will rewrite the reasoning to fit the result.
The baker closes the interval
It is worth following the baker through all three moves, because the sequence matters as much as the parts.
She
opened the interval

because the decision met the tests that justify it: a ten-year lease is hard to reverse, it would affect her staff and family, and she noticed that she was more certain than her evidence warranted. She
examined the conclusion

by asking what it rested on. The central assumption was that her current customers came for her bread rather than for the convenience of her location. A competing explanation, that her success owed as much to the street as to the product, would predict that a second shop elsewhere would struggle. She also found an assumption she had never stated: that she could keep working sixty-hour weeks. The premortem exposed the manager problem.

She then asked what further information would materially change the choice. Two things would: whether a capable manager could be hired, and whether people in the new neighbourhood would buy her bread at her prices. The first could be tested before signing anything, by advertising the role. The second could only be tested by selling there. More analysis of the accountant’s projection would not have changed her decision, so she stopped refining it. She
closed the interval

by choosing the reversible version: a six-month pop-up stall, conditional on hiring a manager first. Before starting, she wrote down what she expected, how confident she was, and what results after six months would lead her to sign the lease, extend the trial or withdraw.

The important point is not that the baker eliminated uncertainty. She did not. She identified which uncertainties mattered, separated those she could investigate from those she could only resolve through experience, and chose an action proportionate to what she knew. Opening the interval prevented premature commitment. Examining it exposed the assumptions behind her confidence. Closing it allowed her to act without pretending that the remaining uncertainty had disappeared. Good judgment does not always produce certainty. Sometimes it produces a better way to proceed without it.
Chapter 15 returns to her a year later, because the decision was not finished when it was made.
Not deciding is a decision

There is one more trap worth naming. Under uncertainty, it can feel safer to do nothing, since doing nothing seems to avoid responsibility for whatever happens. But inaction has consequences too, and they are often simply less visible. The baker who never opens a second shop has not avoided risk. She has chosen one set of risks, such as being overtaken by a competitor or stagnating, over another. A patient who declines a treatment has not avoided a medical decision. A manager who defers a hard choice until it is made by events has made a choice about who or what decides.

Treating inaction as one option among others, with its own outcomes and uncertainties, costs nothing, and it often changes which option looks safest. It removes the illusion that delay is neutral, and it puts the real trade-off in view.
The decision and the futures

Under uncertainty, we never learn how good a decision was in the way we learn whether a factual claim was true. We see only the future that actually arrived, not the others that might have. A decision that worked may have been fortunate. A decision that failed may have been wise.

The quality of a decision under uncertainty therefore lies in how it would have fared across the range of futures that might reasonably have arrived, and in whether it kept open the possibility of learning and adjusting as the real one unfolded. That is a different standard from being right. It asks whether we understood the shape of what we did not know, protected ourselves against the outcomes we could not afford, matched our commitment to our confidence, and left room to change course. Those are things that can be done before the outcome is known, which is precisely when they matter.

sections.title: Building a Life of Better Judgment
sections.label: 15. Building a Life of Better Judgment

runs.text: How deliberate thinking becomes a sustainable practice through reflection, feedback, repetition and supportive environments.

Picture a hypothetical project lead who has just finished a good book on reasoning. She can define confirmation bias, explain why base rates matter and describe how to run a premortem. In the following week she hires a candidate after one confident conversation, accepts a striking figure in a board paper without asking what it is out of, and waves away a colleague’s doubt about a plan she already favours. She has not forgotten anything she read. None of those moments presented itself as the kind of moment the book was about.

The gap between knowing a principle and applying it is not confined to readers of books. It appears among highly trained professionals, and one of the clearest demonstrations of how to narrow it comes from surgery.

Between October 2007 and September 2008, surgical teams in eight hospitals, in cities as different as Toronto, New Delhi, Amman, Auckland, Manila, Ifakara in Tanzania, London and Seattle, began using a 19-item checklist developed with the World Health Organization. The checklist was simple. Before anaesthesia, confirm the patient’s identity, the site and the procedure. Before the incision, have every team member introduce themselves by name and role, and confirm that antibiotics have been given. Before the patient leaves the operating room, count the instruments and sponges. Almost nothing on the list was new to the surgeons, anaesthetists and nurses who used it. They knew all of it already.
The results, published by Alex Haynes and colleagues in the
New England Journal of Medicine
in January 2009, were striking. (Atul Gawande, one of the study’s authors, later described the project in
The Checklist Manifesto

.) Across the participating hospitals, the rate of major complications fell from 11.0 per cent to 7.0 per cent after the checklist was introduced, and the rate of death fell from 1.5 per cent to 0.8 per cent. The study had limitations: it compared periods before and after rather than randomly assigning hospitals, and some of the improvement may have come from the attention the study itself brought. But the effect was large, and it appeared in both high-income and lower-income settings.

What makes the study instructive is not that a checklist helped. It is what the checklist reveals about the people who used it. These were highly trained professionals who knew every principle on the list. What they lacked was not knowledge but consistency: a reliable way of ensuring that what they knew was applied every time, under ordinary pressures, by people who were busy, tired and confident. The checklist did not teach them anything. It changed when and how their knowledge was brought to bear.
This final chapter asks a question the earlier chapters could not answer: how does someone who understands good reasoning become someone who consistently practises it?
The recognition problem
I want to begin with an argument about why knowledge of good reasoning so often fails to show up when it is needed.

Most discussions of thinking errors assume that the main obstacle is ignorance: people make mistakes because they do not know the relevant principle. The research reviewed in this book suggests that this is only part of the story. People who know about confirmation bias still show it. Physicians who understand base rates still misread test results. The experienced captain at Tenerife, described in Chapter 11, knew the importance of take-off clearance. Knowledge of the principle is necessary, but it is rarely what is missing at the moment of error.

What is usually missing is recognition: noticing, in the middle of an ordinary situation, that this is one of the moments when a principle applies. Situations do not announce themselves. A decision to hire, a figure in a board paper, a colleague’s doubt, a fluent answer from an AI system: none of these arrives labelled “examine your assumptions here”. They arrive looking like ordinary work, and they are handled by whatever habits ordinary work has built.

This changes what the goal of practice should be. If the problem were ignorance, more reading would solve it. Because the problem is largely recognition, the goal is to connect principles to the recognizable features of situations, so that the right kind of attention is triggered by the situation itself rather than by an effort of memory. The surgical checklist works in exactly this way. It does not rely on any team member remembering to check antibiotics. It ties the check to a moment, before the incision, that cannot be missed.

I think this is the central idea of the chapter. Good judgment, as a dependable capacity, is less a trait a person possesses than a property of a system: the person, together with the cues, routines, feedback and environment that determine when and how their knowledge is brought to bear. Improving judgment means improving that system.
What habits are
Psychologists who study habits describe them as behaviours that have become automatic responses to particular cues in the environment. In a 2007 review in
Psychological Review

, Wendy Wood and David Neal argued that habits are triggered by context, such as a place, a time or a preceding action, rather than by conscious goals, and that this is why they persist even when intentions change.

Habits also take longer to form than popular advice suggests. In a study published in 2010, Phillippa Lally and colleagues at University College London asked 96 volunteers to perform a simple new eating, drinking or exercise behaviour daily in response to a consistent cue. Among participants whose data could be modelled, the median time to reach near-maximum automaticity was 66 days, with a range from 18 to an estimated 254 days, and missing an occasional day did not seriously disrupt the process. The participants chose their own simple behaviours and rated their own automaticity, so these figures describe one kind of habit measured in one way.

Thinking habits are harder to study than eating or exercise habits, and I do not want to overstate how directly these findings transfer. But they suggest that a habit of examining assumptions will form, if at all, from repeated practice tied to consistent cues, not from reading about it.
Tying examination to cues
The psychologist Peter Gollwitzer has studied what he calls implementation intentions: plans of the form “if situation X arises, then I will do Y”. In a 1999 article in
American Psychologist

, he argued that such plans help people act on their goals by linking the intended action to a specific situation, so that the situation itself prompts the action. A later meta-analysis by Gollwitzer and Paschal Sheeran, published in 2006, found that forming implementation intentions had a substantial effect on goal attainment across many studies.

The approach applies naturally to judgment. Instead of intending in general to “think more carefully”, a person can identify the specific situations in which careful thought matters most in their own life and attach a specific check to each. Some examples, offered as illustrations rather than prescriptions:
If I am about to make a decision that will be hard to reverse, then I will write down the two or three assumptions it depends on most.
If I find myself certain within minutes about a complex question, then I will ask what else could explain what I am seeing.
If a number is about to settle a decision, then I will ask what it is out of and what it is compared with.
If I am about to pass on a claim I have not checked, especially one from an AI system, then I will trace it to a source or say that I have not.
If I feel strong emotion about a decision, then I will wait before committing to it, if waiting is possible.

The value of such rules lies in their specificity. A general resolution to be more careful competes with everything else for attention and usually loses. A specific link between a situation and an action has a chance of firing when the situation occurs.
Feedback

No skill improves without feedback, and judgment is unusual among skills in how little feedback it naturally receives. Many judgments are never checked against outcomes. Others are checked so long after the fact that the connection is lost. Still others are checked against outcomes that depend heavily on luck, which, as Chapter 14 described, can teach the wrong lesson.

The contrast with fields that have good feedback is instructive. Weather forecasters are a frequently cited example of good calibration: when experienced forecasters say there is a 70 per cent chance of rain, it tends to rain on roughly 70 per cent of such days. Research by Allan Murphy and Robert Winkler in the 1970s documented this kind of calibration in precipitation forecasts. Forecasters are not inherently wiser than other professionals. They make many similar judgments, receive clear feedback within a day, and are scored on their accuracy. Chapter 10 described Kahneman and Klein’s conclusion that expert intuition develops in exactly such conditions.

Most personal and professional judgments do not come with this structure, but some of it can be built. The simplest tool is a written record of important judgments: what was decided, what was expected to happen, how confident one was, and why. Reviewing that record later, against what actually happened, provides feedback that memory alone would distort. Chapter 12 described how memory edits the past to make our earlier selves look wiser. A written record does not, which is why it is useful and why it can be uncomfortable to read. It helps most when predictions are recorded in a form that can be checked: not “this project will probably be late” but “about a 70 per cent chance it misses the March deadline”. Over many such entries, one can learn whether one’s 70 per cent judgments come true about 70 per cent of the time.

Consider again the hypothetical baker from Chapter 14. A year after her decision, she reads what she wrote down before the pop-up opened. She had expected weekend sales to reach a certain level within three months, and she had put her confidence at about 70 per cent. They reached it in five. The manager she hired was excellent. On the strength of the trial, she signed a shorter lease than the one first offered.

The review is useful because it separates things that memory would blur. Her central assumption, that customers came for the bread, held up. Her estimate of the timeline was optimistic, and she can see that it was the third time in her written record that she had underestimated how long something would take. That pattern is worth more to her than the success of this particular decision. She also notices that the decision went well partly for a reason she had not foreseen, a nearby office reopening after a refurbishment, and she resists the temptation, described in Chapter 14, to credit her reasoning with an outcome that luck helped produce. Her habit for next time is specific: add a margin to her own timelines, and ask what outside event could change the result.
Reflection that changes something
Feedback is only useful if it is reflected on, and reflection is only useful if it changes something. Many organizations hold reviews after projects end. Fewer change what they do as a result.
The United States Army developed a practice called the after-action review, set out in its 1993 training circular
A Leader’s Guide to After-Action Reviews

and since adopted by many other organizations. In its common form, a team that has completed an activity asks a few questions: what was supposed to happen, what actually happened, why there was a difference, and what should be sustained or changed next time. The questions are simple. The discipline lies in asking them routinely, soon after the event, with an emphasis on learning rather than blame, and in carrying the answers into the next activity.

Individuals can do the same. A brief, regular review of recent decisions, asking not “Did it work out?” but “Was my reasoning sound given what I knew, and what would I do differently?”, turns experience into feedback. Its value depends less on depth than on regularity. A ten-minute review done every week is more useful than a thorough review done once and never repeated.
Can judgment be trained?

It is fair to ask whether any of this works. The research on training people to reason better is mixed, and some earlier reviews were pessimistic. In 2009 Scott Lilienfeld, Rachel Ammirati and Kristin Landfield argued in
Perspectives on Psychological Science
that efforts to reduce bias through education had produced limited and inconsistent results, and that much more research was needed on what actually works.

More recent evidence is somewhat more encouraging. In two experiments published in 2015, Carey Morewedge and colleagues found that a single training session, using either an interactive computer game or an instructional video, reduced participants’ susceptibility to several well-known biases, with effects that persisted for at least two months. The game, which gave personalized feedback and opportunities for practice, produced larger effects than the video. A follow-up study published in
Psychological Science

in 2019 by Anne-Laure Sellier, Irene Scopelliti and Morewedge reported that business students who had played the game were less likely, weeks later, to show confirmatory reasoning in a realistic business case in their coursework.

These findings should not be overstated. They concern specific biases, measured in specific ways, and they do not show that a single intervention produces generally better judgment. But it is worth noticing that the training which combined practice with personalized feedback did better than instruction alone. My own conclusion, which goes beyond these studies, is that reading a book like this one is closer to the video than to the game. It can help, but only if what is read is later practised, with some way of finding out how one’s judgments actually turn out.
Arranging disagreement

Chapter 9 suggested that people are poor judges of their own reasoning and better judges of other people’s. If that is right, one of the most practical habits of judgment is to arrange, in advance, for someone to disagree.

This can be informal. A person facing a significant decision can name one or two people who are likely to see it differently, not because they are contrarian but because their position, experience or values differ, and ask them a specific question: what would make this a mistake? A team can rotate the role of the person whose job in a meeting is to make the strongest case against the preferred option. A couple can agree that before a large purchase each will state the best argument for not making it.

What makes such arrangements work is that they are set up before anyone is attached to an answer. Disagreement invited in advance is information. Disagreement that arrives after a commitment is usually heard as opposition. The habit, then, is not to tolerate disagreement when it appears but to schedule it.
Environments that make good judgment easier

The most powerful influence on everyday judgment may not be individual effort at all, but the environment in which judgments are made. A person working in an environment that rewards quick confident answers, punishes dissent and never reviews outcomes will find it very hard to maintain good habits of judgment, however committed they are. A person working in an environment that builds in pauses, invites challenge and reviews decisions will find good judgment easier, even on bad days.

An environment matters here for a specific reason: it can do some of the recognizing that individuals fail to do. A routine that requires assumptions to be stated before approval does not depend on anyone noticing that this is a moment for examining assumptions. Where people have the power to shape their environment, this is often the most durable way to close the gap between what they know and what they do. In organizations, that means checklists for high-stakes decisions, routines that require assumptions to be stated, meetings that collect views before discussion so that seniority does not dominate, reviews that examine reasoning and not only results, and leaders who visibly change their minds when evidence warrants. In personal life, it may mean seeking out friends who will disagree honestly, slowing down the channels through which information arrives, or simply keeping important decisions away from the times of day when attention is lowest.
The surgical checklist was, above all, a change to an environment. It made it harder for good surgeons to skip steps they knew mattered.
Choosing where to spend attention

A person who tried to apply every principle in this book to every judgment would exhaust themselves within a day and abandon the effort within a week. Sustainable practice requires triage, the habit form of the book’s first two questions (which conclusions deserve examination, and how much): careful examination for the decisions that are hard to reverse, high in stakes, unfamiliar, or made under strong emotion or pressure, and ordinary habits for the rest. Triage is itself a recognition task, and perhaps the first habit worth building. Appendix B sets out questions for the first kind. A small number of well-chosen habits, applied consistently where they matter, will do more for judgment than an ambitious programme that collapses under its own weight.
Maintenance

Habits of judgment, like other habits, can fade. Routines lapse when circumstances change, checklists become rituals performed without attention, and teams that once welcomed dissent grow comfortable and stop. Practices need occasional review: are they still used, do they still fit, have they become empty forms?

This is perhaps the most important difference between knowing a principle and practising it. Knowledge, once acquired, tends to stay. Practice has to be maintained. The person who read about confirmation bias ten years ago still knows what it is. Whether they still check for it depends on whether anything in their life still prompts them to.
Practice as a way of living with fallibility

The hypothetical project lead at the start of this chapter did not need another book. She needed something in her week that would have caught the hire, the board paper and the dismissed doubt at the moment they happened: a rule, a habit, a colleague or a routine that turned a principle she knew into a question she asked.

None of this guarantees good decisions. The surgical checklist reduced complications and deaths. It did not eliminate them. Habits of judgment work the same way. They shift the odds, catching some errors that would otherwise have slipped through, and they make it more likely that when a mistake does happen, it will be noticed and learned from. That is a modest promise, and I think an honest one. The answer to this chapter’s question, then, is less dramatic than one might hope. People who understand good reasoning become people who practise it by attaching a few checks to the moments that matter, writing down what they expect, arranging for someone to disagree, reviewing what happened, and repeating this for long enough that it stops feeling like effort. None of it requires exceptional intelligence. It requires deciding, in advance and in ordinary weeks, what one will do in the moments that are not ordinary.

sections.title: The Mind That Remains Open
sections.label: Conclusion — The Mind That Remains Open

runs.text: The phrase “an open mind” is usually meant as praise, and it is easy to misunderstand. It can suggest a mind without convictions, one that treats every view as equally plausible and every question as permanently unsettled. That is not what this book has argued for. A mind that never reaches conclusions is not open. It is merely undecided, and an undecided mind is as poorly placed to act well as a closed one. G. K. Chesterton made the point in his
Autobiography
: “The object of opening the mind, as of opening the mouth, is to shut it again on something solid.”

The kind of openness this book has been concerned with is more specific. It is the willingness to examine a belief before letting it carry weight, and the capacity to keep that belief revisable after it has been adopted. It applies at two moments: before a conclusion is reached, and after. Between those moments lies the conclusion itself, which should be reached, acted on and, where the evidence supports it, held with confidence.
How sure we feel and how sure we are entitled to be
If the book has one insight beneath its many particular ones, I think it is this: the feeling of being sure is produced by processes that have little to do with whether we are right.

The zipper in Chapter 1 felt understood because it was familiar. The shipowner in Chapter 2 felt sure because his doubts had been soothed, not answered. The flight instructor in Chapter 6 felt that experience had taught him something, when it had shown him regression. The diligent readers of evidence in Chapter 9 felt fair because they had worked hard, without noticing that they had worked hard in only one direction. The lawyer in Chapter 13 felt that the citations were real because they looked exactly like real citations. In each case the sense of certainty was genuine. What it lacked was any reliable connection to the grounds.

Familiarity, fluency, repetition, agreement, effort, the confidence of others: these produce the feeling of knowing, and none of them is evidence. They are often correlated with good grounds, which is why we rely on them, and why the failures are hard to notice from the inside. The deliberate interval is the moment in which that connection is checked rather than assumed: in which we ask not “How sure do I feel?” but “What would make me entitled to feel this sure, and do I have it?”

Seen this way, examining a belief is not an act of self-doubt. It is an attempt to make confidence honest, so that we can be fully confident where the grounds allow it and appropriately tentative where they do not.
The limits of the project

It would contradict the spirit of the book to end with an overstatement of what it can achieve. The research reviewed here offers no method for eliminating bias, and I am not aware of any that exists. People who know the most about reasoning errors still make them. Training can help, as Chapter 15 described, but its effects are partial and specific. Environments can support good judgment, but they can also erode it, and most of us have only limited influence over the environments in which we work and live.

There are also genuine disagreements that no amount of careful reasoning will dissolve. Some questions turn on values rather than facts. Some turn on evidence that does not yet exist and may never exist. Reasonable people examining the same information can reach different conclusions, and the existence of disagreement is not by itself evidence that someone has reasoned badly. One of the quieter dangers of a book like this is that it can tempt readers to explain every disagreement as the other side’s failure of reasoning. The tools in these chapters are meant first for examining one’s own beliefs. Turned only outward, they become another way of being certain.
Why it matters now

I suggested at the start that the examination of belief has become more urgent. The insight above explains why more precisely than the usual worry about misinformation. The cues that produce the feeling of knowing, fluency, specificity, confident tone, the look of a citation, can now be produced at almost no cost by sources that have no grounds at all. A habit of judging conclusions by how sure they make us feel was always risky. It is now exploitable at scale, whether by accident or by design. If the link between confidence and grounds is to be checked, it now has to be checked deliberately.

This is not a reason for alarm. People have adapted to every previous change in how information is produced and spread, from printing to broadcasting to search engines, and they will adapt to this one. But adaptation is not automatic. It consists of exactly the habits this book has described, practised by enough people, often enough, in the situations that matter.
The recurring question
The title of this book is
Before You Reach a Conclusion

, and its recurring concern has not been whether people can reach conclusions. Everyone can, and does, many times a day. The concern has been whether, in the cases that matter, we have examined our reasoning sufficiently before doing so.

Sufficiently is the important word. It does not mean exhaustively, which is impossible, or until all doubt is gone, which would mean never. If the book can be carried away in a form small enough to use, it is as three questions, asked in the moment before a conclusion is allowed to carry weight:
Does this conclusion matter enough to examine?
What would I need to know before trusting it?
When will I have learned enough to act?

The first protects against wasting effort on what does not matter. The second is where most of the book’s tools belong. The third protects against the opposite failure, examination that never ends, and it is the question that distinguishes judgment from mere doubt.

The mind that remains open, in the sense I have meant, is not one that refuses to conclude. It is one that concludes carefully, holds its conclusions honestly, and keeps a door open for the evidence that might show it was wrong. That is not a temperament that some people have and others lack. It is a practice, available to anyone, and it begins in a small, familiar moment: the moment just before we decide that we already know.

sections.title: A Practical Framework for Examining Important Claims
sections.label: Appendix A — A Practical Framework for Examining Important Claims

runs.text: This appendix is a reusable framework for examining a claim before you rely on it, repeat it or act on it. It works for a statistic in a news report, a recommendation from a colleague, a finding in a research summary or an answer from an AI system. It does not replace judgment. It organizes it.

Use the full framework only for claims that matter: those that will support a significant decision, be passed on to others or be hard to correct later. For everyday claims, the first three steps are often enough. The chapter references after each step point to a fuller discussion, but every step is written to be used without them.
The framework follows the book’s three moves. Deciding to use it at all is the first:
open the interval
only for claims that matter. Steps 1 to 9
examine the claim
. Step 10
closes the interval
by deciding what follows.
The framework at a glance

rows: Step
Core question
Warning signs
1. State the claim
What exactly is being claimed, about whom, over what period?
Vague wording; no numbers; scope that shifts when questioned
2. Trace the provenance
Where did this originate, and can I reach the original?
Many repetitions of one source; no primary source; “studies show” with no study named
3. Separate observation from interpretation
What was actually observed or measured, and what has been added?
A conclusion presented as if it were the observation
4. Surface the assumptions
What must be true for this claim to follow from the evidence?
An assumption that is both load-bearing and fragile
5. Assess the source
Is the source reliable on this specific question?
Expertise outside its domain; undisclosed incentives; no track record
6. Consider alternatives
What else could produce the same evidence?
Only one explanation considered; evidence that fits every explanation equally
7. Check the numbers
Out of how many, compared with what, from what base rate?
Relative risk without absolute risk; no denominator; averages with no spread
8. Identify what is missing
What would I want to know that is not here?
No comparison group; no failures counted; selected cases only
9. Set justified confidence
How confident should I be, and what would change my mind?
Certainty about a complex claim; no evidence that could count against it
10. Decide what follows
What, if anything, should I do or say on the basis of this?
Action out of proportion to confidence; passing on claims not checked

runs.text: The steps in more detail
1. State the claim precisely.

Rewrite the claim in your own words, as specifically as possible. Include who or what it concerns, what is said to be true of them, by how much, and under what conditions. Vague claims are hard to check and easy to defend whatever happens. If you cannot state the claim precisely, you do not yet know what you are evaluating.
(Chapters 1 and 4.)
2. Trace the provenance.

Find out where the claim originated. Is the source you are reading the person or organization that did the work, or a report of a report? Can you reach the original study, document, dataset or statement? If many sources repeat the claim, check whether they trace back to one origin. A claim that cannot be traced has not been established, however often it appears. This step is especially important for AI-generated content, which often arrives without a reliable trail.
(Chapters 2, 10 and 13.)
3. Separate observation from interpretation.

Identify what was actually seen, measured or recorded, and distinguish it from what the source concludes. Many claims fuse the two. “Customers love the new feature” may rest on the observation that usage of the feature rose. The observation is checkable. The interpretation goes beyond it.
(Chapter 5.)
4. Surface the assumptions.

Ask what would have to be true for the evidence to support the conclusion. Write down the assumptions you find, and mark which ones the conclusion depends on most and which are most likely to be false here. Pay particular attention to assumptions built into measures, definitions and categories.
(Chapter 3.)
5. Assess the source.

Ask whether the source has relevant expertise on this specific question, a record of being right on similar questions, and incentives that could shape how the evidence is presented. Ask whether other qualified sources, working independently, reach similar conclusions. Distinguish signals of credibility, such as confidence and polish, from signals of reliability.
(Chapter 10.)
6. Consider alternative explanations.

List at least two other ways the same evidence could have come about. Then ask which observations would distinguish between the explanations, and whether those observations are available. Include mundane explanations: chance, measurement error, selection, a change in how something was recorded. For causal claims, ask three further questions. Could the effect be causing the supposed cause? Could a third factor be causing both? And were the cases chosen because they were unusually high or low, in which case they would tend to move back towards the average on their own, whatever was done to them?
(Chapters 6 and 7.)
7. Check the numbers.

For any statistic, ask what it is out of, what it is compared with, and how common the thing was to begin with: a test that is right 99 per cent of the time will still produce mostly false alarms if what it looks for is rare. Convert relative changes into absolute ones: “twice the risk” means little until you know whether the risk went from 1 in 100 to 2 in 100 or from 1 in a million to 2 in a million. Ask what an average hides. Ask whether groups of different composition have been pooled, and whether the data include only cases that passed some filter.
(Chapter 8.)
8. Identify what is missing.

Ask what you would want to know before relying on the claim, and whether it is absent. Common gaps include the comparison group, the failures, the cases that did not fit, the time period before and after, and the source’s own statement of its limitations. Absence of information is itself information, especially when the missing piece is one a careful source would normally provide.
(Chapter 5.)
9. Set your confidence and name what would change it.

Decide how confident the evidence justifies being, using rough degrees rather than yes or no. Then state what new evidence would raise or lower that confidence. If nothing could lower it, the belief is no longer responsive to evidence. Check whether you are applying the same standard you would apply if the claim pointed in the direction you prefer.
(Chapters 9 and 12.)
10. Decide what follows.

Decide what to do with the claim. You might act on it, act cautiously in a reversible way, seek one more piece of information, hold it as unconfirmed, or set it aside. If you pass it on, pass on your level of confidence with it. Match the size of any commitment to the strength of the evidence.
(Chapter 14.)
Worked example: a health claim shared online
The following example is hypothetical. The claim, study and figures are invented for illustration.
A colleague shares a post that reads: “New study proves that people who drink three cups of green tea a day cut their risk of dementia by 40%. Everyone over 40 should start now.”
1. State the claim.

The post makes two claims. The first is factual: a study found that people who drink three cups of green tea daily have a 40 per cent lower risk of dementia. The second is a recommendation: everyone over 40 should start drinking green tea to reduce their risk. Stating them separately shows that even if the first is accurate, the second does not automatically follow.
2. Trace the provenance.

The post links to a news article, which mentions a study by researchers at a university, published in a named journal. Searching for the study finds the journal’s abstract. It reports a cohort study following about 12,000 adults aged 60 and over in one country for eight years. The original source exists, which is a good sign. It also differs from the post in important ways: the participants were over 60, not over 40, and the abstract says the study “was associated with” lower risk, not that tea “cut” risk.
3. Separate observation from interpretation.

The observation is that, over eight years, participants who reported drinking three or more cups of green tea a day were diagnosed with dementia less often than those who reported drinking little or none. The interpretation in the post is that the tea caused the difference. The study, being observational, did not test that.
4. Surface the assumptions.

For the post’s recommendation to follow, several assumptions must hold: that the association is causal; that it applies to people aged 40 to 60, who were not studied; that self-reported tea drinking was accurate; and that starting to drink tea in midlife has the same effect as long-standing habits. The causal assumption is the most load-bearing and, given the design, the most fragile.
5. Assess the source.

The journal is peer reviewed and the researchers work in the relevant field, so the study itself appears credible within its limits. The post’s author is not identified and has no visible expertise. The news article accurately reports the numbers but uses causal language in its headline. A quick check finds no obvious financial interest, though it would be worth seeing whether the study disclosed funding from a tea producer.
6. Consider alternatives.

Several other explanations could produce the same association. People who drink a lot of green tea may differ in diet, physical activity, education, social contact or wealth, all of which are associated with dementia risk. People in the early, undiagnosed stages of cognitive decline may change their habits, including what they drink, which would be reverse causation. The abstract says the researchers adjusted for age, sex, education and smoking. It does not mention diet or physical activity, so those confounders remain possible.
7. Check the numbers.

A 40 per cent reduction is a relative figure. The abstract reports that about 5 per cent of the low-tea group and about 3 per cent of the high-tea group were diagnosed over eight years. The absolute difference is about two percentage points: roughly two fewer diagnoses per hundred people over eight years. That is not trivial, but it is a much smaller-sounding effect than “cut your risk by 40%”, and it applies to people over 60.
8. Identify what is missing.

The post and the article do not mention whether other studies have found similar results, whether any randomized trials exist, or whether the effect was consistent across subgroups. A search for a systematic review would be the natural next step.
9. Set confidence.

A reasonable conclusion is moderate confidence that, in this population, green tea drinking was associated with somewhat lower dementia rates, and low confidence that drinking green tea causes the reduction. What would raise confidence in a causal effect: consistent findings across several cohorts in different countries, a dose-response relationship that survives adjustment for diet and activity, and ideally a randomized trial of a plausible mechanism. What would lower it: evidence that the association disappears after adjusting for lifestyle factors.
10. Decide what follows.

For a person who enjoys green tea and has no medical reason to avoid it, there is little harm in drinking it, and the claim offers no strong reason to stop. As a basis for a recommendation to everyone over 40, the evidence is not sufficient. If the colleague asks for an opinion, a fair reply would be that the study is real and interesting, that it shows an association in older adults rather than proof of an effect, and that the headline figure overstates what was found.
A short version for everyday use
When there is no time for the full framework, three questions catch a large share of problems:
Where did this come from, and can I reach the original?
What else could explain this?
Out of how many, and compared with what?

sections.title: Questions Worth Asking Before Major Decisions
sections.label: Appendix B — Questions Worth Asking Before Major Decisions

runs.text: This appendix is a set of questions to work through before a major decision: one that is costly, hard to reverse, affects other people, or will shape what options are available later. It is designed to be used on its own, by an individual or a group, without reading the rest of the book first.

How long to spend depends on what is at stake and how hard the decision would be to undo. For a reversible decision, a quick pass through the table may be enough. For one that cannot be undone, it is worth working through every area, ideally with someone who does not share your preference. Stop when nothing further you could reasonably learn would change the decision, or when waiting would cost more than it could reveal.

Chapters 14 and 15 follow one hypothetical decision through this sequence from start to finish: a baker deciding whether to open a second shop, choosing a reversible trial, and reviewing the result a year later.

The questions are grouped into eight areas. Not every question will apply to every decision. The aim is to make sure that the areas most often neglected are at least considered before a commitment is made.
The questions

rows: Area
Questions to ask
1. The decision itself
What exactly am I deciding? What am I trying to achieve? Am I answering the real question or an easier one?
2. Options
What are all the realistic options, including doing nothing and doing something partial? Is this framed as “whether or not” when it could be “which of several”?
3. Uncertainties
What do I not know that matters? Which uncertainties could I reduce before deciding, at what cost? Which can only be resolved by acting?
4. Assumptions
What must be true for my preferred option to work? Which of those assumptions are both load-bearing and fragile? What has changed since they were last checked?
5. Consequences
What is the best realistic outcome of each option, and the worst? Could I survive the worst? Who else is affected, and how?
6. Reversibility
How easily could each option be undone? Is there a more reversible version of the option I prefer?
7. Opportunity costs
What am I giving up by choosing this? What else could the same money, time or attention achieve?
8. Signals to change course
What evidence would tell me, after deciding, that I should change direction? When will I check for it, and who will I ask?

runs.text: Notes on each area
The decision itself.

Many poor decisions are good answers to the wrong question. Write the decision down in one sentence, and then write down what you are trying to achieve by making it. Often the goal suggests options the original framing excluded. Ask whether a hard question, such as “Will this succeed?”, has quietly been replaced by an easier one, such as “Do I feel good about this?”
Options.

Decisions framed as a yes-or-no choice exclude every alternative but one. Try to list at least three realistic options, including doing nothing, which always has consequences of its own, and doing a smaller or staged version of the preferred option. Ask what someone with a very different background would suggest.
Uncertainties.

List the things you do not know that would change the decision if you knew them. For each, ask whether it could be learned before deciding and at what cost. Pursue those that are cheap to learn and decisive if learned. Accept the rest as uncertainties to be managed. Some uncertainties can only be resolved by trying something small.
Assumptions.

Write down what would have to be true for the preferred option to work as hoped. Mark the assumptions that the decision depends on most, and those that are most likely to be false in this situation. Ask especially about assumptions that were once safe and may no longer be: about markets, technology, people’s intentions, and your own capacity.
Consequences.

For each option, describe a realistic best case and a realistic worst case, not only the expected case. Ask whether the worst case could be survived and recovered from. Give extra weight to outcomes that are severe and irreversible, on every side of the decision, including the side of inaction. Ask who else is affected, and whether they would see the consequences the same way you do.
Reversibility.

Distinguish decisions that are hard to undo from those that can be adjusted later. Make the hard-to-undo decisions slowly and carefully. Make the reversible ones more quickly, and learn from them. Look for ways to make a hard-to-undo decision more reversible: a trial period, a smaller first commitment, a break clause, a pilot.
Opportunity costs.

Every choice uses resources that could have been used elsewhere. Ask what else the same money, time, attention or goodwill could achieve. A decision that looks attractive on its own can look different when compared with its best alternative use.
Signals to change course.

Before deciding, write down what you expect to happen, how confident you are, and what evidence would show that the decision is not working. Decide when you will check. This makes it much harder to explain away disappointing signs later, and much easier to change direction while change is still cheap.
Before committing
Three final checks are worth a few minutes before any major commitment.
Imagine failure.
Suppose it is a year from now and the decision has turned out badly. Write down the most likely reasons. If one reason stands out, address it before committing.
Check the conditions of the decision.
Are you deciding under time pressure, strong emotion, fatigue or social pressure? If so, and if waiting is possible, wait.
Record the reasoning.
Write down what you decided, why, what you expected and how confident you were. Judge the decision later by this record, not only by how it turned out.
Worked example 1: a professional decision
The following example is hypothetical.

The head of customer support at a mid-sized software company is considering replacing most of the first-line support team with an AI assistant that answers customer questions automatically. A vendor has demonstrated the system, and it handled sample questions fluently. Senior management is enthusiastic about the projected cost savings.
The decision itself.

Written down, the decision is “Should we replace first-line support with the AI assistant?” The underlying goal, on reflection, is “Resolve customer problems quickly and accurately at a sustainable cost.” The goal makes clear that the question is not really about the AI assistant. It is about how best to resolve customer problems.
Options.

Restating the goal produces more options: full replacement; using the assistant to draft responses that staff review; using it only for a defined set of simple questions; running it alongside the existing team for a trial period; or improving the existing team’s tools without the assistant.
Uncertainties.

The key unknowns are how accurately the assistant handles the company’s real questions, not the vendor’s samples; how customers will respond; and what happens when it is wrong. The first can be tested cheaply before deciding, by running the assistant on a sample of last month’s real tickets and having staff grade its answers. The second can only be learned by trying it with real customers.
Assumptions.

The plan assumes that the assistant’s fluency in the demonstration reflects accuracy on real questions; that customers will accept automated answers; that incorrect answers will be noticed and corrected; and that the cost projections include the work of monitoring and correcting the system. The first and third assumptions are the most load-bearing. The demonstration does not test either.
Consequences.

The best realistic case is faster responses at lower cost with similar accuracy. The worst realistic case is that the assistant gives confident but wrong answers about billing, refunds or data, customers act on them, and the company becomes responsible for the consequences, as courts and tribunals have held in comparable situations. That worst case would be costly and damaging to trust.
Reversibility.

Dismissing most of the support team would be very hard to reverse, since experienced staff and their knowledge would be lost. Running the assistant alongside the team, or using it to draft responses for review, is highly reversible.
Opportunity costs.

The money and management attention required for a full transition could alternatively go to better internal tools or training for the existing team, which might achieve part of the savings with less risk.
Signals to change course.

Before deciding, the head of support writes down the thresholds that would justify expanding or abandoning the assistant: accuracy on graded real tickets, the rate of escalations, customer satisfaction scores, and the number of incorrect answers that reach customers. She sets dates for review at one and three months.
The decision.

She proposes a staged approach: first, a test on historical tickets; then a three-month trial in which the assistant drafts responses for a defined set of simple question types, reviewed by staff before sending; then a decision about expansion based on the recorded thresholds. Senior management gets most of the projected learning for a fraction of the risk, and the company keeps the ability to change direction.
Worked example 2: an everyday decision
The following example is hypothetical.

A couple with two school-age children are deciding whether to move to another city, where one of them has been offered a job with a substantially higher salary and better long-term prospects. The other works locally in a role they enjoy. The children are settled in school, and grandparents live nearby.
The decision itself.

Initially the question is “Should we move?” When they write down what they are trying to achieve, it becomes clearer: greater financial security and career growth for one partner, without sacrificing the other partner’s work satisfaction or the children’s stability more than necessary.
Options.

The options turn out to be more varied than move or stay: move now; move in a year, at a natural school transition; one partner commutes or works partly remotely for a trial period while the family stays; negotiate a later start date or a remote arrangement; decline but use the offer to seek a better local position.
Uncertainties.

They do not know how the children will adjust, whether the second partner can find satisfying work in the new city, what the cost of living really is, or whether the new job will be as good as it looks. Some of these can be investigated cheaply before deciding: visiting schools, speaking to people in the second partner’s field in the new city, and asking to speak with future colleagues in the new role.
Assumptions.

The case for moving assumes that the higher salary will not be absorbed by higher housing costs, that the new role is stable, and that the second partner will find comparable work. The case for staying assumes that local career prospects will remain adequate. Both sets of assumptions deserve checking.
Consequences.

The best case for moving is a better life for the whole family. The worst is a lonely, financially stretched year with one partner unemployed and unhappy children, far from family support. The worst case for staying is a missed opportunity and lingering resentment. Neither worst case is catastrophic, but the worst case of moving is harder to recover from quickly.
Reversibility.
Selling a house and moving the children is hard to reverse. A trial period of commuting or remote work is much more reversible, though it has costs of its own.
Opportunity costs.
Moving now uses up the family’s savings and goodwill for change. A trial period postpones the salary gain but preserves the option to move later with better information.
Signals to change course.
If they choose a trial, they agree in advance on what would lead them to move fully, and what would lead them to return to the status quo, and they set a date six months ahead to review it together.
The decision.

They negotiate a later start date with partial remote work for the first six months. During that time the second partner explores the job market in the new city and the family visits regularly. The decision about a full move is postponed until they know more, but it is not deferred indefinitely. It has a date, criteria and a record of what they expected.
When to use this appendix

The full set of questions takes time, and most decisions do not need it. It is most valuable when a decision is hard to reverse, when a lot of money, time or trust is at stake, when the situation is unfamiliar, when strong feelings or pressure are present, and when you notice that you feel unusually certain about a complex choice. In those situations, an hour spent on these questions is rarely wasted.
